# Funke — agent guide

Funke is a 2D game engine: C++20 native core (MSVC v143, premake) + C# scripting on .NET 10.
The user writes German; answer in German.

## Layout

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `Funke-Engine/` | Engine DLL (`Funke-Engine.dll`), PCH `src/pch.hpp` |
| `Funke-EditorRuntime/` | Static lib shared by editor/launcher/runtime |
| `Funke-Editor/`, `Funke-Launcher/`, `Funke-Runtime/` | Executables; Runtime is the shipped game player |
| `Funke-CLI/` | `funke.exe` command-line tool (create/build/validate/convert/prefab/sprite/package); compiles `Funke-Editor/src/Build/GameBuilder.cpp` and other UI-free editor sources directly |
| `Funke-ScriptCore/` | C# API (`dotnet`, SDK-style csproj) |
| `Funke-ScriptCompiler/` | Editor-only in-process Roslyn compiler for C# hot reload (Roslyn from the project's SDK, not shipped) |
| `Tests/Funke-Engine-Tests`, `Tests/Funke-Editor-Tests` | doctest suites; `Tests/Funke-ScriptCore-Tests` is xUnit |
| `packages/` | Engine packages (`funke-package.lua`) |
| `premake5.lua`, `*/premake5.lua`, `Dependencies.lua` | Project generation; `.vcxproj` files are generated and git-ignored |
| `Github-Docs/Documentation/` | User docs; `CHANGELOG.md` for user-visible changes |

## Inner loop — use these, not raw MSBuild

```powershell
scripts\dev\Build.ps1 Engine                    # incremental; errors as path(line): code msg; log in bin-int\_agent\
scripts\dev\Build.ps1 Editor,ScriptCore         # Tests | Runtime | Launcher | CLI | ScriptCompiler | PackageTool | All also work
scripts\dev\Build.ps1 -File Funke-Engine\src\Scene\Scene.cpp   # compile one TU only (seconds)
scripts\dev\Test.ps1                            # build + run engine/editor doctest, failures only
scripts\dev\Test.ps1 -Filter "*Prefab*"         # doctest test-case filter; -Suite CSharp|All
scripts\dev\Run.ps1                             # launch Editor on a sandbox project, screenshot, close, report log warnings/errors + crash dumps (--background: never focused, behind other windows; -Foreground opts out)
scripts\dev\Run.ps1 -App Runtime -Project <dir> -Seconds 5 -Shots 3
scripts\dev\Run.ps1 -App Runtime -Project <dir> -ScreenshotAt 2s,5s -FixedStep 60   # game-time shots; -InputScript for scripted input
funke editor status --project <dir>             # Editor Bridge: drive an editor that is already open (Funke-CLI\funke.exe)
funke editor play --size 1080x2400; funke editor tap 0.5 0.4; funke editor screenshot shot.png   # offscreen, works minimized
funke editor exec "<console cmd>"; funke editor recompile; funke editor logs --level warning; funke editor stop
```

- `funke editor` (doc: `Github-Docs/Documentation/Editor/Editor-Bridge.md`) never moves/focuses windows or sends OS input; screenshots render offscreen. Only drive editors you launched yourself (`Run.ps1 -KeepOpen`) or the user asked you to; `funke editor list` shows which ones run. Exit codes: 3 busy/timeout, 4 no editor. `scripts\dev\Editor.ps1 <command> ...` runs the repo's freshly built `funke editor`.
- `Build.ps1` regenerates premake automatically when a new `.cpp` or a changed `*.lua` needs it, and after building it copies `Funke-Engine.dll` (and, for `ScriptCore`, `Funke-ScriptCore.dll`) into every consumer output (Editor/Launcher/Runtime/tests) — a stale DLL there silently hides fixes, including in game builds staged from the editor.
- Default config is **Release**: the user runs the Release editor (`bin\Release-windows-x86_64\Funke-Editor\`).
- Warnings are shown only for files changed in git (`-Warnings all|none` to change). C4251/C4275 are permanent noise.
- `Run.ps1` screenshots land in `bin-int\_agent\run\*.png` — open them with Read to see the result. The run's log slice is `bin-int\_agent\run\<App>.log`. Without `-Project` it uses `bin-int\_agent\SandboxProject`, never the user's projects. Runtime runs use the player-data profile `agent`, so a game's real PlayerPrefs/SaveData stay untouched. If the editor is already open the build can't overwrite locked DLLs; the script says so.

Full logs: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Funke\Logs\<exe>.log` (format `[time] [logger] [level] msg`). Crash dumps: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Funke\CrashDumps\`.

## Definition of done

1. `Build.ps1` for every project the change touches (engine headers → also `Editor`, since it compiles against them).
2. `Test.ps1` (add `-Suite CSharp` when `Funke-ScriptCore` changed). Add/extend a doctest case when the change is testable.
3. Anything visible at runtime (rendering, editor UI, scene load, scripting): `Run.ps1` and look at the screenshot + reported warnings.
4. User-visible change → `CHANGELOG.md` and `Github-Docs/Documentation`.

## Rules that bite

- Use VS2022 MSBuild (`C:\Program Files\Microsoft Visual Studio\2022\Community\MSBuild\Current\Bin\MSBuild.exe`); `vswhere -latest` finds VS "18" (the user's IDE). VS 18 builds get their own `bin-int\<cfg>\<project>-vs18.0\` (premake/compat.lua + Directory.Build.props), because a PCH built by one install breaks the other's compiles (C2375); keep agent builds on VS2022 so they reuse `bin-int\<cfg>\<project>\`. Build `.vcxproj` files, not `-t:<proj>` on `Funke.sln` (MSB4057); the sln also can't build the SDK-style C# projects.
- Never include `Core/BuildIdentity.hpp` from a header or PCH (forces full rebuilds); use `Engine::GetVersionLong()`.
- Don't reintroduce `/Zm` or `/Zi`/`/ZI`; parallel builds depend on `/Z7` and `Directory.Build.props` defaults.
- Symbols used across the DLL boundary need `FUNKE_API`.
- Other sessions may edit and build in this tree at the same time. A sporadic `LNK1104 cannot open ...obj` is a concurrent build — rerun. Never revert changes you didn't make.
- Text with backslashes (Windows paths, `\n` in literals): edit with Edit/Write, not sed/heredoc via Bash.
- Style: PascalCase methods, `m_`/`s_`/`k_` prefixes, `FNK_*` logging/assert macros; terse "why" comments only (see skills `funke-code-style`, `funke-comment-style`).

## Git

Commit only when asked. Commits are authored as `Ben Schneider <benscr.email@gmail.com>` via `git -c user.name=... -c user.email=... commit` and pushed with the `Ben-Scr` gh account. Never add Co-Authored-By/Claude/AI lines to commits or PRs.

## Skills

`.claude/skills/` (mirrored in `.agents/skills/`) covers engine work (`funke-add-component`, `funke-serialize-field`, `funke-add-system`, `funke-scene-workflow`, `funke-engine-scripting`, `funke-rendering`, `funke-add-editor-panel`, `funke-add-profiler`, `funke-debug`, `funke-code-style`, `funke-author-package`, `funke-inspector-ruleset`, `funke-build-engine`) and game-making with Funke (`funke-make-a-game` is the entry point, incl. pre-production and Data Assets; art, pixel art and UI art: `funke-game-art`; phone apps that aren't games: `funke-make-a-mobile-app`). Keep both mirrors identical: `scripts\dev\SyncSkills.ps1`.
CONTRIBUTING.md:
# Contributing to Funke

Bug reports, documentation fixes and focused pull requests are welcome.

## Reporting bugs

Use the **Bug report** issue template. Attach the log from `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Funke\Logs\` and, for crashes, the dump from `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Funke\CrashDumps\`. Check [Known Limitations](Github-Docs/Documentation/Known-Limitations.md) first.

## Building from source

Follow **Getting Started** in the [README](README.md). Before opening a pull request, run:

```powershell
.\scripts\RunTests.bat --release
dotnet test Tests\Funke-ScriptCore-Tests\Funke-ScriptCore-Tests.csproj -c Release
```

## Pull requests

- Keep each pull request to one change, and describe how you tested it.
- Follow the style of the surrounding code: PascalCase methods, `m_`/`s_`/`k_` member prefixes, short "why" comments instead of narration.
- Add or update tests where the change is testable, and update `Github-Docs/Documentation` plus `CHANGELOG.md` for user-visible changes.
- New `.cpp`/`.cs` files need a Premake regeneration (`scripts\Setup.bat`) because project files list sources explicitly.

## License

Funke is licensed under the [MIT License](LICENSE.txt). By submitting a contribution you agree that it is licensed under the MIT License as well.
Funke-Engine/README.md:
# Funke-Engine

The Funke engine static/shared library, implemented in C++20. **Funke supports game development in both C++ and C#.** This README specifically documents the public C++ application and SDK entry path for users who want to ship a game without the editor. For editor-based C++ and C# game development, see the [scripting guide](../Github-Docs/Documentation/Scripting/Scripting.md). For build setup, dependency installation, and submodule init see the top-level [README.md](../README.md).

## Quick start (for game developers)

A minimal Funke game is one translation unit: a subclass of `Funke::Application` plus a `CreateApplication()` factory. The engine owns the entry point — you never write `main()`.

```cpp
// MyGame.cpp — the single TU that owns the process entry point.

#include <Funke.hpp>              // Public game API.
#include <EntryPoint.hpp>         // Defines main()/WinMain(). See warning below.

using namespace Funke;

class MyGame : public Application {
public:
    ApplicationConfig GetConfiguration() const override {
        // Pick a runtime profile; see "Configuring what the engine starts up" below.
        ApplicationConfig config = ApplicationConfig::Game();
        config.WindowSpecification = WindowSpecification(
            1280, 720, "My Game", /*resizable*/ true, /*decorated*/ true, /*fullscreen*/ false);
        return config;
    }

    void ConfigureScenes() override {
        SceneManager::RegisterScene("Main").SetAsStartupScene();
    }

    void Start() override      {} // Called once after subsystems are up.
    void Update() override     {} // Per-frame, variable timestep.
    void FixedUpdate() override{} // Fixed-timestep tick (physics step interval).
    void OnPaused() override   {} // Window lost focus / minimized / explicit pause.
    void OnQuit() override     {} // Final teardown hook before subsystems shut down.
};

Funke::Application* Funke::CreateApplication() {
    return new MyGame();
}
```

With the 2D renderer enabled, a raw native app automatically gives its active
scene a runtime `Camera2D` after `OnLoad` and before systems start. A camera
created by the scene, including a disabled one, suppresses that fallback. Use
`WithoutDefaultCamera2D()` for intentionally camera-free definitions:

```cpp
SceneManager::RegisterScene("ServerState")
    .WithoutDefaultCamera2D()
    .SetAsStartupScene();
```

> **Warning (audit E29):** `EntryPoint.hpp` defines `main()` (or `WinMain()` in Dist Windows builds) at file scope. Including it in two translation units triggers a duplicate-symbol linker error — and the header guards against this with a sentinel that produces a `#error` if the header is re-included after the symbol has been emitted. **Include it in exactly one `.cpp`.** Every other TU should use `<Funke.hpp>` (or `<Funke/Core.hpp>` for core-only utilities).

The canonical end-to-end example lives in [`Funke-Runtime/src/RuntimeApplication.cpp`](../Funke-Runtime/src/RuntimeApplication.cpp): it loads `project.json` next to the executable, registers project scenes, and falls back to a built-in sample if no project is found.

## Native SDK for external Visual Studio projects

Build a self-contained Dist SDK from the current engine binaries:

```bat
scripts\BuildNativeSdk.bat -Verify
```

The output is `bin\FunkeSDK-Dist-windows-x86_64`. In an empty Visual Studio
2022 C++ project, open **Property Manager** and add its `FunkeSDK.props` to the
`Dist | x64` configuration. That one property sheet provides the single public
include root, ABI defines, `Funke-Engine.lib`, required Windows libraries, and
post-build deployment of the runtime DLLs and `FunkeAssets`.

The SDK layout is deliberately independent of the repository layout:

```text
FunkeSDK-Dist-windows-x86_64/
|-- include/              # the only consumer include directory
|-- lib/Funke-Engine.lib  # the only engine import library without Tracy
|-- runtime/              # DLLs and FunkeAssets, copied by FunkeSDK.props
|-- FunkeSDK.props        # import this in Visual Studio
|-- FunkeSDK.targets      # applies ABI/link settings after project defaults
`-- examples/MinimalApp/  # buildable raw C++ reference project
```

`BuildNativeSdk.bat` inspects the actual `Funke-Engine.dll` and emits matching
Tracy headers, defines, import library, and runtime DLL only when that binary
uses the profiler ABI. The `-Verify` option builds and runs the included
120-frame smoke test entirely through the packaged SDK surface.

## Picking an umbrella header

Three umbrella headers ship today. Pick one based on what your TU actually uses:

| Include | Use when |
|---|---|
| `<Funke.hpp>` | Recommended game-facing umbrella. Exposes the application loop, scenes, entities, systems, concrete components, input, math, rendering, audio, physics, and native scripting enabled by the current module profile. It deliberately does not define `main()` or import the `Funke` namespace globally. |
| `<Funke/App.hpp>` | Smaller application umbrella for hosts that want `Application` plus Core without the complete game-facing surface. Requires `FUNKE_WITH_APPLICATION=1`. |
| `<Funke/Core.hpp>` | Linking the engine for utility code only — no `Application` loop. Gives you `Collections/` (Vec2/Vec4/Color/Mat2/Viewport), `Core/Time`, `Core/Log`, `Core/Assert`, `Core/Version`, `Core/Base`, `Core/Exceptions`, `Core/Export`, and `ApplicationConfig` (the type — not the runtime). Safe in any module profile, including `core`. |

`EntryPoint.hpp` is a fourth header but **not an umbrella**: it exists solely to define `main()`/`WinMain()` and call your `CreateApplication()` factory. Include it in one TU only.

## Configuring what the engine starts up

`Funke::ApplicationConfig` is a plain struct with one bool per subsystem. Your `Application` subclass returns a populated config from `GetConfiguration()`; the engine reads it once during `Application::Initialize()`.

Four factories cover the common cases:

```cpp
ApplicationConfig::Minimal();  // Window host without scenes, workers, arenas,
                               // built-in asset registration, scene renderers,
                               // audio, physics, scripting or packages.
                               // Texture manager stays on for the window icon.

ApplicationConfig::Headless(); // No window or graphics backend. Keeps scenes,
                               // jobs, physics, audio, scripting and packages;
                               // disable individual services your tool omits.

ApplicationConfig::Game();     // Today's default: full rendering, audio,
                               // physics, scripting, package host. Equivalent
                               // to a default-constructed ApplicationConfig.

ApplicationConfig::Editor();   // Editor-host defaults; scene content remains
                               // responsible for its cameras.
```

`Minimal()` still runs the application's `Start`, `Update` and `OnQuit` hooks, but does not call `ConfigureScenes`. Use it for a host that manages its own UI. For a tool without a window, start from `Headless()` or set `EnableWindow = false` on a minimal configuration. These runtime choices do not remove compiled modules or change the library's binary size.

Per-subsystem flags on `ApplicationConfig` (override individually after a factory call):

| Field | Effect when `false` |
|---|---|
| `EnableWindow` | Skips the OS window and graphics backend; initialization disables dependent rendering services. |
| `EnableScenes` | Skips scene/component-registry initialization, `ConfigureScenes` and startup scenes. |
| `EnableJobSystem` | Starts no worker pool; submitted jobs run inline on the caller. |
| `EnableFrameArenas` | Skips frame and persistent arena allocation. |
| `RegisterBuiltInAssets` | Skips GUID registration of engine assets; `funke:` asset references and pickers cannot resolve them. |
| `EnableGuiRenderer` | Skips `GuiRenderer` (ImGui plumbing the engine owns; editor brings its own context). |
| `EnableGizmoRenderer` | Skips `GizmoRenderer2D` construction; gizmo draw calls become no-ops. |
| `EnablePhysics2D` | Skips `PhysicsSystem2D`; Box2D world is never created. |
| `EnableAudio` | Skips miniaudio device init; `AudioSource` components are inert. |
| `EnableScripting` | Skips CoreCLR + ScriptCore + user-assembly load. `ScriptSystem` still attaches but bails in `Awake`. |
| `EnableRenderer2D` | Skips `Renderer2D` construction; `BeginFrame`/`EndFrame` null-check it. |
| `AutoCreateDefaultCamera2D` | Disables the fallback; active camera-free scenes remain unchanged. |
| `EnableTextureManager` | Skips `TextureManager::Initialize`/`Shutdown`. Window-icon falls back to Win32 resource. |
| `EnablePackageHost` | Skips `PackageHost::LoadAll`. Native packages next to the exe are not discovered. |
| `SetWindowIcon` | Suppresses the icon load entirely. |
| `Vsync` | Disables swap-interval vsync; framerate is governed by `TargetFrameRate`. |
| `RunInBackground` | Pauses application updates while the window is unfocused. |
| `UseTargetFrameRateForMainLoop` | When false, the loop runs uncapped and ignores `TargetFrameRate`. |

The `TargetFrameRate` field sets the initial main-loop cap in frames per second; `0` disables the cap. Runtime calls may change it later.

The `WindowSpecification WindowSpecification` field controls the SDL3 window — width, height, title, resizable, decorated, fullscreen. See [`Core/WindowSpecification.hpp`](src/Core/WindowSpecification.hpp).

These are runtime feature requests. Enabling a flag does nothing if the corresponding module was stripped at build time (next section).

## Build-time module profiles

The Premake build supports module-level slicing. Pass these to `premake5`:

```bat
vendor\bin\premake5.exe vs2022 --module-profile=full
vendor\bin\premake5.exe vs2022 --module-profile=core
vendor\bin\premake5.exe vs2022 --module-profile=custom --with-editor
```

Profiles (defined in [`premake5.lua`](../premake5.lua)):

| Profile | Enables | Defines |
|---|---|---|
| `full` *(default for compatibility)* | Render, Audio, Physics, Scripting, Editor | All `FUNKE_WITH_*=1` plus `FUNKE_ALL_MODULES=1` plus `FUNKE_WITH_APPLICATION=1`. Includes `Funke-Launcher` and `Funke-Runtime` projects in the solution. |
| `core` | (none) | All `FUNKE_WITH_*=0`, `FUNKE_CORE_ONLY=1`. No third-party module dependencies pulled in. `<Funke/App.hpp>` will fail to compile in this profile (Application requires the full surface). |
| `custom` | No modules, or the complete application surface with `--with-editor` | With no module flags this is core-equivalent. `--with-editor` enables render, audio, physics, and scripting, but does not define the legacy `FUNKE_ALL_MODULES`. Partial custom combinations fail during project generation. |

Per-module flags (only meaningful with `--module-profile=custom`, or implicitly enable `custom` when used without `--module-profile`):

- `--with-render` — Selects Dawn/WebGPU, `Graphics/`, `Gui/GuiRenderer`, and particle/gizmo systems. Partial custom profiles are not currently supported, so this must be combined with `--with-editor`.
- `--with-audio` — Selects miniaudio, `Audio/`, `Components/Audio/`, and `AudioUpdateSystem`. Partial custom profiles are not currently supported, so this must be combined with `--with-editor`.
- `--with-physics` — Selects Box2D, Jolt, `Physics/`, and `Components/Physics/`. Partial custom profiles are not currently supported, so this must be combined with `--with-editor`.
- `--with-scripting` — Selects the .NET host, `Scripting/`, `Funke-ScriptCore`, and `Funke-Sandbox` projects. Custom profiles must also pass `--with-editor`.
- `--with-editor` — ImGui static lib. Implicitly turns on render, audio, physics, and scripting (the editor depends on all of them).

Engine feature modules (`Funke.2D`, `Funke.3D`; source lists in [`EngineModules.json`](EngineModules.json), also read by `cmake/FunkeEngine.cmake`) are switched off per runtime variant rather than per profile:

- `--without-2d`, `--without-3d` — Generate an isolated workspace in `premake/generated/variant-<modules>` (Engine, EditorRuntime, Runtime and their dependencies only) that builds into `bin/<cfg>-<system>-<arch>-<modules>` with `FUNKE_WITH_2D=0` / `FUNKE_WITH_3D=0`, without the module's sources and without Box2D (2D) or Jolt (3D). The game builder generates and builds these for projects that leave a module out; see [Engine Modules](../Github-Docs/Documentation/Engine-Core/Engine-Modules.md).

Other build-shaping flags:

- `--no-profiler` — Strip Tracy and the `Profiling/` folder entirely. `FUNKE_PROFILER_ENABLED` is undefined; the in-engine ProfilerPanel is excluded.
- `--with-imgui-demo` — Compile `imgui_demo.cpp` into the ImGui static lib (editor only).
- `--funke-project=PATH` — Read the project's `entityBits` setting when generating the engine workspace. Project-local packages are generated into their own workspace:

```powershell
vendor/bin/premake5.exe --file=premake/project-packages.lua --funke-project="<project>" vs2022
```

The editor and Launcher run that project-package command automatically.

The exact wiring lives in [`premake5.lua`](../premake5.lua) (see `ResolveFunkeModules`, `GetFunkeModuleDefines`) and per-module dependency sets in [`Dependencies.lua`](../Dependencies.lua).

## Distribution checklist

A shipped game must include the following next to its executable. The runtime's [`premake5.lua`](../Funke-Runtime/premake5.lua) post-build steps do this for `Funke-Runtime.exe` — your own game project should do the same.

Always required:

- `<YourGame>.exe` — your game binary.
- `Funke-Engine.dll` — the engine shared lib. Built as a `SharedLib` from `Funke-Engine/premake5.lua`. Consumers define `FNK_IMPORT_DLL`; the engine builds with `FNK_BUILD_DLL`.
- `SDL3.dll` (`libSDL3.so.0` / `libSDL3.0.dylib`) — windowing, input and platform services. Shared so engine and exe share its global state; built by `scripts/sdl/SetupSDL.py`.
- `FunkeAssets/` directory — engine default assets (`Fonts/`, `Localization/`, `Textures/`). Source of truth is [`Funke-Runtime/FunkeAssets/`](../Funke-Runtime/FunkeAssets); the post-build copies it next to the exe. Built-in WGSL shaders are embedded in [`Shader.cpp`](src/Graphics/Shader.cpp).

Conditional:

- `nethost.dll` — required when scripting is enabled. The runtime's post-build copies it from `External/dotnet/lib/nethost.dll`.
- `Tracy.dll` — required when the profiler is enabled (i.e. when `--no-profiler` was *not* passed). Stripped builds skip this.
- `project.json` — your project manifest. The runtime auto-detects it via `FunkeProject::Validate(exeDir)` and loads it through `ProjectManager`. **If absent, the runtime logs a warning and falls back to a built-in `SampleScene`** — that warning is the only signal a packaging mistake gives you (audit E30). Always ship the project file.
- Your project's scene files, package DLLs (`Pkg.<Name>.Native.dll`), C# script assemblies, and any user assets referenced by `project.json`.

# Assets

This page explains the **whole asset system** of Funke: what an asset is, how Funke keeps track of them, how you reference them from components and scripts, and how they get loaded while your game runs.

If you just want the short version: every file in your project's `Assets` folder is given a permanent ID. Components and scripts store that ID (not the file path), so you can freely move or rename files without breaking anything. The engine loads the actual data on demand and caches it.

---

## What is an asset?

An **asset** is any content file your game uses — a sprite, a sound, a font, a scene, and so on. In Funke you don't "import" assets through a wizard; you simply **drop files into your project's `Assets` folder** and the engine discovers them automatically.

Funke recognizes these asset kinds (from the `AssetKind` list):

| Kind | Typical file types | Used for |
|------|--------------------|----------|
| **Texture** | `.png`, `.jpg`, `.jpeg`, `.bmp`, `.tga` | Sprites and images |
| **Audio** | `.wav`, `.mp3`, `.ogg`, `.flac` | Sound effects and music |
| **Font** | `.ttf`, `.otf` | Text rendering |
| **Scene** | `.scene` | A level / screen of your game |
| **Prefab** | `.prefab` | A reusable, saved entity (with children) |
| **Script** | `.cs` (and C/C++ source) | Game logic |
| **Shader** | `.wgsl`, `.vert`, `.frag`, … | Custom rendering |
| **Data Asset** | `.dataasset` | Shared game data — items, stats, config (see [Data Assets](Data-Assets.md)) |
| **Other** | anything else | Tracked but not specially handled |

Anything with an unknown extension is still tracked as **Other**, so nothing in your project is invisible to the engine.

---

## How assets are identified: GUIDs and `.meta` files

This is the most important idea in the whole system.

Every asset gets a permanent **GUID** (a 64-bit unique ID, also called an Asset ID). Once a file has a GUID, *that* is how everything refers to it — your scenes, prefabs, components, and scripts all store the GUID, **never the file path**.

Why? Because paths change. If references used paths, renaming `player.png` to `hero.png` would break every sprite using it. With GUIDs, you can rename and move files freely and references keep working.

### The `.meta` file

To make a GUID *stick* to a file, Funke writes a small companion file next to it with a `.meta` extension:

```
Assets/
  player.png
  player.png.meta     ← created automatically
```

The `.meta` is a small JSON file that stores:

- the asset's **GUID** (so it stays the same forever), and
- **import settings** for that asset (for a texture: filter mode, wrap mode, and any sprite slices you've defined).

A texture's filter mode also decides which [graphics settings](../Engine-Core/Graphics-Settings.md) reach it: **Point** (pixel art) stays crisp at every setting, **Bilinear** follows *Texture Quality*, and **Trilinear** / **Anisotropic** follow *Texture Quality* and *Anisotropic Filtering*.

> **Keep `.meta` files.** When you move or copy an asset, move its `.meta` too, and commit them to version control. The `.meta` is what preserves the asset's identity and its import settings. If a `.meta` goes missing, the engine generates a new one — but the new GUID won't match old references.

### Two kinds of GUID

- **Project assets** (your files) get a GUID derived from the file. These live alongside your `.meta` files.
- **Built-in engine assets** (things shipped with Funke, like the default font and the default white texture) get fixed, stable GUIDs so they're identical on every machine. The default font, for example, always has the same ID.

---

## How assets are discovered (the "import" step)

There is no manual import button. Discovery is automatic:

1. The engine **scans** your project's `Assets` folder.
2. Each file is **classified** into an `AssetKind` by its extension.
3. If the file already has a `.meta` with a valid GUID, that GUID is used. If not, the engine **generates a GUID and writes a new `.meta`**.

This is handled by the **Asset Registry**, the engine's central index of all known assets. It keeps two lookups — *GUID → file* and *file → GUID* — so it can answer "where is asset X?" and "what is the ID of this file?" instantly.

In the **editor**, the registry watches the `Assets` folder. When you add, delete, or change a file, the registry marks itself dirty and re-scans, so newly added assets show up without restarting.

---

## Referencing assets from components

Built-in components that use an asset store its **GUID**, plus a transient runtime handle that is *not* saved. For example, a sprite component stores:

- `TextureAssetId` — the GUID, written to the `.scene` file. **This is the real reference.**
- a `TextureHandle` — a lightweight runtime handle to the loaded GPU texture. Rebuilt each run, never saved.

The same pattern is used across the engine: audio sources store an audio GUID, text components store a font GUID, and so on.

**When a scene loads**, the deserializer reads the GUID and asks the right manager to load it — for example, "load the texture with this GUID." It resolves the GUID to a file, applies the import settings from the `.meta`, and hands back a handle. (If a GUID can't be found, the engine falls back to an older saved path if one exists, so projects keep working across changes.)

---

## Referencing assets from C# scripts

Scripts use small **reference types** that wrap a GUID, so you can expose an asset slot in the Inspector and assign it by drag-and-drop:

- `TextureRef`, `AudioRef`, `FontRef`, `SceneRef`, … — each holds an asset GUID and knows how to resolve it.
- `Texture`, `Audio`, `Material` and `Mesh` fields get the same asset slot, filtered to that kind; lists of them (`List<Material>`, `Mesh[]`) work too, e.g. a skin catalog:

```csharp
public class SkinPicker : EntityScript
{
    public List<Material> Skins = new();      // drag .material files onto the list
    public Mesh? Trophy;                      // an .obj mesh
    public Entity CoinPrefab;                 // an Entity field also takes a prefab asset
}
```

You can also load assets in code through the script `AssetManager`:

```csharp
// Load by path (resolved to a GUID internally)…
Texture tex = AssetManager.Load<Texture>("Sprites/player.png");

// …or directly by GUID.
Audio sfx = Audio.FromAssetUUID(myAudioGuid);
sfx.PlayOneShot();
```

Under the hood these always end up working with GUIDs — the path form is just a convenience that looks up the GUID for you. See [Scripting](../Scripting/Scripting.md) for the full API and the Inspector attributes that create asset slots.

`AssetManager.Load<T>` and `LoadByGUID<T>` combine path/GUID resolution, kind checking and any required loading into one managed-to-native call for the usual asset reference types. C# then creates the reference wrapper directly; reference-only types retain their lazy loading behavior. Data Assets use the already-loaded shared managed instance, including the expected subtype check; retrieving that instance does not load it again or rerun `OnValidate()`.

### Asynchronous loading

Use `LoadAsync<T>` to prepare an asset while gameplay continues. Start the call on the engine's main thread; normal `await` continuations return through the engine's synchronization context.

```csharp
Texture? texture = await AssetManager.LoadAsync<Texture>("Sprites/player.png", token);
Audio? audio = await AssetManager.LoadByGUIDAsync<Audio>(audioGuid, token);
Mesh? mesh = await AssetManager.LoadByGUIDAsync<Mesh>(meshGuidString, token);
```

`token` is an optional `CancellationToken`. `LoadByGUIDAsync<T>` accepts either a `ulong` or a GUID string, using the same parsing rules as `LoadByGUID<T>`.

| Type | Prepared in the background |
|------|----------------------------|
| `Texture` | File reading and image decoding |
| `Audio` | File reading and audio decoding |
| `Font` | File reading and rasterizing the 32 px font cache bucket |
| `Mesh` | File reading and mesh parsing |

GUID/path resolution and import metadata access still run on the main thread. Workers prepare owned CPU data; the main thread publishes it into the existing managers and performs GPU uploads. Completion means that publication has finished. Fonts at other sizes and additional Unicode glyphs retain their normal on-demand behavior.

Each C# async load starts with one managed-to-native request containing the expected kind and the path or GUID. Pending assets require no per-asset native status polling. When results are ready, the engine delivers them together in one native-to-managed completion callback, creates the managed references and completes their tasks. Cancellation requests are also sent in batches. The public loading APIs and their return values are unchanged.

Missing assets, mismatched kinds, decoding failures and rejected requests return `null`. Unsupported generic types, such as `Material`, `Entity` or a `DataAsset` subclass, throw `NotSupportedException`; a build without the necessary asset module or thread support also reports that exception. Starting a load outside the engine synchronization context throws `InvalidOperationException`.

Cancellation produces a cancelled task, so awaiting it throws `OperationCanceledException`. It affects only that request; another request for the same asset can still complete. Once publication succeeds, a later cancellation does not undo it. Cancellation discards an unused result without interrupting a decoder in the middle of its work. Changes to the requested asset, its import metadata, its mesh dependencies or the current project can also cancel pending requests, as can clearing the relevant asset cache. Unrelated registry changes preserve the request.

The loader shares pending work for the same asset, runs at most **two preparations concurrently**, and accepts at most **256 unreleased requests**. Requests from C# are released automatically as their completion batch is delivered, without a separate release call for each asset. Cache eviction and ordinary asset ownership rules still apply after loading; an async result does not pin an asset permanently.

### Native asynchronous requests

Include `Assets/AssetLoader.hpp` and call `AssetLoader::LoadAsync(assetId)` on the main thread. It returns an operation ID, or `0` when the request is rejected. `Application` initializes the loader and calls `Pump()` once per frame; a custom host must call `Initialize()`, `Pump()` and `Shutdown()` itself on the same thread.

```cpp
uint64_t operation = AssetLoader::LoadAsync(assetId);

// Poll during a later update; do not block the frame waiting for completion.
if (operation != 0) {
    const AssetLoadResult result = AssetLoader::GetResult(operation);
    if (result.Status != AssetLoadStatus::Pending) {
        if (result.Succeeded()) {
            texture = TextureManager::LoadTextureByUUID(result.AssetId);
        }
        AssetLoader::Release(operation);
        operation = 0;
    }
}
```

`GetResult()` supplies the asset ID, status and an error message when available. Call `Release()` for every accepted request, including failed or cancelled ones; releasing pending work cancels that observer. `Cancel()` marks a pending request cancelled without releasing its result. `Shutdown()` cancels pending requests and waits for CPU preparation to finish before asset managers and the renderer are destroyed; workers never publish resources during teardown.

---

## Loading, caching, and handles

You don't load the same file twice. Each asset type has a **manager** (Texture Manager, Audio Manager, Font Manager, Shader Manager) that:

1. **Loads** the data the first time it's requested (decode the PNG, upload it to the GPU, etc.).
2. **Caches** it and returns a small **handle** (a cheap value you pass around instead of the heavy data).
3. **Reuses** the cached copy on every later request for the same asset.

Handles are designed to be safe: if an asset is unloaded and its slot later reused, old handles won't accidentally point at the new asset (each slot carries a generation counter).

The built-in default font is **IBM Plex Sans Condensed Regular**. Its stable asset GUID is unchanged, so existing references to the engine default resolve to IBM Plex. Explicit project, text-component and Editor font selections continue to take precedence.

Fonts are cached per **pixel size** — text at 16px and 48px has separate glyph atlases. ASCII and Latin-1 are baked initially; other Unicode glyphs are rasterized from the same font file and uploaded on first use, then reused from the cache. Additional atlas pages keep existing glyph positions stable and count toward the Font Manager's cache budget. Each size allows up to 16 MiB of additional pages and 65,536 dynamic glyph entries; exceeding those limits uses replacement glyphs.

Assign a font that contains the characters you need. The engine does not automatically search other fonts: missing glyphs use the assigned font's U+FFFD replacement character or `?`. Glyphs are loaded synchronously on first use, so displaying a new language can incur rasterization and upload work. Unicode character coverage does not add complex-script shaping, bidirectional layout or color-emoji support.

### Hot-reload (editor)

In the editor, changing an asset file on disk updates it live. For example, editing `player.png` in an image editor and saving triggers the Texture Manager to re-decode it and re-upload to the GPU, so the change appears in the editor without a restart. Thumbnails in the Asset Browser refresh the same way.

This covers every file another program can change while the editor is open: an image or audio editor, a text editor, a `git pull`, or an AI agent working on the project.

| File | What happens when it changes on disk |
|------|--------------------------------------|
| Textures (`.png`, `.jpg`, `.bmp`, `.tga`) | Re-decoded and re-uploaded. |
| Audio (`.wav`, `.mp3`, `.flac`) | Re-decoded; Audio Sources keep the clip, and sources that were playing restart. |
| Fonts (`.ttf`, `.otf`) | Every baked size is dropped and re-baked from the new file. |
| Data Assets (`.dataasset`) | Field values are re-read onto the live instance, so script references to it stay valid. |
| Prefabs (`.prefab`) | New instances use the new file. |
| Scenes (`.scene`) | A loaded scene without unsaved edits reloads (selection is kept, undo history is cleared). A scene with unsaved edits asks first: **Reload from Disk** or **Keep Editor Version**; auto-save waits until you choose. During Play the decision waits until Stop. |

The editor only reacts to changes it did not make itself: its own saves are recognized and ignored. To be asked about every changed scene instead of reloading unsaved-free scenes automatically, turn off **Preferences › Behavior › External Changes › Reload scenes changed on disk**.

### Unloading and purging

Managers can free assets that nothing is using anymore. Systems that hold references (scenes, components, plugins) can register as "reference providers," and a `PurgeUnreferenced()` pass unloads anything no provider still needs — keeping memory in check during long sessions.

---

## The Asset Browser (editor)

The **Asset Browser** is the editor panel where you work with assets directly. From it you can:

- Browse folders with a breadcrumb trail and a thumbnail grid.
- See prefabs as preview images: each `.prefab` tile renders the prefab once it has loaded, with its fonts baked. Sprites, world text and UI are framed from the front. Meshes are shown at a three-quarter angle if the project has Funke.3D enabled. Until the preview is ready, and for prefabs that draw nothing or fail to load, the tile keeps the file icon. A preview re-renders when its `.prefab` file changes (also when saved from Prefab edit mode) or when a texture is reloaded.
- **Create** new scenes, prefabs, scripts, and folders.
- **Drag and drop** assets onto components (e.g. drop a texture onto a sprite) or onto the scene.
- Rename, duplicate, delete, copy/paste, and open files in an external editor.
- **Slice sprite sheets** — define multiple sprites inside one texture; the slices are stored in that texture's `.meta`.
- Drop external files into the window to bring them into the project.

### Native-size sprites and pivots

By default a Sprite Renderer stretches its sprite over the entity's scale: scale (1, 1) is a 1×1 unit quad, whatever the texture size. Set the renderer's **Pixels Per Unit** above 0 to draw the sprite at its native size instead — slice width / Pixels Per Unit units wide (times the scale), like Unity's sprite import setting — placed on the slice's **pivot** from the `.meta` (`"pivot": [x, y]`, 0..1 from the bottom-left corner; a whole texture without a slice uses its centre). A tree with a pivot at its trunk then stands on the entity position, and frames of different sizes keep their anchor while an animation swaps them. **Flip X / Flip Y** mirror the sprite around that pivot. Scene keys: `pixelsPerUnit`, `flipX`, `flipY`; C#: `SpriteRenderer.PixelsPerUnit`, `FlipX`, `FlipY` (also on `NativeSpriteRenderer` for ECB and `QueryRef` code).

See [Editor](../Editor/Editor.md) for how the Asset Browser fits with the other panels.

---

## Assets at runtime vs. in the editor

| | Editor | Runtime (shipped game) |
|---|--------|------------------------|
| Where assets come from | The project's `Assets` folder | The `Assets` folder shipped next to the game |
| Discovery | Scanned + watched live | Loaded on demand as scenes deserialize |
| Hot-reload | Yes — edits apply live | No — files are read once |
| Form on disk | Loose files | **Loose files** (no archive/pack step) |

Funke ships assets as **loose files** — there is no "cook" or archive step that bundles everything into one package file. When you build a game, the project's assets are copied alongside the runtime executable, and the game reads them from disk as scenes load. (See the Build flow in [Editor](../Editor/Editor.md).)

---

## Summary

- Drop files into `Assets/` — no import wizard.
- Each file gets a permanent **GUID**, stored in a `.meta` file beside it.
- Everything references assets **by GUID**, so you can move/rename freely. Keep the `.meta` files.
- The **Asset Registry** indexes everything; per-type **managers** load, cache, and hand out **handles**.
- The editor hot-reloads changed assets; the runtime reads loose files on demand.

## Related pages

- [Scenes](../Engine-Core/Scenes.md) — scenes and prefabs are assets too, and they store the GUIDs of the assets they use.
- [Scripting](../Scripting/Scripting.md) — loading and referencing assets from C#.
- [Editor](../Editor/Editor.md) — the Asset Browser and the build process.

# Data Assets

A **Data Asset** is a reusable, shared piece of game data that lives on its own — not attached to any entity or scene. Item definitions, character stats, loot tables, dialogue, difficulty settings: anything you'd want to author once and reference from many places.

If you've used Unity, this is Funke's equivalent of a **ScriptableObject**.

If you just want the short version: write a C# class that inherits from `DataAsset`, create instances of it in the editor as `.dataasset` files, fill in their fields, and reference them from your scripts.

---

## Why use them?

Imagine 50 enemies that share the same stats. You *could* copy those numbers onto every enemy — but then changing one value means editing 50 entities. Instead, put the data in a single **Data Asset** and have every enemy reference it. Change the asset once, and everyone updates.

Data Assets are good for:

- **Definitions** — items, weapons, spells, enemy types.
- **Tuning data** — stats, curves, difficulty presets.
- **Content** — dialogue lines, quest descriptions, loot tables.
- **Shared config** — anything multiple objects should read from one source of truth.

The key idea: the data is **decoupled** from entities and scenes. One asset, referenced anywhere, edited in one place.

---

## How they work

A Data Asset has two halves:

1. **A C# class** you write (a subclass of `DataAsset`) — this defines *what fields the data has*.
2. **`.dataasset` files** — individual instances of that class, each saved with a permanent **GUID**, just like any other [asset](Assets.md).

So the class is the *template*, and each `.dataasset` file is one filled-in copy. `ItemData` is a class; `Sword.dataasset` and `Potion.dataasset` are instances of it.

At runtime, the engine keeps **one shared live instance** per `.dataasset` file. Everything that references `Sword.dataasset` gets the *same* object — so they all see the same values, and there's no duplication. References are stored as the asset's GUID (not a copy of the data), exactly like texture and audio references.

> Data Assets are part of the **scripting layer**, not the engine core. A build with scripting stripped out simply doesn't include them.

---

## Authoring a Data Asset class

Write a class that inherits from `DataAsset` and add `[CreateDataAsset(...)]` so it shows up in the editor's create menu. Here's the sample from the Sandbox:

```csharp
using Funke;

[CreateDataAsset("Gameplay/Item Data")]
public class ItemData : DataAsset
{
    public string DisplayName = "New Item";
    public int MaxStack = 99;
    [ClampValue(0f, 1000f)] public float Weight = 1.0f;
    public Color Tint = new Color(1f, 1f, 1f, 1f);
    public Texture? Icon;

    public override void OnValidate()
    {
        if (MaxStack < 1)
            MaxStack = 1;   // keep the value sane after edits
    }
}
```

A few things to notice:

- **`[CreateDataAsset("Gameplay/Item Data")]`** puts an entry in the editor's *Create → Data Asset* menu. The path is slash-separated for submenus. Without this attribute the class still works, but it won't appear in the create menu.
- **Fields** use the same rules and [attributes](../Scripting/Scripting.md#exposing-fields-to-the-inspector) as script fields — `[ClampValue]`, `[ShowInEditor]`, `[Header]`, `[ToolTip]`, and so on. Public fields are editable by default.
- **`OnValidate()`** runs after the fields are edited in the editor or loaded from disk. Override it to clamp or recompute values — it's the analogue of Unity's `OnValidate`.

### What field types are allowed?

The same set as script fields:

- primitives (`int`, `float`, `bool`, …) and `string`,
- enums,
- the built-in math/color types (`Vector2/3/4`, `Color`, …),
- asset references like `Texture` and `Audio`,
- and **other `DataAsset` subclasses** — a Data Asset can reference another Data Asset (e.g. an `ItemData` that points at a `RarityData`).

---

## Creating and editing instances (editor)

Once your class exists and the project is built:

1. In the **Asset Browser**, right-click → **Create → Data Asset → Gameplay/Item Data** (your menu path).
2. A new `.dataasset` file appears. Name it (e.g. `Sword`).
3. Select it — its fields show in the **Inspector**, starting from the class's default values.
4. Edit the values. They're saved to the `.dataasset` file.

Each file is an independent instance with its own values, but all share the class you wrote. See [Assets › The Asset Browser](Assets.md#the-asset-browser-editor).

---

## Referencing a Data Asset from a script

Just declare a field of your Data Asset type. The editor shows a picker so you can assign an asset by drag-and-drop, and the reference is saved (by GUID) with the scene:

```csharp
using Funke;

public class ItemHolder : EntityScript
{
    public ItemData? Item;   // shows a Data Asset picker in the Inspector
    public int Count = 1;

    public override void OnStart()
    {
        if (Item != null)
            Log.Info($"{Count}x {Item.DisplayName} (weight {Item.Weight})");
        else
            Log.Warn("ItemHolder has no Item assigned.");
    }
}
```

Because every holder that points at the same asset shares one instance, reading `Item.DisplayName` always reflects the asset's current values. (And as noted above, one Data Asset can reference another the same way.)

---

## Loading a Data Asset from code

You don't have to assign assets in the Inspector — you can load them at runtime through the [`AssetManager`](Assets.md#referencing-assets-from-c-scripts):

```csharp
// Load a specific one by its project path:
ItemData? sword = AssetManager.Load<ItemData>("Items/Sword.dataasset");

// Or get every ItemData in the project (optionally under a folder):
IReadOnlyList<ItemData> allItems = AssetManager.FindAll<ItemData>();
IReadOnlyList<ItemData> weapons  = AssetManager.FindAll<ItemData>("Items/Weapons");
```

`FindAll<T>` is handy for things like building a catalog of every item at startup.

---

## What's in a `.dataasset` file

A `.dataasset` file is small and self-describing. It stores:

- the **type** name of the class it's an instance of (e.g. `"ItemData"`),
- a format **version**, and
- the **field values**.

Like scenes and prefabs, it's written as text (JSON) or in a compact binary form depending on your project's asset-serialization setting. The file on disk is always the source of truth; the engine loads it into the shared live instance on demand.

---

## Hot reload

Data Assets play nicely with C# [hot reload](../Scripting/Scripting.md#hot-reload). When you rebuild your scripts, the live managed instances are swapped out and then **re-created from disk**. The engine creates every instance first and *then* replays their field values, so cross-references between Data Assets resolve correctly even when assets point at each other.

In practice this means you can tweak a Data Asset class, reload, and keep working — your `.dataasset` files and their values are preserved.

Editing a `.dataasset` file outside the editor (a text editor, a `git pull`, an AI agent) also applies live: the editor re-reads the changed file and writes its values onto the existing instance, so scripts holding a reference see the new values without a recompile — in edit mode and during Play.

---

## Data Asset vs. the alternatives

It helps to know when to reach for a Data Asset versus something else:

| Use… | When you want… |
|------|----------------|
| **Data Asset** | Shared data, decoupled from any entity — one source of truth referenced from many places. |
| **Prefab** | A reusable *entity* (with components, children, transforms) you stamp into scenes. See [Scenes › Prefabs](../Engine-Core/Scenes.md#prefabs). |
| **Plain script fields** | Per-instance values that belong to one specific entity and aren't shared. See [Scripting](../Scripting/Scripting.md). |

Rule of thumb: if several objects should read the **same** data and you want to edit it in **one** place, use a Data Asset.

---

## Summary

- A **Data Asset** is shared game data in its own file — Funke's **ScriptableObject** equivalent.
- Write a `class X : DataAsset`; add `[CreateDataAsset("Menu/Path")]` to get a create-menu entry.
- Each instance is a `.dataasset` file with a permanent **GUID**; the engine keeps **one shared live instance** per file.
- Fields follow the script-field rules (primitives, strings, enums, vectors/colors, `Texture`/`Audio`, and other Data Assets); `OnValidate()` runs after edits.
- Create and edit them in the **Asset Browser/Inspector**; reference them from scripts by declaring a field, or load them with `AssetManager.Load<T>` / `FindAll<T>`.

## Related pages

- [Assets](Assets.md) — the wider asset system Data Assets are part of (GUIDs, the Asset Browser, loading).
- [Scripting](../Scripting/Scripting.md) — the C# layer, field attributes, and hot reload.
- [Scenes](../Engine-Core/Scenes.md) — prefabs, the entity-shaped alternative.

# Building and Shipping

The editor exports games for the desktop platform it runs on: **Windows x64**, **Linux** or **macOS**. **Android, iOS and Web** exports come from platform packages; see [Platform Packages](Platform-Packages.md) for their requirements.

## Build a game

Before exporting:

1. Open **Project Settings** and set the executable name, company, version, window mode, icon, and splash screen.
2. Add every required scene to **Build Scenes** and choose a valid startup scene.
3. Select a build profile for your desktop platform (new projects get `Windows`, `Linux` and `macOS` profiles).
4. Use **Development** while testing and **Release** for distribution. **Debug** adds debug binaries and symbols for attaching a debugger. Build profiles can carry their own configuration, defines and test switches; see [Test Builds and Debug Tools](Testing.md).
5. Choose an empty output directory (outside the project or under its `Builds` folder) and click **Build**.

The output directory defaults to `<project>/Builds/<Platform>`. While its last folder is a platform name (`Windows`, `Linux`, `MacOS`, `Android`, `Web`, ...), it follows the active profile's platform; any other folder name is kept as typed.

What the build produces:

| Platform | Output |
|---|---|
| Windows | `<Name>.exe` with `Funke-Engine.dll`, `SDL3.dll`, `nethost.dll` and the game content next to it. |
| Linux | `<Name>` (executable) with `libFunke-Engine.so`, `libSDL3.so.0`, `libwebgpu_dawn.so` and the game content next to it. Ship the folder, e.g. as a `.tar.gz`. |
| macOS | `<Name>.app`: the executable and libraries in `Contents/MacOS`, the game content in `Contents/Resources`, an `Info.plist` with the app id and version, and the icon as `AppIcon.icns`. The bundle is ad-hoc signed; sign and notarize it with your Developer ID before distributing it outside your own Macs. |

From a source checkout the editor compiles a fresh runtime for the export first (MSBuild on Windows, `make` on Linux and macOS). That runtime contains only the [engine modules](../Engine-Core/Engine-Modules.md) the project enables, so a 2D game ships without the 3D renderer and Jolt and a 3D game without sprites and Box2D. The first export with a new module set compiles the engine once. A build stops when a shipped scene uses a component of a module the project leaves out.

On Windows that runtime is compiled with the MSBuild of Visual Studio 2022 when it is installed, because the engine itself is built with it; otherwise Visual Studio 2026 with the MSVC v143 toolset is used. Set `FUNKE_MSBUILD` to the full path of an `MSBuild.exe` to choose one yourself.

The build is fail-closed: invalid paths, missing scenes, incomplete scripting artifacts, package failures, and incomplete runtime payloads stop the export instead of publishing a partial folder. The completed directory is staged first and then moved into place.

Do not remove files from the result. The executable depends on the adjacent engine, SDL3, .NET host, ScriptCore, project assembly, package libraries, project configuration, assets, and license folders produced by the build.

For the current demo release, list every native package dependency directly in the project's `packages` array. Native runtime loading does not yet expand transitive package dependencies.

## Which assets ship

A build only contains the files from `Assets/` and the engine's `FunkeAssets/` that the game can reach:

- The enabled **Build Scenes**, and everything they reference: textures, audio, fonts, prefabs, Data Assets and other scenes (by GUID, asset path or scene name). References inside those assets are followed too.
- Paths in `project.json` (splash images, cursors).
- Files and folders whose path appears as a string literal in a C# script, e.g. `Path.Combine(Application.DataPath, "Levels/Official")` ships the whole `Levels/Official` folder. A literal scene name, e.g. `SceneManager.LoadScene("Credits")`, ships that scene.
- `AssetManager.FindAll<T>("Prefix")` ships every asset of that type under the prefix. Without a literal prefix, every asset of that type ships.
- Everything in **`Assets/StreamingAssets/`**, unchanged.
- The engine's default font, default shape textures, splash logo and localization files.

`.cs` sources, scenes not in the build list, and assets nothing refers to are left out, along with their `.meta` files. The build log lists how many files were skipped and their total size.

Built-in files always come from the engine you build with, so engine updates (a new splash logo, fixed default textures) reach older projects too. The project's own `FunkeAssets/` folder, a copy made when the project was created, only replaces an engine file when you changed that file in the project (it is newer than the engine's).

Files your code finds through a computed path (`"Level" + i + ".json"`, a path from a config value) cannot be detected. Put them in `Assets/StreamingAssets/`. If the project cannot be scanned completely (unreadable file, missing build scene), the build logs a warning and ships all assets.

## Asset bundles

In **Build Profiles › Asset Packaging**, enable **Bundle Assets** to ship the staged
`Assets/` and `FunkeAssets/` as `Assets.fbundle` and `FunkeAssets.fbundle`.
**Compress Bundles** separately enables lossless LZ4 compression. Both switches
default to off, including for older profiles.

```json
{
  "bundleAssets": true,
  "compressAssetBundles": true
}
```

Pruning and binary scene conversion run before bundling. GUIDs and `.meta` data
are preserved. The runtime reads individual files directly from the bundles;
compressed files are decompressed only when requested. Files that do not shrink
are stored uncompressed. Bundles have a versioned index and per-file checksums;
invalid indices reject startup and corrupt payloads fail asset loading.

`Assets/StreamingAssets/` stays loose. Use it for direct C# `System.IO` access or
third-party libraries that require real filenames; bundled assets are available
through Funke's asset APIs. Bundle entries are limited to 2,113,929,216 bytes per
file. Keep larger external files in StreamingAssets.

The settings apply to desktop and platform-package content staging. Ship the
complete output directory, including bundles, StreamingAssets and licenses.
Turning bundling off restores loose assets on the next successful build.

## App icon and cursors

**Project Settings › Branding › App Icon** accepts PNG, JPG, BMP or ICO at any size; use a square image of 1024×1024 or larger. Non-square images are centred on a transparent square. Each build places it next to `project.json` as `AppIcon.png`, so the shipped game finds it even if the source file sits outside `Assets/`.

| Target | Where the icon appears |
|---|---|
| Windows | Embedded in the `.exe` at 16–256 px (Explorer, taskbar, title bar). An `.ico` source is embedded unchanged. The window also gets icons at the exact size for the monitor's DPI. |
| Android, iOS, Web | Passed to the platform package as a PNG, together with the app id. |
| macOS | `AppIcon.icns` in the app bundle (Finder, Dock), made with `iconutil` from the PNG. |
| Linux, macOS (runtime) | Set on the window at several sizes. GNOME on Wayland only shows icons from an installed `.desktop` file; there the window is grouped by the app id. |

The app id is `com.<company>.<name>`, built from **Company** and the project name as lowercase letters and digits, e.g. `com.benscr.geometrydash`. Without a company it is `com.funke.<name>`.

To show players another name than the project name, set `"productName"` in `project.json` (e.g. `"Marble Run"`, spaces allowed). It becomes the app's label on Android, iOS and macOS and the window title. The project name stays the identity: app id, save-data folder and file names do not change, so a game can be renamed after release without becoming a new app or losing saves.

**Branding › Cursors** sets the default cursor and the cursor over Interactable UI elements. Each has a **Hotspot**: the click point in image pixels, measured from the top-left corner (**Center** for crosshairs). The image keeps its aspect ratio and is 32 px on its longest side at 100 % display scaling. Larger scaling uses sharp images up to 400 %, so source images of 128 px or more look best. On Android and iOS cursor settings are ignored. From C#: `Cursor.SetTexture(texture, new Vector2(x, y))`.

## Player prerequisites

A Windows player machine needs:

- Windows x64 with a WebGPU-capable D3D12 or Vulkan graphics driver.
- The [.NET 10 x64 Runtime](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/en-us/download/dotnet/10.0), only when **Include .NET Runtime** is off in the build profile.
- The [Microsoft Visual C++ 2015-2022 x64 Redistributable](https://aka.ms/vs/17/release/vc_redist.x64.exe).

A Linux player machine needs a Vulkan driver and the operating-system dependencies of .NET. A macOS player needs macOS 11 or later. When **Include .NET Runtime** is off, both also need the .NET 10 Runtime for their CPU (`dotnet-runtime-10.0` on Linux; Arm64 on Apple Silicon).

Desktop build profiles enable **Include .NET Runtime** by default (`"bundleDotNetRuntime": true` in the `.build` file). The exporter copies the newest installed stable patch of ScriptCore's required major/minor version, its matching hostfxr and license notices into `dotnet/` beside the game's ScriptCore files. It checks the native runtime architecture and refuses incomplete installations. The export uses the installed runtime offline; update .NET on the build machine and export again to ship security updates. The SDK and unrelated runtimes are not included.

The player explicitly loads that private runtime, including after moving the game folder or the macOS `.app`. A damaged private runtime fails instead of silently switching to a machine-wide version. Turn the option off for smaller downloads when an installer supplies .NET separately; without an installed runtime that build shows a download prompt. Windows still needs the Visual C++ Redistributable; this option bundles .NET only.

Funke is MIT-licensed ([LICENSE.txt](../../../LICENSE.txt)): you may ship and sell games made with it freely. The license only asks that its notice travels with the engine, which the build already does by placing it, together with the third-party notices, in the output's `Licenses` folder. Keep that folder when you distribute the game.

Saved data (`PlayerPrefs`, `SaveData`) is stored in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\<Company>\<Name>`, taken from **Project Settings**. Set both before your first release: changing them later moves players' saves to a new folder.

## Standalone editor prerequisites

The standard installer and public archives contain compiled applications, assets and `EngineSDK/FunkeSDK.json`. They do not contain engine sources, native headers or a ScriptCore source project. Ordinary C# project creation, Editor play mode and desktop export need the **stable .NET 10.0 SDK**; Roslyn comes from that SDK. Git and a native compiler are not required for this workflow.

Additional tools depend on the work:

- The matching optional Native SDK plus Visual Studio or Build Tools with MSVC v143 14.44 or newer for native scripts and packages.
- Visual Studio 2026 (18.0+) for C# IntelliSense when Visual Studio is selected as the script editor.
- Python 3.10 or newer for the package scaffolding commands.
- CMake for a project's `NativeScripts` target.

Premake and the package authoring scripts are included in `EngineSDK`.

Installed desktop exports select the declared Development or Release runtime directly. An available prebuilt module variant is used when compatible; otherwise the declared full runtime is used without invoking an engine build. Missing configurations and damaged declared runtimes fail explicitly. Cross-platform builders that compile the engine still require a complete source checkout and the target toolchain.

Use [Standalone Verification](Standalone-Verification.md) for the automated Launcher/create/edit/play/export/player gate and the separate Windows Sandbox recipe. A restricted host run is recorded separately from a clean-machine result.

## Validate a game release

Test the exact folder or archive you plan to upload:

1. Copy it to a clean Windows x64 VM that has no Funke source checkout and no developer SDKs.
2. Install only the player prerequisites above.
3. Launch the executable from a path containing spaces and non-ASCII characters.
4. Exercise the startup scene, scene changes, C# scripts, native and managed packages, audio, input, save data, fullscreen/window switching, and shutdown.
5. Confirm no absolute developer paths appear in logs or configuration.
6. Unzip the final archive into a second clean directory and repeat the launch test.
7. Scan the archive and record its checksum before publishing.

Treat the clean-machine run as a release gate. Repository CI can verify structure and startup behavior, but it cannot prove that an arbitrary customer machine has the expected drivers and runtimes.

Desktop CI also creates and exports a small C# game, moves its output to a path containing spaces and non-ASCII characters, and runs it with global .NET discovery redirected to a missing directory. It requires the game's script marker and the bundled-runtime log message. Two negative checks remove the framework or the entire private runtime and require startup to fail without falling back to the build machine's installation. Run this check locally with `python scripts/ci/desktop_export_smoke_test.py --cli <path-to-funke>`.

For real browser, Android and iOS simulator runs of already exported games, use [Platform Export Testing](Platform-Export-Testing.md). Those checks require C# success markers and rendered pixels, and retain evidence for each run. The Web workflow is opt-in and consumes an export artifact; mobile checks need an explicitly selected device or simulator.

## Build the standalone engine distribution

Engine maintainers need Visual Studio with MSVC v143 14.44 or newer, the .NET 10 SDK, Python 3.10 or newer, Git, CMake, and a recursive submodule checkout.

After a fresh clone, build the git-ignored Dawn/WebGPU dependency once. A release-only Dawn build is sufficient for the publish bundle:

```powershell
$env:DAWN_BUILD_CONFIGS = "Release"
$env:DAWN_SKIP_PREMAKE = "1"
.\scripts\dawn\SetupDawn.bat
Remove-Item Env:DAWN_BUILD_CONFIGS
Remove-Item Env:DAWN_SKIP_PREMAKE
```

Generate project files once:

```powershell
.\scripts\Setup.bat
```

Build the Release editor/runtime, the stripped Dist runtime, the package tool, ScriptCore, Launcher, SDK payload, notices, and then run the structural verifier:

```powershell
.\scripts\BuildWindows.ps1 -PublishBundle
```

The verified folder and upload artifacts are:

```text
bin\Release-windows-x86_64\Funke-Launcher\
bin\Release-windows-x86_64\Funke-Editor-<version>-Windows-x64.zip
bin\Release-windows-x86_64\Funke-Editor-<version>-Windows-x64.zip.sha256
bin\Release-windows-x86_64\PrivateSymbols\Funke-Editor-<build-id>-Windows-x64-symbols.zip
```

The version comes from `Version.props`. The build ID combines that version with the exact Git commit and is embedded in native and managed binaries plus `BuildMetadata.json`. The build extracts the ZIP into a temporary path containing spaces and non-ASCII characters, verifies that extracted copy, and records its SHA-256. The archive includes:

- Launcher, Editor, and Development Runtime executables.
- The prebuilt `EngineSDK\Runtime-Dist` runtime used for Release game exports.
- Funke-ScriptCore and Funke-PackageTool artifacts.
- Premake, the package workspace scripts, and package create/remove/version tools.
- A versioned SDK manifest with the installation's capabilities and runtime paths.
- Funke, third-party, Dawn, font, and .NET redistribution notices.

Maintainers can add native headers, import libraries and required third-party headers with `BuildWindows.ps1 -PublishBundle -IncludeNativeSdk`, `BuildInstaller.ps1 -IncludeNativeSdk`, or `PackagePosix.py --include-native-sdk`. Developer Launcher staging retains this optional Native SDK; public archives and installers omit it by default.

PDB files are excluded from the public archive. A separate build-ID-keyed private symbols archive contains the exact Release and Dist PDBs, a binary hash manifest, and the build identity needed to diagnose crash dumps.

The CI artifact's 90-day retention is transfer storage only. Copy every private symbols archive to durable, access-controlled storage and retain it for the full supported lifetime of that exact release, plus any longer crash-report retention period.

The structural verifier can also be run directly:

```powershell
.\scripts\verify-standalone-zip.bat Release
```

## Engine release checklist

Before tagging a public release, update `Version.props`, add the exact version to `CHANGELOG.md`, and use the matching `v<version>` tag. Prerelease and final versions are distinct: for example, `v2026.1.0-rc.1` requires `FunkeVersion` to be `2026.1.0-rc.1`.

For unsigned local candidates, the normal publish command is sufficient. Official tags require Authenticode signing and a detached CMS signature over the checksum. CI reads the PFX and password from `FUNKE_SIGNING_CERTIFICATE_BASE64` and `FUNKE_SIGNING_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD`; configure `FUNKE_SIGNING_TIMESTAMP_URL` as a repository variable when timestamping is required. Credentials stay outside the repository.

Before tagging a public release:

1. Confirm GitHub rulesets protect the default branch and release-tag path and require both the `windows-build` and `linux-build` CI jobs. This repository setting is external to the checkout; do not publish a tag while either required check is absent.
2. Run `.\scripts\RunTests.bat --release`, then `.\scripts\RunTests.bat` to cover both Release and Debug native tests.
3. Run `dotnet test Tests\Funke-ScriptCore-Tests\Funke-ScriptCore-Tests.csproj -c Release`.
4. Run the project-local package smoke test:

   ```powershell
   .\scripts\ci\project_package_smoke_test.ps1 -Configuration Release
   ```

5. Run `.\scripts\ci\core_module_build.ps1` so the isolated core-only Engine must link as a complete shared library.
6. Create and verify the release-candidate artifacts with `.\scripts\BuildWindows.ps1 -PublishBundle`.
7. Copy the Launcher bundle to a clean Windows VM, install the standalone editor prerequisites, and create, open, play, build, and run a small project containing both a C# and native package.
8. Run the packaged Launcher, Editor, and Dist Runtime smoke tests and require their natural zero exit after the stable-frame marker.
9. Review the bundled licenses and the matching `CHANGELOG.md` section.
10. Move the private symbols artifact to durable, access-controlled storage under its build ID, and retain it for the release's full supported lifetime. Do not treat the 90-day CI artifact as the archive of record.
11. Verify the archive checksum and detached signature:

   ```powershell
   .\scripts\VerifyRelease.ps1 `
       -ArchivePath .\Funke-Editor-<version>-Windows-x64.zip `
       -ChecksumPath .\Funke-Editor-<version>-Windows-x64.zip.sha256 `
       -ExpectedSignerThumbprint <published-code-signing-thumbprint> `
       -RequireSignature
   ```

CI runs on pushes, pull requests and manual dispatch. Python tooling tests and C# ScriptCore tests run independently on Windows, Linux and Apple Silicon macOS; the C# jobs use AnyCPU and upload TRX results without waiting for Dawn or native builds. Native jobs build and test the desktop engine, and runtime smoke tests cover Release/Dist on macOS, Release/Debug/Dist on Linux, and the packaged Windows applications and installer. The Windows standalone job downloads the public archive onto a fresh runner whose sparse checkout contains only the verification script. A draft release requires this gate, all desktop jobs and the managed-test matrix to pass.

Android helper tests, iOS/Web export orchestration tests and Web preview tests run in the Python matrix. The export tests substitute external compilers and downloads: they do not compile APKs, sign iOS apps or execute WebAssembly in a browser. Device and browser export checks remain part of release validation. A public tag should be created only after the clean-machine engine and exported-game checks pass.

CI regenerates `--module-profile=core` into `premake/generated/core` and builds the isolated Engine on Windows and Linux. Linux CI also runs the Debug engine tests in separate `--sanitize` and `--coverage` variants. AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer fail the job on runtime defects; lcov publishes the engine coverage report. The core, sanitizer, and coverage object directories are distinct, so none of these gates can reuse full-profile or uninstrumented objects.
