# Test Builds and Debug Tools

These tools are for testing a game without changing its code. You can:

- build your own test, demo or QA variants with build profiles,
- type commands in a developer console while the game runs,
- see colliders and contacts in the running game,
- keep test runs away from the player's save data,
- record reproducible test runs with scripted input and screenshots at fixed points in game time.

## Configurations

A game build uses one of three configurations:

| Configuration | Binaries | C# define | Overlays and console by default | For |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Debug** | Debug engine and runtime, plus PDBs for the runtime, the engine, ScriptCore and your scripts | `FUNKE_BUILD_DEBUG` | on | Attaching Visual Studio or Rider, stepping through engine code |
| **Development** | Optimized (the editor's own configuration) | `FUNKE_BUILD_DEVELOPMENT` | on | Everyday testing on your machine and devices |
| **Release** | Fully optimized Dist binaries | `FUNKE_BUILD_RELEASE` | off | Distribution |

Pick it in the Build window under **Configuration**, in the build profile (see below), or with `funke build --debug | --development | --release`. The order of precedence is: the command line, then the build profile, then the Build window.

**Debug builds:**

- **Engine sources required.** Debug builds need the engine sources: the editor compiles the Debug runtime the first time, which takes a while. The SDK editor without sources needs a `Runtime-Debug` folder next to it.
- **Developer machines only.** They link the Visual C++ *debug* runtime, which only machines with Visual Studio have. Give testers Development builds.
- **Console window.** The Debug runtime opens a console window that shows the log.
- **Android, iOS and Web.** These platforms have no Debug engine. A Debug profile there ships the Development runtime with Debug-compiled scripts.

In C#, `Engine.BuildConfiguration` is `Editor`, `Development`, `Release` or `Debug`.

## Build profiles for test variants

Besides platform and rendering API, a build profile (`BuildProfiles/<Name>.build`) can carry its own settings. Edit them in **Build Profiles › Configuration & Testing**. Any field left at *Project Default* keeps the project's setting.

```json
{
  "name": "AndroidTest",
  "platform": "Android",
  "renderBackend": "Vulkan",
  "configuration": "Development",
  "defines": [ "FUNKE_TEST", "DEMO" ],
  "showRuntimeStats": true,
  "showRuntimeLogs": false,
  "devConsole": true,
  "isolatedPrefs": true
}
```

| Field | Effect |
|---|---|
| `configuration` | `Debug`, `Development` or `Release` for builds with this profile. |
| `defines` | Extra C# defines, added to the project's `customDefines`. Use them for `#if DEMO` code. |
| `showRuntimeStats`, `showRuntimeLogs` | The runtime stats and log overlays; see [keyboard shortcuts](#runtime-keyboard-shortcuts). |
| `devConsole` | The developer console and physics overlay. |
| `isolatedPrefs` | Saves to a separate player-data profile named after the build profile (see below). |

`funke build --profile AndroidTest` builds that variant. The settings go into the build's own `project.json` only. Your project stays unchanged.

`project.json` itself accepts `devConsole` (true/false) and `prefsProfile` (a name) for every build. **Project Settings › Build › Diagnostics** has a switch for the console.

## Platform-specific code in the editor

The editor compiles and plays your C# scripts as the platform of the **active build profile** (the one chosen in the Build window or with **Set Active** in Build Profiles). With an Android profile active, scripts get `FUNKE_ANDROID` instead of `FUNKE_WINDOWS`, so code like this runs in Play mode and can be debugged there:

```csharp
#if FUNKE_ANDROID
    ShowTouchControls();
#else
    ShowKeyboardHints();
#endif
```

- **Which defines.** The platform define of the profile (`FUNKE_WINDOWS`, `FUNKE_LINUX`, `FUNKE_MACOS`, `FUNKE_ANDROID`, `FUNKE_IOS`, `FUNKE_VISIONOS`, `FUNKE_WEB`) and the profile's `defines`, besides `FUNKE_EDITOR`, `FUNKE_BUILD_DEVELOPMENT` and the project's custom defines. Without an active profile the editor uses its own platform.
- **Switching.** Changing the active profile, its platform or its defines recompiles the scripts within a second. `Packages/FunkeDefines.props` follows, so Visual Studio and Rider grey out the right `#if` branches.
- **Shown in the toolbar.** While the editor plays another platform than its own, a **Simulating Android** (or iOS, Web, …) badge sits next to the Play button. Clicking it opens Build Profiles.
- **At runtime.** `Application.Platform` is the platform the scripts run as: the simulated one in the editor, the real one in a built game. `Application.IsSimulatingPlatform` is true while the editor simulates. `Engine.Platform` always reports the machine itself.
- **Only scripts change.** The engine keeps running as the editor's own platform: its native code, input devices, file paths and graphics backend are the desktop ones. Calls that need the real device (for example `AndroidBridge` or permissions) behave as on the desktop. Test those in a build.

## Runtime keyboard shortcuts

Shortcuts follow the platform the engine and runtime are built for. On macOS, the diagnostic overlays use number keys with Cmd+Shift, without requiring the function-key row.

| Action | Windows / Linux | macOS |
|---|---|---|
| Stats overlay | F6 | Cmd+Shift+6 |
| Log overlay | F7 | Cmd+Shift+7 |
| Physics overlay | F8 | Cmd+Shift+8 |
| Profiler | Ctrl+F6 | Cmd+Shift+P |
| Toggle fullscreen | F11 | Ctrl+Cmd+F |
| Minimize window | Ctrl+M | Cmd+M |

These actions are available when their respective runtime features are enabled. Fullscreen and minimize also apply to engine applications that enable those window shortcuts.

## Developer console

Development and Debug builds have a console. To open it, press **`** (the key left of 1, `^` on German keyboards) or tap the screen with three fingers. **Esc** closes it.

While the console is open, it takes the game's keyboard and mouse input. **Tab** completes command names. **↑** and **↓** go through earlier commands. Separate several commands with `;`.

| Command | Does |
|---|---|
| `help [filter]` | Lists every command with its arguments |
| `scene [name]` | Lists the loaded scenes, or loads (restarts) one |
| `timescale [x]` | Shows or sets `Time.TimeScale` (`0` freezes the game) |
| `physics.debug [on\|off]` | Collider wireframes, triggers and contacts (also **F8**, or **Cmd+Shift+8** on macOS) |
| `physics.contacts [on\|off]` | Contact points and normals in that overlay |
| `stats [on\|off]`, `logs [on\|off]` | The stats/log overlays, even in builds that start without them |
| `screenshot [file]` | Saves the next frame as PNG |
| `audio.spatial [x y z ...]` | The audio listener and every playing 3D sound (distance, gain, pan, left/right volume); with a position, how a sound there would be heard. See *Scripting › 3D sound* |
| `prefs.clear`, `prefs.path` | Deletes the PlayerPrefs, or shows the data folder in use |
| `echo <text>`, `clear`, `quit` | Prints text, clears the console, quits |

### Your own commands

Any **static** method with `[DevCommand]` becomes a command. Its parameters are read from the words you type:

- string, bool (`on`/`off`), int, long, float, double, enums, and `Vector2`/`Vector3` (written `1,2,3`).
- Optional parameters can be left out.
- A string as the last parameter takes the rest of the line.
- A single `string[]` parameter gets the raw words.
- If the method returns a value, the console prints it.

```csharp
using Funke;

public static class CheatCommands
{
    [DevCommand("coins.add", Description = "Gives the player coins")]
    static string AddCoins(int amount = 100)
    {
        Wallet.Coins += amount;
        return $"Coins: {Wallet.Coins}";
    }

    [DevCommand("level.goto")]
    static void GoTo(int level) => SceneManager.LoadScene($"Level{level}");
}
```

From a script that needs its instance, register a handler:

```csharp
DevConsole.Register("player.teleport", args => { Teleport(args[0]); return "ok"; }, "Moves the player to a named spawn");
```

`DevConsole.Execute("timescale 0.5")` runs any command from code, in every build. You can use it for debug menus that reuse the same commands. `DevConsole.IsAvailable` and `DevConsole.IsOpen` tell you whether the console is shown.

## Stats overlay

**F6** (**Cmd+Shift+6** on macOS) in a running game, or **Stats** in the Game View toolbar, shows the frame rate and frame time, memory, playing sounds, entities and the geometry drawn per frame:

- **Tris** and **Verts** count Mesh Renderers and Skinned Mesh Renderers (every instance), 3D particles, 2D sprites and 2D particles. A sprite or particle is 2 triangles and 4 vertices; a mesh adds its own triangles and vertices once per instance. UI, text and gizmos are not counted.
- **Shadow tris** appears while a light casts shadows: the triangles the shadow map draws again for the shadow casters. They are not part of **Tris**, so **Tris** matches what the cameras show.

In a game, the numbers include every camera and are averaged over the frames since the last refresh (about 30 times per second). The Game View shows only what its own render drew, without the Editor View. The Profiler's **Triangles** and **Vertices** rows show everything drawn in a frame, in the editor including the Editor View.

## Physics overlay

**F8** (**Cmd+Shift+8** on macOS), or `physics.debug on` in the console, draws over the running game:

- every collider in green,
- triggers in light blue,
- Fast 2D colliders in cyan,
- the current contact points with their normals in orange.

The overlay works for both 2D (Box2D) and 3D (Jolt). It is independent of `Gizmo.IsEnabled`.

## Isolated player data

A player-data profile moves `Application.PersistentDataPath` to `…/<Company>/<Game>/Profiles/<name>`. `PlayerPrefs` and `SaveData` live in that folder, so a test run never changes real coins, stars or best times. Ways to set it:

- `isolatedPrefs` in a build profile (the profile name becomes the profile),
- `"prefsProfile": "QA"` in `project.json`,
- `--prefs-profile=<name>` on the command line. An empty name switches a build's profile off again.

`Application.PrefsProfile` tells scripts which profile is active. `prefs.clear` resets it.

## Automated test runs

The runtime and every built game read these command-line options:

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--input-script=<file.json>` | Timed input and actions (see below) |
| `--screenshot-at=<t>[,<t>...]` | PNG screenshots at game time (`2.5s`, `2.5`, `500ms`) or frame (`120f`) |
| `--screenshot-dir=<dir>` | Where screenshots go (default `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Funke\Screenshots`) |
| `--fixed-step=<fps>` | Every frame advances exactly 1/fps seconds, however long it really took |
| `--quit-at=<t>` | Quit at a game time or frame |
| `--exec="<cmd>; <cmd>"` | Console commands on the first game frame, e.g. `"physics.debug on; timescale 2"` |
| `--prefs-profile=<name>` | Isolated player data (see above) |
| `--background` | The window never takes focus: it opens behind your other windows and keeps running while unfocused, even with **Run in background** off. Fullscreen and maximized windows become a plain window filling the screen, and `Window.Focus()` does nothing. The editor and launcher accept it too |
| `--sound` | Keep the sound of an automated run on (see below) |
| `--mute` | Silence any run, automated or not |

**Automated runs are silent.** A run with any of the options above except `--screenshot-dir`, `--sound` and `--mute` (a `--prefs-profile` only with a name) counts as automated: the engine mutes its sound, so several test windows next to your work stay quiet, and the log says `Sound muted: automated run`. Pass `--sound` to listen anyway. Scripts can ask with `Application.IsAutomatedRun`, e.g. to skip an intro, an ad or a tutorial; the game's own volume settings (`Audio.MasterVolume`) don't unmute such a run.

**How game time is counted:**

- Game time starts on the first frame after the startup scene loaded, so the splash and loading screens don't shift it.
- With `--fixed-step` every frame adds the same amount, so the same input lands on the same frame on every machine.
- Screenshots and `quit` follow this clock, not the wall clock.

### Input scripts

```json
{
  "fixedStep": 60,
  "steps": [
    { "at": "0.5s", "key": "D", "action": "down" },
    { "at": "2.0s", "key": "D", "action": "up" },
    { "at": "2.1s", "key": "Space" },
    { "at": "3s",   "mouse": [0.5, 0.8], "button": "left" },
    { "at": "4s",   "touch": [0.2, 0.8], "finger": 0, "action": "down" },
    { "at": "4.5s", "touch": [0.3, 0.8], "finger": 0, "action": "move" },
    { "at": "5s",   "touch": [0.3, 0.8], "finger": 0, "action": "up" },
    { "frame": 330, "command": "level.goto 5" },
    { "at": "8s",   "screenshot": "level5-start.png" },
    { "at": "8s",   "log": "Level 5 loaded" },
    { "at": "9s",   "quit": true }
  ]
}
```

Each step needs a time, written as `"at"` (seconds, or a string like `"2.5s"`, `"500ms"`, `"120f"`) or as `"frame"`. It also needs exactly one of these actions:

| Step | Fields |
|---|---|
| `key` | Key name: `A`–`Z`, `0`–`9`, `Space`, `Enter`, `Esc`, `Tab`, `Left`/`Right`/`Up`/`Down`, `LeftShift`, `Ctrl`, `Alt`, `F1`–`F25`, ... `action`: `press` (default: down for one frame), `down` or `up` |
| `mouse` | Window position `[x, y]` from 0 to 1, top-left origin. With `button` (`left`, `right`, `middle`) it clicks, without it the mouse only moves |
| `touch` | Position `[x, y]` from 0 to 1, `finger` (id), `action`: `tap`, `down`, `move` or `up` |
| `command` | A console line, including your `[DevCommand]`s |
| `screenshot` | File name (optional), saved in the screenshot folder |
| `log` | A line in the log, tagged with the step's time |
| `quit` | Ends the run |

Scripted input goes through the same path as real input. `Input.GetKey`, the C# input events, UI buttons and the console all see it. Gamepads can't be scripted yet; use the keys of `Input.GetAxis`.

A broken script stops nothing: the log names the step and the problem, and the game runs without it.

A touch's first finger also moves and clicks the mouse, as on a real touch screen, so `tap` and `touch` drags reach UI buttons and scroll views.

The same scripts run in an open editor with `funke editor input <script.json>`, without building or starting the runtime ([Editor Bridge](Editor-Bridge.md)).

### From the command line and `Run.ps1`

```powershell
funke run --input-script Tests\level5.json --fixed-step 60 --prefs-profile qa
.\Builds\Windows\MarbleSky.exe --screenshot-at=2s,5s --quit-at=6s --prefs-profile=qa
scripts\dev\Run.ps1 -App Runtime -Project <dir> -ScreenshotAt 2s,5s -FixedStep 60
scripts\dev\Run.ps1 -App Runtime -Project <dir> -InputScript Tests\level5.json -Exec "physics.debug on"
```

Engine contributors and agents can drive runs from `scripts\dev\Run.ps1`:

- Every run starts with `--background`, so test windows never pull focus from what you are doing; `-Foreground` turns that off.
- Its runtime runs use the player-data profile `agent` unless `-RealPrefs` is passed.
- With `-ScreenshotAt`, `-InputScript` or `-QuitAt` the game takes its own screenshots into a new `bin-int\_agent\run\shots-<time>-<pid>\` folder and quits by itself.
- Without a quit step, it quits half a second after the last screenshot.

# 3D

Funke started as a 2D engine. This page covers the 3D foundation: what exists, how it fits next to 2D, and what is still missing.

## Components

| Component | Fields | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Transform 3D** (`Transform3D`) | Position, Rotation (Euler degrees: X pitch, Y yaw, Z roll), Scale | Local to the parent's Transform 3D. Conflicts with Transform 2D and Rect Transform 2D. |
| **Camera 3D** (`Camera3D`) | Projection (Perspective / Orthographic), Field Of View (vertical, degrees), Orthographic Size, Near Clip, Far Clip, Background (Skybox / Solid Color), Clear Color, Skybox Material, Sky Top / Sky Horizon / Sky Ground, Sun Size, Sky Ambient, Ambient From Skybox, Fog, Fog Color, Fog Start, Fog End | Looks down its local −Z axis. The first enabled Camera 3D of the loaded scenes renders the game. See [Sky](#sky) and [Fog](#fog). |
| **Mesh Renderer** (`MeshRenderer`) | Mesh (Cube, Sphere, Plane, Cylinder), Material, Color, Lit, Cast Shadows | Built-in primitives, 1 unit in size. Plane lies flat (XZ) and faces +Y. Color tints the material. Lit only applies without a material. |
| **Skinned Mesh Renderer** (`SkinnedMeshRenderer`) | Model, Material, Color, Lit, Cast Shadows, Clip, Speed, Loop, Play On Awake, Preview In Edit Mode, Culling Mode, Distance Rate, Half / Quarter Rate From | Draws an animated glTF model and plays one of its clips. See [Skeletal animation](#skeletal-animation). Can't share an entity with a Mesh Renderer. |
| **Directional Light** (`DirectionalLight`) | Color, Intensity, Ambient, Cast Shadows | Shines along its local −Z axis. The first enabled one is the *main* light: its Ambient is the flat ambient, it draws the sun disc and it is the only light that casts shadows. |
| **Point Light** (`PointLight`) | Color, Intensity (default 4), Range (default 10) | Shines in all directions from its position and fades to zero at Range. |
| **Spot Light** (`SpotLight`) | Color, Intensity (default 6), Range (default 15), Inner Angle (default 20°), Outer Angle (default 30°) | Cone along its local −Z axis; full intensity inside Inner Angle, fading to zero at Outer Angle (both half angles). |

Every 3D component needs a Transform 3D; the editor adds it when you add them from **Add Component**. An entity holds at most one light component. A scene without any light component gets a default light from above, so meshes are never black.

World matrices come from `Transform3DHierarchySystem`, which runs before the scripts every frame. A child of an entity without a Transform 3D (for example an empty grouping entity) still inherits the transform of the nearest ancestor that has one.

Scene JSON keys: `Transform3D` (`posX/posY/posZ`, `rotX/rotY/rotZ`, `scaleX/scaleY/scaleZ`), `Camera3D` (`projection`, `fov`, `orthoSize`, `near`, `far`, `background`, `clearColor`, `skyTop`, `skyHorizon`, `skyGround`, `sunSize`, `skyAmbient`, `fog`, `fogColor`, `fogStart`, `fogEnd`), `MeshRenderer` (`mesh` 0–3, `customMesh`, `material`, `color`, `lit`, `castShadows`), `SkinnedMeshRenderer` (`model`, `material`, `color`, `lit`, `castShadows`, `clip`, `speed`, `loop`, `playOnAwake`, `previewInEditMode`, and only when changed `cullingMode`, `distanceRate`, `halfRateDistance`, `quarterRateDistance`), `DirectionalLight` (`color`, `intensity`, `ambient`, `castShadows`), `PointLight` (`color`, `intensity`, `range`), `SpotLight` (`color`, `intensity`, `range`, `innerAngle`, `outerAngle`). Missing keys take the defaults, so scenes saved before these fields existed still load.

## Materials

A material is a `.material` asset: a small JSON file with a GUID in its `.meta`, like every other asset. Its **Shader** field can pick your own `.wgsl` shader instead of the standard PBR shader described here; see [Custom Shaders](Custom-Shaders.md). Create one with **Create → Material** in the Asset Browser, select it to edit it in the Inspector (every change is saved to the file right away), and drag it onto a Mesh Renderer's **Material** slot or pick it there.

| Field | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Lit | on | Off ignores lights, exposure and tone mapping and shows Base Color (plus emissive) exactly. |
| Surface | Opaque | **Transparent** blends the surface over what is behind it (see [Transparency](#transparency)). |
| Base Color | white | sRGB color; its alpha is the opacity of a Transparent material. |
| Base Color Texture | none | Texture asset multiplied into Base Color; sampled with repeat wrapping (point filtering if the texture's import filter is Point, linear otherwise). |
| Metallic | 0 | 0 = plastic/wood/stone, 1 = metal. |
| Roughness | 0.5 | 0 = mirror-like highlight, 1 = fully matte. |
| Emissive Color / Intensity | black / 1 | Light the surface gives off itself (not lighting other objects). |
| Tiling / Offset | (1,1) / (0,0) | UV scale and shift of the texture. |

On disk (`Assets/Materials/Gold.material`):

```json
{
  "type": "Material", "version": 1, "lit": true, "surface": 0,
  "baseColor": { "r": 1.0, "g": 0.78, "b": 0.34, "a": 1.0 },
  "baseColorTexture": "0",
  "metallic": 1.0, "roughness": 0.3,
  "emissiveColor": { "r": 0, "g": 0, "b": 0, "a": 1 }, "emissiveIntensity": 1.0,
  "tiling": { "x": 1, "y": 1 }, "offset": { "x": 0, "y": 0 }
}
```

GUIDs (`baseColorTexture` here, `material` in the scene) are written as decimal strings. All Mesh Renderers that use a material share it: editing the file (in the editor or outside it) updates all of them. A Mesh Renderer without a material uses a white default material (metallic 0, roughness 0.5) tinted by its Color, and its own Lit flag. Build asset pruning keeps every material a shipped scene references and every texture such a material references.

### Transparency

A material with **Surface = Transparent** (`"surface": 1`) is alpha blended. Its opacity is Base Color alpha × texture alpha × the Mesh Renderer's Color alpha, so one glass material can be made more or less see-through per renderer. Transparent meshes are drawn after all opaque ones, sorted per object from the farthest to the nearest (by the centre of the mesh bounds), with depth testing but without writing depth. Lighting, emissive and unlit materials work as for opaque surfaces. Lit transparent surfaces follow Fresnel: reflected light is not filtered by the transparency, so the surface turns more opaque and mirror-like at grazing angles — a low roughness (≈ 0.03) gives water and glass a clear sky reflection.

Limits: sorting is per object, so two transparent meshes that intersect, or one large concave transparent mesh, can show parts in the wrong order. Only front faces are drawn. A transparent mesh with **Cast Shadows** on casts a full (opaque) shadow; turn it off for glass.

## Custom meshes

Besides the built-in primitives a Mesh Renderer can draw a mesh asset: drop a Wavefront `.obj` or a glTF 2.0 file (`.gltf`, `.glb`) into `Assets/` and pick it in the renderer's **Custom Mesh** slot (`"customMesh": "<guid>"` in the scene). While a custom mesh is set the primitive **Mesh** field is ignored; clearing the slot draws the primitive again.

- glTF: every triangle mesh of the file's scene is merged into one mesh, placed by its node transforms. A Mesh Renderer draws an animated model in its rest pose; use a [Skinned Mesh Renderer](#skeletal-animation) to play it. Buffers can be embedded (`.glb`, base64 `data:` URIs) or separate files next to the `.gltf`. Materials, textures, cameras, lights and morph targets in the file are ignored — assign a `.material` as usual.
- Read from an OBJ file: positions, texture coordinates and normals (`v`, `vt`, `vn`, `f`); faces with more than three corners are triangulated, negative (relative) indices work, and all objects and groups in the file become one mesh. Materials (`mtllib`, `usemtl`), lines and points are ignored — assign a `.material` as usual.
- Missing normals are computed as smooth normals per position; missing texture coordinates are 0.
- Faces should wind counter-clockwise seen from outside (the OBJ convention); back faces are culled. The mesh keeps the file's units and origin — scale it with the Transform 3D.
- A file that cannot be read draws nothing and logs a warning; fixing the file reloads it, and edits made outside the editor reload live. Picking, the selection box and **F** (frame) use the mesh's bounds.
- **Mesh Collider 3D** collides with the custom mesh of the entity's Mesh Renderer (**Use Mesh Renderer**), or with its own **Custom Mesh**.

### Meshes built from code

`Mesh.Create()` returns an empty in-memory mesh for geometry a script computes: procedural terrain, a water surface from a fluid simulation, trails. Fill it with `SetData` and assign it like a mesh asset:

```csharp
Mesh surface = Mesh.Create();
GetComponent<MeshRenderer>()!.CustomMesh = surface;

// Any time, as often as every frame: replaces the whole geometry.
surface.SetData(positions, indices);              // ReadOnlySpan<Vector3>, ReadOnlySpan<int> (triangle list)
surface.SetData(positions, indices, normals, uvs); // optional per-vertex normals and UVs
```

- Positions are in the entity's local space; indices are a triangle list wound counter-clockwise seen from outside (back faces are culled). Without normals, smooth normals are computed from the triangles; without UVs they are 0.
- `SetData` throws `ArgumentException` when normals/UVs don't match the vertex count or an index is out of range, and `InvalidOperationException` on a mesh asset or a destroyed mesh. `Clear()` removes all geometry (the renderer draws nothing), `Destroy()` frees the mesh; runtime meshes still alive when Play mode ends are freed then. `IsRuntime` tells them apart from `.obj` assets.
- Rewriting a mesh every frame is cheap: its GPU buffers only grow and are rewritten in place. Lists of vertices can be passed without copying via `CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan(list)`.
- Runtime meshes are not saved: a scene stores the renderer's primitive **Mesh**, so author a placeholder primitive (e.g. a Plane where the water will be) for the Editor View and assign the runtime mesh in `OnStart`.
- A Mesh Collider 3D can use a runtime mesh too; it rebuilds its shape whenever the geometry changes, which is expensive for large meshes updated every frame.

Build asset pruning keeps referenced mesh and skinned-model assets, including external buffer files used by glTF models.

## Skeletal animation

A **Skinned Mesh Renderer** draws an animated glTF model (`.glb` or `.gltf`, exported for example from Blender with *Skinning* and *Animation* enabled) and plays its clips:

1. Drop the model into `Assets/` and pick it in **Model**. The inspector lists the model's clips under **Pick Clip** with their length, plus its vertex, node, joint and clip counts.
2. Leave **Clip** empty to play the first clip, or pick or type a clip name. **Speed** scales playback (negative plays backwards), **Loop** repeats the clip, otherwise it holds its last frame.
3. **Play On Awake** starts the clip when Play begins. In edit mode the renderer shows the clip's first frame; **Preview In Edit Mode** plays it in the editor too.

How it works:

- Skins (up to four joint weights per vertex) and node animation both animate: rigid parts parented to an animated node (a robot arm, a door) move with that node. Translation, rotation and scale channels are read with Linear, Step and Cubic Spline interpolation.
- Animation poses and joint matrices are evaluated on the CPU; vertex skinning uses a GPU compute pass when the model fits the device's limits, with a CPU fallback. The posed mesh goes through the regular mesh pass, so materials, custom shaders, transparency, fog and shadows work as on a Mesh Renderer. A model is re-posed only when its pose changes. Profile the actual model and character count on the target device.
- **Culling Mode** and **Distance Rate** work as on the Animator (see [Animation > Culling and distance rate](Animation.md#culling-and-distance-rate)): off screen (Cull Pose) or far from the camera, the model keeps its last skinned pose and is re-skinned only on its update frames, every 2nd or 4th frame. The play head itself keeps the exact time, so `Time`, `IsPlaying` and the end of a one-shot clip stay right for scripts. Off screen means outside the camera's view with the model's rest-pose bounds plus a margin.
- Picking, the selection box and **F** use the bounds of the pose the model is drawn in (the clip's first frame in edit mode, the current frame while it plays).

From a script:

```csharp
public class PlayerAnimation : EntityScript
{
    private SkinnedMeshRenderer? m_Model;

    public override void OnStart() => m_Model = GetComponent<SkinnedMeshRenderer>();

    public override void OnUpdate()
    {
        bool moving = Input.GetAxis().Length() > 0.1f;
        m_Model!.Play(moving ? "Run" : "Idle", crossFade: 0.2f);
    }
}
```

`Play(clip, crossFade = 0.2f)` blends from the current pose to the new clip over `crossFade` seconds; calling it again for the clip that is already playing does nothing, so it is safe to call every frame. `Pause()`, `Resume()` and `Stop()` (back to the first frame) control playback; `Clip`, `IsPlaying`, `Time`, `Speed`, `Loop`, `PlayOnAwake`, `ClipNames` and `GetClipLength(name)` read or change it. `TryGetBone("Hand.R", out position, out forward, out up)` returns a bone's (or any model node's) world position and axes in the drawn pose, e.g. to place a sword in a hand every frame; while culling or the distance rate holds the pose back, the bone stays with the drawn model. `Model`, `Material`, `Color`, `Lit` and `CastShadows` work like on a Mesh Renderer; `CullingMode`, `DistanceRate`, `HalfRateDistance` and `QuarterRateDistance` like on the Animator.

## Lights and shading

Lighting is physically based (GGX/Cook-Torrance specular with Lambert diffuse) and runs in linear color space: colors you pick are sRGB and converted before lighting. A white light with intensity 1 lights a white surface facing it to full brightness.

- **Directional lights** have no falloff. **Point and spot lights** fall off with the inverse square of the distance, smoothly windowed so they reach exactly zero at Range. Intensity is therefore "brightness at about one unit away"; raise it or the range for larger rooms.
- **Ambient:** the main directional light's Ambient color is added everywhere. With a sky background, the sky colors add hemispheric ambient (top color from above, ground color from below), scaled by the camera's **Sky Ambient**; metals reflect the sky with it. With a Skybox Material, **Ambient From Skybox** takes these colors from the material instead: a Gradient Sky's top/horizon/ground colors, the averaged upper, middle and lower band of a Panoramic Sky's image (× tint × exposure), or a 6-Sided Sky's up, side and down faces (× their colors × exposure). Texture averages are computed once per texture (`ambientFromSkybox` in scenes).
- **Light limit:** each frame uses at most **Max Lights** lights (Project Settings → Graphics → 3D Rendering, default 16, at most 64). Directional lights come first, then the point and spot lights whose range is closest to the camera.
- **Shadows:** the main directional light casts shadows from every Mesh Renderer with **Cast Shadows** on, onto everything within **Shadow Distance** of the camera (default 40 units). The shadow map is soft-edged (3×3 PCF) and fades out at the distance limit. **Shadow Quality** picks the map size (Off, Low 1024, Medium 2048, High 4096). Point and spot lights do not cast shadows.
- **Exposure** and **Tone Mapping** (None, Reinhard, ACES — default ACES) map the lit result to the screen. They do not affect unlit materials or the sky.

## Sky

New Camera 3Ds use **Background = Skybox**: a procedural gradient (Sky Top above, Sky Horizon at the horizon, Sky Ground below) drawn behind all meshes, with a sun disc in the direction of the main directional light, tinted by its color. **Sun Size** is the disc's angular radius in degrees (0 hides it). No texture is needed. **Solid Color** clears to Clear Color instead and also turns off the sky ambient.

**Skybox Material:** assign a `.material` whose shader targets `Skybox` and the camera draws it instead of the gradient (the gradient colors still drive the sky ambient). **Create → Skybox Shader** in the Project panel writes one of three ready-made shaders into the folder:

| Shader | What it shows |
|---|---|
| **Gradient Sky** | The gradient above as a material (top / horizon / ground, curve, sun on or off) |
| **6-Sided Sky** | A cube: per face (front = −Z, back, left, right, up, down) a texture times a color, so a face can be a plain color; rotation and exposure |
| **Panoramic Sky** | An equirectangular (2:1) image around the camera with tint, rotation, exposure and an optional sun |

Then create a material, pick the shader, set its values, and drop the material into the camera's **Skybox Material** (from C#: `Camera3D.SkyboxMaterial`; changing the material's properties with `Material.SetFloat`/`SetColor`/... animates the sky). Your own sky shaders work the same way (see [Custom Shaders](Custom-Shaders.md#skybox)). A material without a Skybox shader shows a magenta sky.

Cameras saved before the sky existed have a `clearColor` but no `background` key; they load as **Solid Color**, so existing scenes look the same. New cameras, cameras whose component is reset, and cameras created from **3D Entity → Camera 3D** use the sky.

## Fog

Enable **Fog** on the Camera 3D to fade meshes into **Fog Color** with distance: nothing changes closer than **Fog Start**, and from **Fog End** on a surface is fully fog colored (smooth in between, measured from the camera in world units). Use it to hide the far end of a long level or to give depth to a valley; a fog color close to the sky's horizon color blends the level into the sky. The fog is applied after lighting and tone mapping, to lit and unlit materials, opaque and transparent ones. The sky and skybox materials are not fogged.

Untick **Fog** on a material (`"fog": false` in the `.material`) for meshes that should stay clear at any distance, e.g. a sky dome mesh, distant scenery that already has the sky's colors, or glowing goal markers. Fog is off on new cameras and on cameras saved before it existed.

```csharp
var cam = Camera3D.Main;
cam.FogEnabled = true;
cam.FogColor = new Color(0.73f, 0.83f, 0.93f, 1f);
cam.FogStart = 40f;
cam.FogEnd = 160f;
```

## Particles

**Particle System 3D** (`ParticleSystem3D`, needs a Transform 3D) emits camera-facing billboards. Create one with **3D Entity → Particle System 3D** or add the component to any 3D entity.

| Group | Fields |
|---|---|
| Particles | Play On Awake, Life Time, Speed, Size (edge length in world units), Life Time / Speed / Size **Variation** (0–1: each particle gets base × (1 ± variation)), Random Rotation, Angular Velocity (°/s), Use Gravity + Gravity (world space), Drag (fraction of velocity lost per second), Random Colors |
| Emission | Emit Over Time (particles per second, fractions accumulate), Simulation Space, **Bursts** (Count every Interval seconds, the first one right after Play) |
| Shape | **Sphere**, **Hemisphere**, **Cone** or **Box**; Radius, Cone Angle (half angle), Box Size, Emit From Surface. Cone and Hemisphere open along the entity's local **+Y**, Box emits along +Y, Sphere outwards. The shape follows the Transform 3D's rotation and scale. |
| Over Lifetime | **Scale over Lifetime** (curve) and **Color over Lifetime** (gradient, multiplied into the start color; fade out with alpha keys) |
| Rendering | Texture (none = soft round dots), Color, **Blend Mode** (Alpha for smoke and dust, Additive for fire, sparks and magic), Max Particles |

**Simulation Space World** leaves particles where they were emitted when the entity moves (trails, smoke); **Local** carries them with the entity. Particles are unlit, depth tested against meshes and drawn after all meshes; Alpha particles are sorted back to front within their system, systems are sorted by distance. The project's **Particle Quality** setting scales emission and the particle limit like it does in 2D.

In the Editor View a selected particle system shows its shape and a **Play / Restart / Stop** overlay that previews the effect without entering play mode; idle emitters show a small marker. In play mode and in games, systems with Play On Awake start by themselves (also when spawned from a prefab).

```json
"ParticleSystem3D": {
  "lifetime": 1.2, "speed": 2.5, "size": 0.4, "emitOverTime": 120,
  "shape": 2, "radius": 0.25, "coneAngle": 12,
  "color": { "r": 1, "g": 0.55, "b": 0.15, "a": 1 }, "blendMode": 1,
  "colorOverLifetimeEnabled": true,
  "colorOverLifetimeAlphaKeys": [ { "t": 0, "a": 1 }, { "t": 1, "a": 0 } ],
  "bursts": [ { "count": 30, "interval": 2 } ],
  "texture": "7100000000000000001"
}
```

Enum values in scene files: `shape` 0 Sphere, 1 Hemisphere, 2 Cone, 3 Box; `simulationSpace` 0 Local, 1 World; `blendMode` 0 Alpha, 1 Additive. Missing keys use the defaults. Curves and gradients use the same keys as Particle System 2D (`scaleOverLifetimeKeys`, `colorOverLifetimeColorKeys`, `colorOverLifetimeAlphaKeys`).

## Rendering

`Renderer3D` is a forward renderer on the same WebGPU backend as the 2D renderer. Per frame it:

1. clears the screen to the main Camera 3D's clear color and draws the sky if its background is Skybox,
2. renders the shadow map of the main directional light (if enabled),
3. draws every opaque Mesh Renderer with depth testing, instanced per (mesh, texture) pair with the material values per instance, lit by up to Max Lights lights, then the transparent ones back to front with alpha blending,
4. draws the Particle System 3D billboards (depth tested, not depth writing),
5. hands over to the 2D renderer, which draws sprites, particles and world text on top (without clearing), followed by UI.

A scene can therefore mix a 3D world with a 2D HUD: the scene's Camera 2D draws the 2D layer with its own orthographic projection (Orthographic Size, position), unaffected by the Camera 3D. When a scene has a Camera 3D, no default Camera 2D is created for it, so add one for a HUD made of sprites.

**MSAA 4x** renders the 3D scene into a multisampled target and resolves it before the 2D layer and UI. **FXAA** is also available. A Post Processing component on the Camera 3D applies the shared post-processing effects, including custom WGSL effects, to the 3D image. See [Graphics Settings](Graphics-Settings.md#anti-aliasing) and [Custom Shaders](Custom-Shaders.md).

## Editor

- **3D toggle** (Editor View toolbar, top right): switches the scene camera. 3D projects start in 3D mode; once toggled, the choice is saved per project (`editorView3D` in `project.json`).
- **Camera:** hold the right mouse button to orbit (add **W/A/S/D** to fly, **Q/E** down/up, **Shift** faster), hold the middle mouse button to pan, use the wheel to zoom, press **F** to frame the selected entity (also while the Entities or Inspector panel has focus).
- **Selection:** click a mesh, camera or light, or a sprite or UI element (they are drawn on the z = 0 plane, over the meshes, and win the click). Clicking the same spot again selects the next entity behind it. Ctrl/Shift-click toggles. The orange selection box surrounds every mesh the entity and its enabled children draw, turned with the entity, so selecting a character's root (an empty parent of its model) frames the whole character; **F** frames the same box. An entity that draws nothing, such as a light or an empty, gets a small box at its origin. A selected 2D entity gets an outline on that plane, and **F** frames it.
- **Gizmo:** the Move / Rotate / Scale tools work in 3D. Snapping uses the grid, rotation and scale snap settings; hold **Left Ctrl** to snap temporarily. Every drag is one undo step.
- **Create menu:** **3D Entity** offers Empty, Cube, Sphere, Plane, Cylinder, Camera 3D, Directional Light, Point Light, Spot Light and Particle System 3D. In 3D mode, **Create (Entity)** and **Camera** create 3D entities.
- **Collider gizmos:** the selected entity's 3D colliders are outlined in green (triggers in light blue): boxes, spheres and capsules as their physics shape, mesh colliders as their triangle edges (a convex custom mesh or a mesh over 20,000 triangles as its bounds). The outlines stay visible inside and behind meshes, faded where they are hidden.
- **Particle gizmos:** the selected Particle System 3D shows its emission shape (sphere, hemisphere, cone or box) and a Play / Restart / Stop overlay for an edit-mode preview.
- **Light gizmos:** point lights show a small sphere and, while selected, their range sphere; spot lights show their cone (to their range while selected, with the inner angle).
- **Camera gizmo:** a selected Camera 3D shows its view volume from Near Clip to Far Clip at the Game View's aspect ratio (perspective: a frustum, orthographic: a box of Orthographic Size half height). Other cameras show a short piece of it with a triangle on top marking the camera's up side.
- **Sky:** the Editor View shows the background and sky ambient of the scene's main Camera 3D (a grey background when the scene has none, and in prefab edit mode).
- **Game View** renders through the scene's Camera 3D; a Camera 2D draws the 2D layer over it exactly as in builds (also in `funke editor screenshot` and the project preview).

## Scripting

```csharp
public class Mover : EntityScript
{
    private Transform3D? m_Transform;

    public override void OnStart() => m_Transform = GetComponent<Transform3D>();

    public override void OnUpdate()
    {
        Vector2 input = Input.GetAxis();
        m_Transform!.Position += new Vector3(input.X, 0.0f, -input.Y) * (4.0f * Time.DeltaTime);
    }
}
```

`Transform3D` exposes `Position`, `Rotation`, `Scale`, `WorldPosition` and `Forward`. `Camera3D.Main` returns the active 3D camera; `Camera3D` also has `Background`, `SkyTopColor`, `SkyHorizonColor`, `SkyGroundColor`, `SunSize`, `SkyAmbient`, `AmbientFromSkybox`, `SkyboxMaterial` (a `Material` or null for the gradient, e.g. `camera.SkyboxMaterial = AssetManager.Load<Material>("Materials/Night.material")`) and `FogEnabled`, `FogColor`, `FogStart`, `FogEnd`. `MeshRenderer` has `Mesh` (a `PrimitiveMesh`), `CustomMesh` (a `Mesh` asset or null), `Material`, `Color`, `Lit` and `CastShadows`. A `Mesh` (`AssetManager.Load<Mesh>("Meshes/Rock.obj")`) reports `IsValid`, `VertexCount`, `TriangleCount`, `BoundsMin` and `BoundsMax`. `PointLight` (`Color`, `Intensity`, `Range`) and `SpotLight` (plus `InnerAngle`, `OuterAngle`) work like `DirectionalLight` (`Color`, `Intensity`, `Ambient`, `CastShadows`).

```csharp
Material? gold = AssetManager.Load<Material>("Materials/Gold.material");
GetComponent<MeshRenderer>()!.Material = gold;
gold!.EmissiveIntensity = 2.0f;           // shared: every renderer using Gold changes, the file does not
RenderSettings.ShadowQuality = ShadowQualityLevel.High;
RenderSettings.Exposure = 1.2f;
```

```csharp
var sparks = GetComponent<ParticleSystem3D>()!;
sparks.Emit(60);                              // one-shot, works while stopped; uses the emitter's current position
sparks.BlendMode = ParticleBlendMode3D.Additive;
sparks.Texture = AssetManager.Load<Texture>("Textures/Spark.png");
```

`ParticleSystem3D` has `Play`, `Pause`, `Stop` (stops emitting, live particles finish), `Restart`, `Clear`, `Emit(count)`, `IsPlaying`, `ParticleCount`, and the properties `LifeTime`, `Speed`, `Size`, `EmitOverTime`, `Color`, `UseGravity`, `Gravity`, `Drag`, `AngularVelocity`, `MaxParticles`, `PlayOnAwake`, `BlendMode`, `SimulationSpace`, `Shape`, `Radius`, `ConeAngle` and `Texture`. Curves, gradients and bursts are authored in the Inspector or the scene file.

`Material` properties (`BaseColor`, `BaseColorTexture`, `Metallic`, `Roughness`, `EmissiveColor`, `EmissiveIntensity`, `Lit`, `Surface`, `Tiling`, `Offset`) change the live shared material and are not saved. `RenderSettings` (and `GraphicsSettings`) also carry `ShadowDistance`, `MaxLights` and `ToneMapping`, and the animation distance rate (`AnimationDistanceRateEnabled`, `AnimationHalfRateDistance`, `AnimationQuarterRateDistance`). Texture quality, anisotropic filtering and anti-aliasing work in 2D and 3D: see [Graphics Settings](Graphics-Settings.md).

## Not available yet

- FBX models, materials and textures from glTF files, morph targets (blend shapes), and animation layers/masks. OBJ and glTF meshes, skeletal animation, and GPU skinning with CPU fallback are supported.
- Dedicated normal/metallic/roughness maps and alpha-cutout settings in the standard material, and per-triangle transparency sorting. Custom WGSL shaders can implement their own surface shading.
- Shadows from point and spot lights, cascaded shadow maps, and environment-cubemap reflections. Gradient, panoramic and six-sided skybox materials are supported.
- Lit, soft (depth-faded), stretched or mesh particles, particle collisions, sub-emitters and GPU simulation.
- A complete quaternion API in C#; Transform 3D rotations use Euler degrees.

Spatial audio is available through Audio Sources and `Audio.PlayOneShotAt`. 3D physics is covered in [Physics 3D](Physics-3D.md).

# Animation

The **Animator** component plays keyframe animations on an entity and its children. A clip can animate any component property the Inspector shows (position, rotation, scale, colors, light intensity, UI rects, sprites ...) and the visible fields of C# scripts. An **Animator Controller** switches between clips with a state machine driven by parameters that scripts set.

For flip-book sprite animation, assign a looping clip directly to the Animator and switch slices with a discrete **Sprite Renderer > Texture** track.

## The pieces

| Asset / component | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Animation Clip** (`.anim`) | Tracks of keyframes over time, plus animation events. |
| **Animator Controller** (`.animctrl`) | States (each plays a clip), parameters and transitions with conditions. |
| **Animator** (component) | Plays a controller, or a single clip when it has no controller. Its entity is the root that track paths start from. |

Create clips and controllers from the Project panel (**Create > Animation > Animation Clip / Animator Controller**), or from the Animation window: select an entity and click **Create Clip...** (or **New Clip...** in the clip selector). A save dialog asks where to put the `.anim`; it opens next to the clip being edited, or in `Assets/`, and only accepts folders inside `Assets/`. The window then adds an Animator if needed and assigns the clip. A second clip on the same Animator creates a controller with one state per clip, saved next to the new clip. **Create Controller...** in the Animator window works the same way for `.animctrl` files.

### Animator fields

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Controller** | The `.animctrl` to play. Wins over Clip. |
| **Clip** | A `.anim` played on its own (looping per its Loop setting) when there is no controller. |
| **Speed** | Playback speed multiplier. 0 freezes the pose. |
| **Update Mode** | **Normal** follows `Time.TimeScale`; **Unscaled Time** keeps playing while the game is paused; **Fixed** steps in the fixed update, in sync with physics. |
| **Apply In Edit Mode** | Plays the animation in the editor without pressing Play. The scene keeps its authored values: saving never stores an animated value. |
| **Culling Mode** | What happens outside the game camera's view: **Always Animate** (default), **Cull Pose** or **Cull Completely**. See [Culling and distance rate](#culling-and-distance-rate). |
| **Distance Rate** | Fewer updates far from the camera: **Project Setting** (default), **Off** or **Custom** with the component's own **Half Rate From** and **Quarter Rate From**. |

The Animator runs after the scripts each frame, so parameters a script sets in `OnUpdate` take effect in the same frame, and before 3D physics reads kinematic bodies.

## What can be animated

- **Component properties:** every property with a field in the Inspector. Numbers, booleans, vectors and colors use curves, and each vector or color channel is its own track (`Position.x`, `Color.a`). Booleans and integers step from key to key.
- **Assets, text and enums** (a sprite texture, a material, a text) use **discrete keys** that switch the value at each key time.
- **Sprite-sheet slices:** the **Texture** property of a Sprite Renderer or Image holds the texture together with its slice, so a Texture track switches between slices of one sheet. With **Record** on, pick another slice in the Inspector's Texture field (it shows `Sheet > Slice`); each pick becomes a key.
- **Rect Transform 2D:** Anchored Position, Size, Pivot, anchors, Rotation (degrees) and Scale.
- **C# script fields:** the public or `[ShowInEditor]` fields of scripts on the animated entities (`float`, `int`, `bool`, `Vector2/3/4`, `Color`). The script must be on the entity when the Animator starts.
- **Rotations** are animated as Euler angles in degrees, per axis.

Tracks address their entity by a path of child names from the Animator's entity (`"Arm/Hand"`; empty for the Animator's own entity). Renaming a child breaks the path: the Animator then skips that track and logs one warning, and the Animation window shows the track in the warning color.

## Animation window

**Tools > Animation**, or double-click a `.anim` in the Project panel. It edits the clips of the selected Animator, or of the nearest parent that has one. Choosing a time in the window previews that pose in the Editor View and the Inspector without changing the scene.

**Toolbar:** Record, previous key, preview playback (Space), next key, the current time and frame, the clip selector (with **New Clip...**), **Dopesheet / Curves**, the clip's **Length**, **Samples** (the frame rate of the key grid) and **Loop**.

**Creating keys**

- **Record** (the red dot): while it is on, every change to an entity below the Animator becomes a key at the current time. The change can come from the Inspector or a gizmo drag. A property that is keyed for the first time also gets a key with its old value at time 0. Record changes go into the clip; the scene keeps its values.
- **Add Property...** lists the animatable properties and script fields of the Animator's entities and adds tracks with keys at the start and end.
- Drag the value next to a track to key it at the current time.
- Double-click a track row to add a key there; **K** keys the selected tracks (or all) at the current time.

**Editing keys:** click to select (Ctrl adds), drag to move them (they snap to the sample grid; hold Shift to move freely), drag on empty space for a box selection, **Delete** removes them. Right-click a key for **Smooth**, **Flat**, **Linear** and **Constant** interpolation.

**Curves** shows the curves of the selected tracks, or all of them when no track is selected. Drag keys in time and value. Drag a smooth key's tangent handles to shape it; hold Ctrl to break the two tangents apart. **F** frames everything. The mouse wheel zooms time, Shift+wheel zooms values, and the middle mouse button pans.

**Navigation:** Ctrl+wheel (Cmd+wheel on macOS) zooms the dopesheet, Shift+wheel scrolls in time, a click on the ruler moves the playhead, `,` / `.` step one frame, and Home / End jump to the start / end. Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y (Cmd+Z / Cmd+Shift+Z on macOS) undo and redo clip edits while the window has focus. Every edit is saved to the `.anim` file at once.

### Animation events

The row above the tracks holds events. Double-click it (or right-click > **Add Event**) to add one, then drag it in time. Double-click or right-click an event to set its **Function** and **Argument**. During playback the event calls that public method on every script of the Animator's entity:

```csharp
public class Footsteps : EntityScript
{
    public Audio? Step;

    // Event: Function "OnFootstep", Argument "left"
    public void OnFootstep(string foot) => Step?.PlayOneShot();
}
```

The method may take no parameter or one `string`, `int`, `float` or `bool`; the Argument text is converted to it. An event whose method no script has logs one warning. Events fire on every loop, and during a crossfade they fire for both clips.

## Animator window

**Tools > Animator**, or double-click a `.animctrl`. It shows the controller of the selected Animator, or the one you opened.

- **States:** right-click the canvas > **Create State**, or drop a `.anim` from the Project panel onto it. Select a state to edit its name, clip, speed and loop mode (**From Clip**, **Loop**, **Once**) on the right. The orange arrow from **Entry** marks the default state; change it with right-click > **Set as Default State**. Double-click a state to edit its clip in the Animation window.
- **Transitions:** right-click a state (or **Any State**) > **Make Transition**, then click the target. Select a transition to edit it:
  - **Has Exit Time / Exit Time:** waits until the source state has played that far, in clip lengths (0.75 = three quarters through; with looping states it fires each time the loop passes that point).
  - **Duration:** crossfade length in seconds. Properties that both clips animate blend; properties only one of them animates blend from or to their current value.
  - **Conditions:** all must hold. Floats and ints compare with Greater / Less (ints also Equals / Not Equal); bools test True / False; triggers fire when set and are reset by the transition that used them.
  - **Can Transition To Self** (Any State only) lets the transition restart the state that is already playing.
  - A transition without conditions fires at its exit time, or immediately when it has none.
- **Any State** transitions are checked before the current state's own, every frame, except while a crossfade is running.
- **Parameters** (left): **+** adds Float, Int, Bool or Trigger; the value next to each is its start value. Renaming a parameter updates the conditions that use it; deleting it removes them.
- In Play mode, select the playing entity: the window marks the active state with its progress, highlights a running transition, and the parameter column shows live values you can change.

Drag nodes to arrange them, drag the empty canvas (or use the middle mouse button) to pan, use the wheel to zoom, and press **F** to frame everything. **Delete** or **Backspace** removes the selection; Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y (Cmd+Z / Cmd+Shift+Z on macOS) undo and redo.

## Scripting

```csharp
public class Player : EntityScript
{
    private Animator? m_Animator;

    public override void OnStart() => m_Animator = GetComponent<Animator>();

    public override void OnUpdate()
    {
        m_Animator!.SetBool("IsRunning", Input.GetAxis().X != 0f);
        if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space)) m_Animator.SetTrigger("Jump");
    }
}
```

| Member | |
|---|---|
| `SetFloat/GetFloat`, `SetInteger/GetInteger`, `SetBool/GetBool` | Parameters by name. A name that doesn't exist (or has another type) logs one warning. |
| `SetTrigger(name)`, `ResetTrigger(name)` | A trigger stays set until a transition that checks it fires. |
| `HasParameter(name)` | |
| `Play(state, normalizedTime = 0)` | Jumps to a state without blending. |
| `CrossFade(state, duration)` | Blends from the current pose to a state. |
| `CurrentStateName`, `NextStateName` | The playing state, and the target of a running crossfade (empty when none). |
| `NormalizedTime` | Time in the current state in clip lengths (1.5 = halfway through the second loop). |
| `IsInTransition`, `TransitionProgress` | The running crossfade and its 0..1 progress. |
| `Speed`, `Controller`, `Clip` | The component's fields; `Controller` / `Clip` take `AnimatorController` / `AnimationClip` assets. |
| `CullingMode`, `DistanceRate`, `HalfRateDistance`, `QuarterRateDistance` | See [Culling and distance rate](#culling-and-distance-rate) (`AnimationCullingMode`, `AnimationDistanceRate`). |

Script fields of type `AnimationClip` and `AnimatorController` show as asset slots in the Inspector, so a script can swap controllers (e.g. per character skin): `GetComponent<Animator>().Controller = Skins[i];`. `AssetManager.LoadByGUID<AnimationClip>(guid)` and `FindAll<AnimatorController>(...)` work as for other assets.

## Culling and distance rate

Animated characters cost time every frame, also when they are off screen or far away. Two options on the Animator, and the same two on the [Skinned Mesh Renderer](3D.md#skeletal-animation), let them skip that work. Both are off by default, so existing scenes animate exactly as before.

**Culling Mode** decides what happens while the animation is outside the game camera's view:

| Mode | Off screen |
|---|---|
| **Always Animate** (default) | Animates as usual. |
| **Cull Pose** | The clock, transitions and animation events keep running (at most every 4th frame), but no pose is written and no bones are computed. Back in view, the current pose is written at once, as if it had played all along. |
| **Cull Completely** | Pauses. Back in view it continues where it stopped. |

"In view" means that a renderer on the Animator's entity or its children (Mesh Renderer, Skinned Mesh Renderer, Sprite Renderer) is inside the view of the main camera: the first Camera 3D of the loaded scenes for 3D entities, the main Camera 2D for 2D entities. The test uses the renderers' bounds plus a margin for limbs that swing out between two checks, and it is repeated every few frames. An Animator without such a renderer below it (UI, lights) always counts as visible.

**Distance Rate** updates animations less often the farther they are from the camera:

| Distance from the camera (world units) | Updates |
|---|---|
| below **Half Rate From** | every frame |
| **Half Rate From** (default 20) up to **Quarter Rate From** | every 2nd frame (30 per second at 60 fps) |
| **Quarter Rate From** (default 40) and farther | every 4th frame |

- The time of the skipped frames is added to the next update, so the tempo, transition times and exit times stay the same, and no animation event is lost: an event that falls between two updates fires with the next one.
- The updates are spread over the frames, so far animations don't all update in the same frame.
- **Project Setting** (the default) follows **Project Settings > Graphics > Animation**: the **Distance Rate** switch (off by default) and its two distances (20 and 40 units). **Off** always updates every frame. **Custom** uses the component's own **Half Rate From** and **Quarter Rate From**.
- Animators in **Fixed** update mode ignore the distance rate: fewer, larger steps would change how the bodies they move behave in physics.

Tips:

- Turn the project's **Distance Rate** on for games with many animated characters, or from a quality menu: `RenderSettings.AnimationDistanceRateEnabled = true;`.
- Keep **Always Animate** where an animation matters off screen: a character whose shadow falls into view, a platform a physics body stands on, an Animator that moves the camera.
- In the editor the game camera decides, also while you watch the scene in the Editor View.
- The Profiler's **Animation** rows show the time of the Animators and Skinned Mesh Renderers and how many of them updated their pose in a frame.

Sprite animations played by an Animator (Texture tracks) also use its culling and distance rate.

## File formats

Both are JSON with a GUID in their `.meta`, like other assets, and can be written by hand or by tools. `funke validate` checks them: tracks need a component and a property, controller states must point at `.anim` files, transitions at existing states, and conditions at parameters. It also checks that an Animator's `controllerAsset` / `clipAsset` point at the right kind of file.

```json
{
  "type": "AnimationClip", "version": 1,
  "length": 1.0, "loop": true, "sampleRate": 60,
  "tracks": [
    { "path": "", "component": "Transform3D", "property": "Position.y",
      "keys": [ { "t": 0, "v": 1, "interp": "bezier" }, { "t": 0.5, "v": 1.6, "interp": "bezier", "in": 0, "out": 0 }, { "t": 1, "v": 1 } ] },
    { "path": "Arm", "component": "SpriteRenderer", "property": "Texture",
      "discrete": [ { "t": 0, "v": "7300000000000000001|slice|arm_0" }, { "t": 0.5, "v": "7300000000000000001|slice|arm_1" } ] }
  ],
  "events": [ { "t": 0.5, "function": "OnFootstep", "argument": "left" } ]
}
```

- `component` is the serialized component name (`Transform3D`, `Transform2D`, `RectTransform2D`, `SpriteRenderer`, `MeshRenderer`, `Image`, `PointLight` ...) or a C# script class name. `property` is the Inspector property name (case-insensitive), with `.x/.y/.z/.w` or `.r/.g/.b/.a` for one channel.
- `interp` is `linear` (default), `step` or `bezier`; `in` / `out` are the bezier tangents (value per second) and default to 0 (flat).
- Discrete values are written as in the Inspector's text form: asset GUIDs as decimal strings, a sprite-sheet slice as `"<texture GUID>|slice|<slice name>"` (a bare GUID shows the whole texture), enum values as numbers, vectors as `"x,y"`. The value field next to a discrete track in the Animation window shows and edits the same text. Sprite Renderer and Image have no separate `SpriteName` property; the slice is part of `Texture`.

```json
{
  "type": "AnimatorController", "version": 1,
  "parameters": [ { "name": "IsRunning", "type": "bool", "default": false }, { "name": "Jump", "type": "trigger" } ],
  "states": [ { "name": "Idle", "clip": "7200000000000000001", "speed": 1, "position": [0, 0] },
              { "name": "Run", "clip": "7200000000000000002", "speed": 1, "loop": "loop", "position": [260, 0] } ],
  "defaultState": "Idle",
  "transitions": [
    { "from": "Idle", "to": "Run", "conditions": [ { "parameter": "IsRunning", "mode": "if" } ], "hasExitTime": false, "duration": 0.2 },
    { "fromAny": true, "to": "Jump", "conditions": [ { "parameter": "Jump", "mode": "if" } ], "duration": 0.1 }
  ]
}
```

- Parameter `type`: `float`, `int`, `bool`, `trigger`. Condition `mode`: `greater`, `less`, `equals`, `notEquals` (with `threshold`), `if`, `ifNot`.
- State `loop`: `clip` (default, use the clip's Loop), `loop`, `once`.
- Transitions reference states by name; `"fromAny": true` makes an Any State transition.

In a scene the component is written as `"Animator": { "controllerAsset": "<guid>", "clipAsset": "<guid>", "speed": 1, "updateMode": 0, "applyInEditMode": false }`. `cullingMode` (0 Always Animate, 1 Cull Pose, 2 Cull Completely), `distanceRate` (0 Project Setting, 1 Off, 2 Custom), `halfRateDistance` and `quarterRateDistance` are only written when they differ from the defaults. Game builds ship the clips and controllers that scenes, controllers and scripts reference.

## Limits

- One layer per controller; there are no blend trees, avatar masks or root motion yet.
- Fields of C# `IComponent` structs can't be animated (fields of `EntityScript`s and managed `Component`s can).
- Crossfades blend each rotation axis separately (Euler angles), which can take a long way around when the angles differ by more than 180°.

# Engine Modules

Funke splits its world features into two optional engine modules. A project lists the ones it uses in `project.json`:

```json
"modules": [ "Funke.2D", "Funke.3D" ]
```

| Module | Contains |
|---|---|
| `Funke.2D` | Transform 2D, Sprite Renderer, Camera 2D, Particle System 2D, 2D physics (Box2D: Rigidbody 2D, colliders, `Physics2D`), world-space text on 2D entities, 2D picking |
| `Funke.3D` | Transform 3D, Camera 3D with sky, Mesh Renderer, materials and meshes, Directional/Point/Spot lights, Particle System 3D, 3D physics (Jolt: Rigidbody 3D, colliders, `Physics3D`) |

UI (Rect Transform 2D and every UI widget), text, images, Post Processing (on a Camera 2D or Camera 3D), audio, scripting, gizmos, input and assets belong to the engine core and are always available. A project may list one module, both, or none (a pure UI app).

## In the editor

The **Package Manager** lists the modules under **Engine Modules**, next to the packages: **Install** turns a module on, **Remove** turns it off. The editor then asks in its main window whether to reload now; **Later** keeps a "Reload pending" hint with a **Reload Now** button in the status bar until the reload happens. Project Settings only shows which modules are on and links there. From the command line, `funke package add Funke.3D` / `funke package remove Funke.3D` do the same.

Packages declare the modules they build on (`modules = { "Funke.2D" }` in `funke-package.lua`). Installing such a package turns those modules on as well, including the ones its dependencies need, and a module can't be removed while an installed package needs it. A package whose module is off is not loaded and the build stops with an error that names it.

The editor offers only the enabled modules:

- the Add Component menu and the **Create** menus (2D Entity, 3D Entity presets, Camera) list their components only while their module is on;
- the Editor View is fixed to 2D or 3D when only one module is on, and shows the **3D** toggle only with both;
- **Create > Material** and the **3D Rendering** graphics settings need `Funke.3D`;
- systems and renderers of a disabled module don't run, and script calls into its API do nothing and log one error.

Turning a module off never deletes data: components of a disabled module stay in scenes and prefabs, and loading such a scene logs a warning that names the module.

Projects created before modules existed have no `modules` field and keep both. New projects get the modules of their template (the built-in starter is `Funke.2D`).

## One world per entity

An entity is either 2D, 3D or UI. Components of the 2D and the 3D module can't be combined on one entity, and neither can sit on an entity with a Rect Transform 2D: the Add Component menu greys them out ("Conflicts with Transform 2D"), and `Entity.AddComponent`, entity command buffers and **Paste Component** refuse them with a warning (`Entity.AddComponent<T>()` returns `null`). Put a 3D object and a 2D object next to each other as separate entities instead.

Scenes saved before this rule may still mix them. They load unchanged, the editor logs which entity combines which components, and the component of the other world stays inactive: a 2D physics body or camera on a 3D or UI entity is not created (it never adds a second transform), and 3D components on a 2D entity are ignored by the 3D renderer and physics.

## In a game build

The game ships a runtime compiled **without** the modules the project leaves out — their code, shaders and third-party libraries (Box2D for `Funke.2D`, Jolt for `Funke.3D`) are not in the executable.

- **Windows, Linux, macOS:** the build generates a runtime variant workspace (`premake/generated/variant-<modules>`) and compiles it into `bin/<config>-<system>-<arch>-<modules>`. The first build of a variant compiles the whole engine once; later builds are incremental.
- **Android, iOS, Web:** the platform package passes the modules to the engine's CMake build (`MODULES` of `funke_add_engine`); each module set gets its own build cache.
- A project whose shipped scenes or prefabs use a component of a module it doesn't list fails the build, with every offending entity in the log.
- Projects with native (C++) packages ship the full engine: those packages are linked against it.
- From an EngineSDK without project files (no MSBuild/`make` workspace) the build falls back to the prebuilt full runtime.

## For engine developers

The module source lists live in [`Funke-Engine/EngineModules.json`](../../../Funke-Engine/EngineModules.json); premake and `cmake/FunkeEngine.cmake` both read it. Code in the core that touches a module guards it with `#if FUNKE_WITH_2D` / `#if FUNKE_WITH_3D` (compile time) and asks `EngineModules::IsActive(EngineModule::TwoD)` (project setting at runtime). Built-in components register inside a `ModuleRegistrationScope` so the editor can hide them. Script bindings of a module live in `Scripting/ScriptBindings2D.cpp` / `ScriptBindings3D.cpp`, and every slot they fill is listed in `Scripting/ScriptBindingModuleSlots.hpp`, which provides signature-matched stubs when the module is off.

Build a variant by hand:

```bat
vendor\bin\premake5.exe --without-3d vs2022
```

then build `premake\generated\variant-2d\Funke-Runtime\Funke-Runtime.vcxproj`, and run it with `scripts\dev\Run.ps1 -App Runtime -Variant 2d -Project <dir>`.

# Graphics Settings

Graphics settings trade image quality for speed: render scale, post-processing, particles, shadows, lights, texture quality, anisotropic filtering, anti-aliasing and the update rate of distant animations. A project sets its defaults in **Project Settings → Graphics**; a game changes them at runtime through `RenderSettings`, for example from its own options menu.

## Where the defaults live

The editor writes the settings to the `graphics` object in `project.json`. Keys you leave out use their default, so older projects keep working.

```json
"graphics": {
  "renderScale": 1.0,
  "upscaleFilter": "Linear",
  "postProcessingEnabled": true,
  "postProcessingQuality": "High",
  "particleQuality": "High",
  "shadowQuality": "Medium",
  "shadowDistance": 40.0,
  "maxLights": 16,
  "exposure": 1.0,
  "toneMapping": "ACES",
  "textureQuality": "Full",
  "anisotropicFiltering": "X16",
  "antiAliasing": "Off",
  "antiAliasingQuality": "High",
  "animationDistanceRate": false,
  "animationHalfRateDistance": 20.0,
  "animationQuarterRateDistance": 40.0
}
```

Settings with a fixed set of values are stored by name. An unknown name falls back to the default; a value of the wrong type (a number where a name belongs) makes the project fail to load with a message naming the key.

| Setting | Values (default **bold**) | Applies to |
|---|---|---|
| Render Scale | 0.25 – **1.0** | 2D scene resolution; UI and gizmos stay at full resolution |
| Upscale Filter | Point, **Linear** | how a reduced Render Scale is stretched to the screen |
| Post-Processing | **on**, off | the camera's Post Processing effects (bloom, color grading, …) |
| Post-Processing Quality | Low, Medium, **High** | blur and bloom sample counts |
| Particle Quality | Off, Low, Medium, **High** | share of 2D and 3D particles drawn |
| Shadow Quality | Off, Low (1024), **Medium (2048)**, High (4096) | 3D shadow map size |
| Shadow Distance | 1 – 1000, **40** | 3D shadow range in world units |
| Max Lights | 1 – 64, **16** | 3D lights per frame |
| Exposure | 0.01 – 16, **1** | 3D brightness before tone mapping |
| Tone Mapping | None, Reinhard, **ACES** | 3D |
| Texture Quality | **Full**, Half, Quarter | scene textures that are not Point-filtered (2D and 3D) |
| Anisotropic Filtering | Off, 2x, 4x, 8x, **16x** | textures filtered Trilinear or Anisotropic |
| Anti-Aliasing | **Off**, FXAA, MSAA4x | FXAA: the 2D and 3D scene image; MSAA4x: edges of 3D geometry |
| Anti-Aliasing Quality | Low, Medium, **High** | FXAA search length and edge sensitivity |
| Animation › Distance Rate | **off**, on | Animators and Skinned Mesh Renderers whose Distance Rate is Project Setting |
| Animation › Half Rate From | 0 – 100000, **20** | world units from the camera from which they update every 2nd frame |
| Animation › Quarter Rate From | 0 – 100000, **40** | world units from the camera from which they update every 4th frame |

## Texture quality

**Half** and **Quarter** make every scene texture skip its top one or two mip levels: a 1024 px texture is sampled at most at 512 px or 256 px. Distant surfaces look the same as before, close-up ones get softer, and the GPU reads less texture memory. The textures themselves stay loaded at full size, so the setting does not lower video memory use and switching back is instant.

What it never touches:

- **Point-filtered textures.** Pixel art keeps every texel crisp at every setting.
- **UI.** Images, text and UI materials keep full resolution.
- **Textures of custom post-processing effects** (LUTs, noise), which are data rather than surface detail.

A texture's filter is its import setting (the `.meta` file, or the texture's Inspector). A data texture on a mesh or sprite material that must keep full detail can use Point filtering.

## Anisotropic filtering

Floors, roads and walls seen at a grazing angle blur with plain trilinear filtering. Anisotropic filtering takes more samples along the stretched direction and keeps them sharp. **Anisotropic Filtering** sets the sample limit for all textures filtered **Trilinear** or **Anisotropic**; at **Off** both behave like plain trilinear filtering. **Bilinear** and **Point** textures are not affected, so a texture needs the Trilinear or Anisotropic filter to benefit. The cost is small on desktop GPUs and noticeable on older phones, which is why games usually offer the setting in their options menu.

## Anti-aliasing

**FXAA** (fast approximate anti-aliasing) smooths the stair-steps along the edges of meshes, rotated sprites and lines in one extra screen pass. It runs on the finished scene image before the camera's post-processing effects; UI, text and gizmos are drawn afterwards and stay sharp. It works the same on desktop, Android and Web.

Because FXAA only sees the final image, it also softens hard color edges inside textures a little, which shows most on pixel art. Pixel-art games often leave it off or offer it as an option. **Low** finds fewer edges and is the cheapest; **High** follows long, shallow edges further.

**MSAA 4x** (multisample anti-aliasing, `MSAA4x` in `project.json` and C#) draws the 3D scene with four coverage samples per pixel and averages them. It smooths the silhouettes and seams of meshes, 3D particles and 3D lines, but each pixel's color is still computed once from the texture, so a pixel inside a surface stays exactly as it is without anti-aliasing: Point-filtered textures (pixel art, voxel worlds) keep every texel crisp. That makes it the choice for 3D pixel-art games. What it does not smooth:

- **2D sprites.** They are drawn after the 3D scene and keep their edges; 2D games use FXAA.
- **Cut-out texels.** Leaves or grass whose transparent texels a shader discards keep hard edges.
- **Shading inside a surface**, such as sharp specular highlights.

Custom shaders that pick an atlas tile from the UV need a small margin under MSAA, see [Custom Shaders › Mesh3D](Custom-Shaders.md#mesh3d).

MSAA 4x is supported by every GPU Funke runs on (desktop, Android and Web). It costs memory and bandwidth rather than an extra screen pass: the 4x color and depth target takes about 65 MB at 1920×1080, and each 3D pass reads and writes four samples per pixel, which phones feel most. **Anti-Aliasing Quality** only applies to FXAA.

In the editor, the Game View shows anti-aliasing as the game will. The Editor View shows it when its **Post Processing** toggle is on.

## Animation distance rate

With **Distance Rate** on, Animators and Skinned Mesh Renderers far from the game camera update every 2nd frame from **Half Rate From** and every 4th frame from **Quarter Rate From**; the skipped time is added to their next update, so they keep their tempo. It applies to components whose own **Distance Rate** is **Project Setting** (the default); **Off** and **Custom** on a component override it. In a scene with 384 skinned models and 160 animated characters it cut the frame time from about 37 ms to 12 ms. See [Animation › Culling and distance rate](Animation.md#culling-and-distance-rate).

## Changing settings at runtime

`RenderSettings` changes take effect at the start of the next frame; texture samplers are rebuilt then, without reloading any texture. Call it from the main thread (any script callback).

```csharp
using Funke;

public class GraphicsOptions : EntityScript
{
    public void ApplyLowPreset()
    {
        RenderSettings.TextureQuality = TextureQualityLevel.Half;
        RenderSettings.AnisotropicFiltering = AnisotropicFilteringLevel.X2;
        RenderSettings.AntiAliasing = AntiAliasingMode.Off;
        RenderSettings.ShadowQuality = ShadowQualityLevel.Low;
    }

    public void ToggleAntiAliasing()
    {
        // MSAA keeps pixel-art textures sharp in a 3D game; FXAA would soften them.
        GraphicsApplyStatus status = RenderSettings.SetAntiAliasing(
            RenderSettings.AntiAliasing == AntiAliasingMode.Off ? AntiAliasingMode.MSAA4x : AntiAliasingMode.Off);
        if (status != GraphicsApplyStatus.Applied)
            Log.Warn($"Anti-aliasing not changed: {status}");
    }
}
```

Every setting is a property (`RenderSettings.TextureQuality = …`). To see whether a change was accepted, use its `Set…` method where there is one (`SetTextureQuality`, `SetAnisotropicFiltering`, `SetAntiAliasing`, `SetAntiAliasingQuality`, `SetRenderScale`, …) or `RenderSettings.Apply(settings)`; both return a `GraphicsApplyStatus`:

| `GraphicsApplyStatus` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Applied` | queued for the next frame |
| `Unchanged` | the value was already set |
| `NotInitialized` / `ShuttingDown` | no running application |
| `WrongThread` | called from a worker thread |

Out-of-range values are clamped (a cast like `(AnisotropicFilteringLevel)99` becomes `X16`). `RenderSettings.Get()` returns all settings as a `GraphicsSettings` struct and `RenderSettings.Apply(settings)` sets them in one call; `RenderSettings.ResetToDefaults()` goes back to the project's values. Runtime changes are not saved: store the player's choice yourself (for example with `PlayerPrefs`) and apply it when the game starts.

The animation distance rate has the properties `RenderSettings.AnimationDistanceRateEnabled`, `AnimationHalfRateDistance` and `AnimationQuarterRateDistance`.

C++ has the same API in `Graphics/RenderSettings.hpp` (`RenderSettings::SetTextureQuality(TextureQualityLevel::Half)`, `RenderSettings::SetAnimationDistanceRateEnabled(true)` and so on).
