# Job System

The **Job System** is Funke's tool for doing work on multiple CPU cores at once. Instead of running everything on the main thread, you hand off chunks of work as **jobs** and let a pool of worker threads run them in parallel.

If you just want the short version: wrap independent work in a job, schedule it, and (optionally) wait for it to finish. Use it for heavy, parallel-friendly work like processing thousands of entities.

---

## What it is

At startup the engine creates a **pool of worker threads** (the count is based on your CPU, leaving a little headroom for other systems). You submit jobs; the workers pick them up and run them. You get back a **handle** you can use to wait for completion or check progress.

If the job system isn't running for some reason, scheduling a job simply runs it inline on the calling thread — so code that uses jobs still works, just without the parallel speedup.

**When to reach for it:** large batches of independent work — moving thousands of objects, generating data, spawning many entities. **When not to:** small amounts of work (the overhead isn't worth it) or anything that must happen in a strict order.

---

## Using jobs from C#

C# is the main way most users touch the job system. There are three job shapes:

| Interface | Runs | Use for |
|-----------|------|---------|
| `IJob` | once | A single chunk of background work. |
| `IJobFor` | once per index, in order | A loop you want as one job. |
| `IJobParallelFor` | once per index, **across threads** | A loop split over all workers. |

### A simple parallel loop

The quickest way to parallelize a loop:

```csharp
// Run body(i) for i in [0, count), spread across worker threads:
Job.ScheduleParallelFor(count, i =>
{
    DoExpensiveWork(i);
}).Complete();   // .Complete() waits for all of it to finish
```

`Complete()` blocks until the work is done. You can also keep the `JobHandle` and check `IsComplete`, or wait later — which lets the main thread do other things while workers run.

### A struct job (the fast path)

For hot code, write the job as a `struct` so there are no per-item allocations:

```csharp
private struct SpinJob : IJobParallelFor
{
    public float Dt;
    public void Execute(int i) { /* ...process item i... */ }
}

var job = new SpinJob { Dt = Time.DeltaTime };
Job.ScheduleParallelFor(job, length: count).Complete();
```

### Chaining jobs (dependencies)

A job can depend on another — it won't start until the first finishes:

```csharp
JobHandle a = Job.Schedule(() => StepOne());
JobHandle b = Job.Schedule(() => StepTwo(), dependency: a);  // runs after a
b.Complete();
```

### Sharing results safely

Worker threads run at the same time, so you **can't** just write to a shared variable — you'd get race conditions. Use the atomic helpers (`AtomicInt`, `AtomicFloat`, …) or a reducer for combining results across threads. Don't write to ordinary fields from inside a parallel job.

---

## Creating entities from jobs

You **cannot** add or remove entities/components directly inside a job — structural changes to the entity world aren't thread-safe. Instead, record the changes into an **Entity Command Buffer** and play them back on the main thread afterward:

```csharp
using var ecb = new EntityCommandBuffer(initialCapacity: 64 * 1024);

var job = new CreateEntityJob { Ecb = ecb.AsParallelWriter(), /* ...data... */ };
Job.ScheduleParallelFor(job, length: count).Complete();

int created = ecb.Playback();   // all the entities are created here, on the main thread
```

Each worker writes into its own slice of the buffer (no locks), and `Playback()` applies everything in one bulk step. This is the standard pattern for spawning lots of entities in parallel. (See `Funke-Sandbox/Source/CreateEntityJobSample.cs` for a complete, runnable example.)

---

## The rules (read these)

Multithreading is powerful but unforgiving. Keep these in mind:

1. **No structural ECS changes inside a job.** Don't create/destroy entities or add/remove components directly — use an Entity Command Buffer.
2. **Don't write to shared state from parallel jobs.** Use atomics or a reducer.
3. **A job's work should be independent.** If item 5 depends on item 4's result, a parallel-for is the wrong tool.
4. **Wait before you read.** Call `Complete()` (or otherwise confirm the job is done) before using its results.
5. **Frame Arenas are main-thread only** (see below) — don't use them from a worker.

---

## Using jobs from C++

The native API mirrors the C# one:

```cpp
JobHandle h = Job::Schedule([]{ DoWork(); });
Job::Wait(h);                       // wait for completion

ParallelFor(0, count, [](size_t i) { Process(i); });  // parallel loop, blocks until done
```

`ParallelFor` automatically splits the range into chunks (aiming for a few chunks per worker). One nice property: `Job::Wait` actively helps run queued work while it waits, so nested waits can't deadlock. Engine systems like the 2D renderer use this to process entities in parallel.

Completion also guarantees that the job's callable and its owned captures have been released, including when the callable throws. Native script DLLs can therefore finish their jobs before unloading without leaving callable destructors in the worker queue. Structural ECS operations use the [native commandbuffer API](ECS.md#batched-structural-changes-in-c), with playback on the main thread after recording jobs finish.

---

## Frame Arenas (related)

Alongside the job system, the engine sets up **Frame Arenas** — fast scratch memory for short-lived, per-frame data. The "frame" arena is wiped automatically at the end of each frame, so you can grab temporary space cheaply without worrying about freeing it.

Frame Arenas are **main-thread only** and not thread-safe — a worker thread must use its own local storage instead. They're an internal performance tool more than a everyday-scripting feature, but it's worth knowing why they exist.

---

## Summary

- The job system runs independent work across **worker threads**.
- In C#, use `Job.ScheduleParallelFor(...)` for loops and struct jobs for hot paths; `Complete()` waits.
- Combine results with **atomics**; create entities via an **Entity Command Buffer** + `Playback()`.
- Never do structural ECS changes or touch Frame Arenas from a worker thread.
- C++ has the same tools: `Job::Schedule`, `Job::Wait`, and `ParallelFor`.

## Related pages

- [ECS](ECS.md) — the entities and components jobs often process.
- [Scripting](../Scripting/Scripting.md) — where you'll write most job code.
- [Startup Processes](Startup-Processes.md) — the job pool starts early in boot.

# Lighting 2D

`Funke.Lighting2D` is an optional external package for world lighting. It adds colored point lights, ambient illumination and rectangular shadow occluders to sprites, tilemaps, terrain, particles and world text. Screen-space UI stays unaffected.

Use an engine build with `Renderer2D::RegisterSceneEffect` and `FullscreenEffect`; older beta binaries need updating. In **Package Manager > Search Packages**, click **Refresh registry**, search for `Funke.Lighting2D` and click **Install**. The editor enables the required `Funke.2D` module and compiles the package against your engine. A native C++ toolchain is required. The [release ZIP](https://github.com/Ben-Scr/Funke-PackageRegistry/releases/tag/Funke.Lighting2D-0.1.0) also supports manual installation through the Package Manager.

## Add lighting

Use **Create > 2D Entity > Lighting** or **Add Component > Lighting 2D**:

| Component | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Light 2D | Color, intensity, radius in world units, falloff and shadow casting. |
| Ambient Light 2D | Base illumination; enabled ambient components add together. |
| Shadow Occluder 2D | A local rectangle with size, offset and opacity, transformed by its entity. |

Lights use their entity's world position; their radius does not inherit transform scale. Occluders follow position, rotation and scale. Add a sprite separately to make an occluder visible. Selecting a component shows its radius or rectangle in the Editor View.

With point lights and no ambient component, base illumination is 10%. Add an ambient component with zero intensity for complete darkness. Without any enabled point or ambient light, rendering bypasses the lighting pass. Disabled entities and components do not contribute.

## Script access

The wrappers are in `Funke.Lighting2D`: `Light2D`, `AmbientLight2D` and `ShadowOccluder2D`. Obtain them through `GetComponent<T>()` or `Entity.AddComponent<T>()`. Their properties match the Inspector and update native state directly. For example, a `Light2D` exposes `Color`, `Intensity`, `Radius`, `Falloff` and `CastShadows`. Non-finite numeric values throw; finite values clamp to the Inspector ranges. Access after removal throws `InvalidOperationException`.

The package owns component registration, serialization, C# bindings, gizmos and shaders. Scene/prefab saving, duplication and Play/Stop use the ordinary component workflow. See the package's `README.md` for a complete script example and reproducible showcase tests.

## Current limits

Each view supports 32 visible point lights and 64 occluders; excess components are selected by distance to the view center and produce a warning. Lighting affects one shared 2D plane before FXAA and camera effects. It leaves alpha unchanged and uses nearest filtering at the scene resolution. Wireframe mode bypasses lighting.

This version has hard rectangular shadows, no polygon occluders, normal maps, per-layer masks, soft shadows or emissive exclusions. It does not light 3D geometry. Keep light and occluder counts modest: the shader tests their intersections per pixel. Windows Editor and Runtime rendering are tested; Android/iOS/Web device validation and performance measurements remain outstanding.

# Localization

This page explains how Funke handles **localization** — translating interface text into multiple languages, choosing a language from a JSON file, switching it at runtime, and downloading languages (and the CJK font) on demand. It also covers the file format, the lookup API, and how to add a language of your own.

If you just want the short version: each language is a JSON file of `key → text`. You look a string up by key with `FNK_TR("some.key")` and set the active language with `Localization::SetLanguage("de")`. Any label that re-reads its key picks up the new language on the next frame, falling back to English for anything it can't find — and to the raw key if even English is missing it, so gaps are visible rather than fatal.

**Making a game?** Your game has its own string tables in `Assets/Localization/`, a C# API (`Localization.Get`, `Localization.SetLanguage`, …) and a **Localized Text** component — jump to [Localizing your game](#localizing-your-game). The rest of this page describes the engine's own (Launcher) tables, which share the file format.

---

## What it is

Funke's localization system is a small, self-contained engine subsystem (namespace `Funke::Localization`, in `Funke-Engine/src/Localization/`) that maps **keys to translated strings**. Each language is a JSON file: a `meta` block describing the language, plus a flat `strings` object of `key → translated text`.

At startup the engine loads the **English fallback table**, scans the languages it can find on disk, and reads the user's saved preference. From then on, a lookup like `Localization::Get("launcher.settings.title")` returns the active language's text for that key — or the English text if the active language is missing it — or, as a last resort, the raw key itself.

English (`en`) is the **built-in fallback**: it is always present, is never downloaded, and is the language every other one falls back to. Other languages ship as bundled JSON files and/or are listed in a manifest for on-demand download.

The bundled localization data ships under `Funke-Runtime/FunkeAssets/Localization/`, which a post-build step copies next to every runnable binary:

```
FunkeAssets/
  Localization/
    en.json          ← English (built-in fallback, always present)
    de.json          ← Deutsch (bundled)
    ja.json          ← Japanese (日本語) (bundled; needs the CJK font)
    manifest.json    ← lists downloadable languages + the CJK font
```

> **Two separate tables.** `Funke::Localization` (this part of the page) holds the engine's own strings: every Funke binary calls `Localization::Initialize()` at startup, but only the **Launcher** reads from it, and all of its keys are in the `launcher.*` namespace. Games use a second, independent table, `Funke::GameLocalization`, loaded from the project's `Assets/Localization/` folder — see [Localizing your game](#localizing-your-game). Launcher keys and game keys never mix, and the two remember their language in different places.

---

## Supported languages

Funke ships three languages out of the box. Two distinctions matter: which ones are **bundled** (work offline, no download) versus listed only for download, and which need the large **CJK font** to render their glyphs.

| Code | Display name | How it ships | Needs CJK font |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **en** | English | Built-in fallback — always present, never downloaded | No |
| **de** | Deutsch | Bundled on disk (also has a download URL for updates) | No |
| **ja** | Japanese (日本語) | Bundled on disk (also has a download URL for updates) | **Yes** |

`en` is special: it is the hard-coded fallback table, it is **not** listed in `manifest.json`, and the language list always sorts it first (the rest sort by display name). `de` and `ja` are bundled so the Launcher works offline; their manifest URLs are an *update* path, not the only way to get them. Only `ja` sets `requiresCjkFont`, because Latin/German glyphs are already in the default UI font but Japanese kana and ideographs are not (see [On-demand downloads and the CJK font](#on-demand-downloads-and-the-cjk-font)).

The shipped `de` and `ja` files are intentionally **partial** — they translate the strings that matter most and lean on English for the rest. That is by design; the fallback chain makes it safe.

---

## The translation file format

A language file has two top-level objects: a `meta` block describing the language, and a `strings` object mapping dotted keys to translated text. Placeholders use `{0}`, `{1}`, … positional markers.

```json
{
  "meta": {
    "code": "de",
    "displayName": "Deutsch",
    "fallback": "en",
    "schemaVersion": 1
  },
  "strings": {
    "launcher.settings.title": "Launcher-Einstellungen",
    "launcher.list.size_prefix": "Größe: {0}",
    "launcher.delete.message": "Projekt '{0}' löschen?"
  }
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **`meta.code`** | The language code (`en`, `de`, `ja`). This is the identity used everywhere — file lookups, the preference file, `SetLanguage`. |
| **`meta.displayName`** | The human-readable name shown in a language picker (e.g. `"Japanese (日本語)"`). |
| **`meta.fallback`** | The language to fall back to; in practice always `en`. |
| **`meta.schemaVersion`** | Format version (currently `1`). |
| **`strings`** | A flat object of `key → translated string`. Only string-valued members are loaded; anything else is skipped. |

When a file is found, only its `meta` block is parsed up front, so a language picker can be populated cheaply without loading every table. The full `strings` table is loaded lazily the moment that language becomes active. Values are substituted at lookup time with `std::vformat`, so `{0}`/`{1}` map to the arguments you pass to `Localization::Format`.

> **`en.json` is the canonical key set.** English is the fallback for every other language, and missing keys resolve *through* it, so a translation file should use the **same keys** as `en.json` — only the values change. If `de.json` lacks a key, the German UI shows the English string; if English also lacks it, the UI shows the raw key (e.g. `launcher.settings.title`) and the engine logs the miss once. A renamed or mistyped key simply won't be found. Keep `en.json` complete and treat its keys as the source of truth.

---

## Choosing and switching the language

### At startup

`Initialize()` reads the saved preference from `locale.json` (at `%LocalAppData%/Funke/locale.json` on Windows). If there is no usable preference — or the saved language is unknown or not actually installed — it falls back to `en` and writes the resolved choice back out. From then on, the active table is whatever the preference says.

### Auto-detecting the system language

`Localization::GetSystemLanguage()` probes the OS UI locale (Windows `GetUserDefaultLocaleName`, or the POSIX `LC_ALL` / `LC_MESSAGES` / `LANG` environment variables), normalizes it to a bare lowercase tag, and returns the matching language code — **but only if that language is already installed**. A system locale that maps to a not-yet-downloaded language quietly returns `en`; it does not auto-trigger a download. The Launcher uses this to offer an "Auto (system)" option that re-pins to the OS language on each launch.

### The fallback chain and missing keys

Every `Get()` lookup walks the same chain:

1. The **active** language's table.
2. The **English** fallback table.
3. On a complete miss: the engine records the key, logs a one-time warning tagged `Localization`, and returns the **raw key string** itself.

That last step means a missing key is never an exception or a blank — it surfaces visibly as the key text (`launcher.settings.title`), which makes gaps easy to spot during development.

### Switching at runtime

`Localization::SetLanguage(code)` does the right thing based on the language's status:

- **Installed** → swaps the active table immediately, persists the new preference, and (for a CJK language) makes sure the CJK font is present — fetching it if not, which can require a restart.
- **Available** (listed in the manifest but not on disk) → records a pending switch and kicks off a download; the switch is applied when the download finishes.
- **Downloading / DownloadFailed**, an unknown code, or the already-current code → no-op.

Switching to an already-installed, non-CJK language is **live**: the active string table is swapped in place, any registered change callbacks fire, and there is no restart. (The CJK font is the one exception — see below.)

---

## On-demand downloads and the CJK font

`manifest.json` (schema version 1) lists the languages and the font that can be fetched at runtime. Each language entry carries a GitHub-release `url`, a `sha256`, a `sizeBytes`, and `requiresCjkFont`. A separate `fonts.cjk` entry describes the shared CJK font — **Noto Sans CJK** (`NotoSansCJK-Regular.ttc`, ~19 MB). The font is large enough that it is *not* bundled; it is downloaded the first time it's needed.

Two download paths exist:

- **A language JSON.** Selecting an **Available** language queues its `<code>.json` for download to `%LocalAppData%/Funke/Localization/<code>.json`. (Because `de`/`ja` are bundled, this path is really their *update* path; it mainly matters for any server-only languages added later.)
- **The CJK font.** Whenever a CJK language is activated and the font isn't already on disk, Funke queues `NotoSansCJK-Regular.ttc` to `%LocalAppData%/Funke/Fonts/NotoSansCJK/NotoSansCJK-Regular.ttc`. This happens even for **Japanese, which ships bundled** — the `ja.json` is already present, but its font is not, so selecting Japanese for the first time still triggers the ~19 MB download.

Downloads run on a single background worker, one job at a time (the actual transfer is delegated to the bundled `Funke-PackageTool`). The host loop calls `Localization::Poll()` each frame to finalize a finished job — which rebuilds the language list, marks the language **Installed**, and applies any pending switch. Each file is staged to a temporary sibling and renamed into place only after its byte length (when the manifest gives one) and **SHA-256** (when the manifest gives one) check out — so a failed or tampered download never overwrites the existing file.

> **A CJK language needs a restart the first time.** The UI font atlas is baked once at startup; there is no dynamic glyph loading, so a CJK font downloaded mid-session can't be merged into the live atlas — its characters would render as boxes until the next launch. Because of this, fetching the CJK font sets a **restart-required** flag, and the Launcher shows a "Restart Required" prompt that can relaunch the app. Ordinary (non-CJK) language switches never require a restart.

A note on platforms: SHA-256 verification is implemented with BCrypt on **Windows**; on other platforms the hash check is not yet implemented, so any manifest entry carrying a `sha256` will fail to verify there. In practice the download path is Windows-centric today — which is consistent with localization being a Launcher feature for now.

User-downloaded files always **override** bundled ones on a code collision, so an updated `de.json` pulled into `%LocalAppData%/Funke/Localization/` takes precedence over the bundled copy.

---

## Using it from code

The public C++ surface lives in `Funke-Engine/src/Localization/Localization.hpp`, all in namespace `Funke::Localization`:

| Function | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **`Get(key)`** | Returns the active translation for `key`, falling back to English, then to the raw key. |
| **`GetFallback(key)`** | Looks up `key` in the **English table only**, ignoring the active language. Used for UI shown *before* a freshly-selected language's font is loaded (e.g. the CJK restart prompt), where localized text would render as missing-glyph boxes. |
| **`Format(key, args...)`** | Looks up `key` and substitutes `{0}`/`{1}`/… with the arguments. Header-only template over `std::vformat`; returns the raw template on a bad format spec rather than throwing. |
| **`FormatFallback(key, args...)`** | The English-fallback counterpart of `Format` (built on `GetFallback`). |
| **`GetAvailableLanguages()`** | The cached list of `LanguageInfo { Code, DisplayName, Status, RequiresCjkFont }`. |
| **`GetCurrentLanguage()`** | The active language code. |
| **`GetSystemLanguage()`** | The OS UI language code, if it's installed; otherwise `"en"`. |
| **`SetLanguage(code)`** | Switches language (or queues a download — see above). |
| **`RequestLanguageDownload(code)`** | Kicks off an async download for an *Available* language (plus the CJK font if required); no-op if a download is already running or the language isn't *Available*. `SetLanguage` calls this for you, so you rarely call it directly. |
| **`GetActiveDownload()`** | A snapshot of any in-flight or recently-finished download (`Code`, `Stage`, `Progress`, `Running`, `Failed`, `RestartRequired`, `Error`) for progress UI. |
| **`Poll()`** | Pumped every frame by the host loop to finalize downloads. **Without a pump, a finished download never transitions** — applies any pending switch and rebuilds the installed list. |
| **`Initialize()`** | Loads the fallback, scans languages, applies the saved preference. Called once at startup by the engine entry point. |
| **`RegisterChangeCallback(fn)` / `UnregisterChangeCallback(h)`** | Run `fn` whenever the active language changes; the handle unregisters it. |
| **`FNK_TR(key)`** | Macro alias for `Get(key)` — the idiomatic way to read a string. |

(`Get`, `GetFallback`, and the rest are `FUNKE_API`-exported symbols; `Format` and `FormatFallback` are header-only templates with no exported symbol.)

A typical call site just re-reads its keys every frame, so live language switches are picked up automatically:

```cpp
#include "Localization/Localization.hpp"
using namespace Funke;

// A label — re-fetched each frame, so it re-localizes on a language switch.
ImGui::TextUnformatted(FNK_TR("launcher.settings.title").c_str());

// A formatted string with positional args ({0}, {1}).
std::string msg = Localization::Format("launcher.asset_library.engine_too_old",
                                       requiredVersion, currentVersion);

// UI that must stay readable before a new font has loaded → use the English fallback.
ImGui::TextUnformatted(Localization::GetFallback("launcher.settings.language.restart_required").c_str());

// Switch language at runtime (live for an installed, non-CJK language).
if (userPickedGerman)
    Localization::SetLanguage("de");
```

Two things to keep in mind. First, `Get()`/`GetFallback()` return a **reference** into the engine's internal tables; **don't hold that reference across a language change** — switching languages rebuilds the active table and can invalidate it. Copy the string if you need to keep it. Second, the change-callback hook is live (it fires on every switch) but the shipped Launcher doesn't register one — it simply re-queries every label through `FNK_TR` each frame, which is the recommended pattern.

These functions only reach the Launcher's tables. Game code — C# scripts and native game code alike — uses the game table described next.

---

## Adding a new language

Adding a language is drop-in — no code changes, no rebuild:

1. **Copy `en.json`** to `<code>.json` (e.g. `fr.json`), using the language's code.
2. **Edit the `meta` block**: set `code` to the same code and `displayName` to the name to show in a picker. Keep `fallback` as `"en"` and `schemaVersion` as `1`.
3. **Translate the `strings` values**, leaving the keys exactly as they are. Any key you omit falls back to English.
4. **Drop the file** into either the bundled folder (`Funke-Runtime/FunkeAssets/Localization/`) to ship it, or the user folder (`%LocalAppData%/Funke/Localization/`) to test it locally. The engine scans both on startup, and **user-dir files override bundled ones** on a matching code.

The new language appears automatically: the scan reads each file's `meta` block, records the language, and the next `GetAvailableLanguages()` includes it with status **Installed**. Languages listed in `manifest.json` but not present on disk show up as **Available** (downloadable) instead.

---

## Localizing your game

A game's translations are separate from the Launcher's: their own table (`Funke::GameLocalization` natively, `Funke.Localization` in C#), their own folder in the project, and the player's choice stored with the game's save data.

### Language files

Put one file per language into **`Assets/Localization/`** — the same format as above:

```
MyGame/
  Assets/
    Localization/
      en.json    ← fallback
      de.json
      fr.json
```

```json
{
  "meta": { "code": "de", "displayName": "Deutsch" },
  "strings": {
    "menu.play": "Spiel starten",
    "hud.score": "Punkte: {0:N1}"
  }
}
```

- Only `*.json` files directly in that folder count. `meta.code` names the language; without it the file name is used (`fr.json` → `fr`), and without `meta.displayName` pickers show the code. `fallback` and `schemaVersion` are optional here.
- The **fallback** language is `en` when the game has an `en.json`, otherwise its first language by code. Lookups go **current language → fallback → the key itself**, and a missing key is logged once (tag `Localization`).
- The files load when the project opens — in the editor, the built game and `funke.exe` — and **always ship** in builds (the build's asset pruning keeps the whole folder). The editor reloads them as soon as you save one, also during Play.
- Text Renderers load Unicode glyphs on demand from their assigned font. Choose a font containing the characters in your translations: the bundled IBM Plex fonts cover Latin Extended, but Greek, Cyrillic and CJK require another font. Missing characters use the font's replacement glyph or `?`; malformed UTF-8 also renders as replacement characters. There is no automatic fallback-font chain or complex-script shaping/bidirectional layout. This game-text path is separate from the Launcher's ImGui font atlas and its CJK-font restart requirement. See [Known Limitations](../Known-Limitations.md) and [font caching](../Assets/Assets.md#loading-caching-and-handles).

### Which language the game starts in

1. The language the player picked with `Localization.SetLanguage` — stored in **`PlayerPrefs`** under `Funke.Language`, so it lives in the game's player-data folder (`Application.PersistentDataPath`) and follows `--prefs-profile` / isolated build profiles like any other save data.
2. Otherwise the **OS language**, if the game has it: an exact match (`pt-BR`), then the bare language (`de` for `de-AT`), then a regional variant (`pt-PT` → `pt-BR`).
3. Otherwise the fallback.

Editor Play Mode and the built game share the player-data folder, so a language chosen while playing in the editor is also the built game's start language on that machine.

### The Localized Text component

Add **Localized Text** (category UI) to an entity with a **Text Renderer** (Add Component adds the Text Renderer for you) and set its **Key**. During Play — and always in a built game — the component writes the translation into the Text Renderer, and writes it again whenever the language changes or the files are reloaded. A script may still set the text itself; that text stays until the key or the language changes.

Outside Play the Text Renderer keeps the text you typed, so translations never leak into saved scenes or prefabs. The inspector's read-only **Translation** row shows what the key resolves to in the current language (or `(missing key)`).

In scene JSON the component is `"LocalizedText": { "key": "menu.play" }`.

### From C#

```csharp
using Funke;
using Funke.UI;

title.Text = Localization.Get("menu.title");
score.Text = Localization.Format("hud.score", points);   // {0}, {1} … formatted for the language's culture

// A language picker:
foreach (LanguageInfo language in Localization.AvailableLanguages)
    AddButton(language.DisplayName, () => Localization.SetLanguage(language.Code));

Localization.LanguageChanged += RefreshLabels;          // unsubscribe in OnDisable/OnDestroy
GetComponent<LocalizedText>()!.Key = "menu.continue";   // switch a Localized Text to another key
```

| Member | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **`Get(key)`** | The translation; the fallback's when the current language lacks it; the key itself when no language has it. Cached until the language changes. |
| **`Format(key, params args)`** | `Get` plus .NET composite formatting (`{0}`, `{0:N1}`, `{{` for a brace) with `Culture`. A malformed translation is returned unformatted instead of throwing. |
| **`Has(key)`** | True when the current or the fallback language has the key. |
| **`CurrentLanguage`** / **`FallbackLanguage`** | Language codes; empty when the game has no language files. |
| **`SystemLanguage`** | The OS UI language as a bare code (`"de"`), whether or not the game has it; `"en"` when unknown. |
| **`AvailableLanguages`** | `LanguageInfo(Code, DisplayName)` for every file, fallback first, then by display name. |
| **`SetLanguage(code)`** | Switches immediately and stores the choice in PlayerPrefs; `false` (nothing changes) for a language the game doesn't have. |
| **`Culture`** | `CultureInfo` of the current language for your own number/date formatting; invariant when .NET doesn't know the code. |
| **`LanguageChanged`** | Raised after a language switch and after the editor reloaded edited files. |
| **`PreferenceKey`** | `"Funke.Language"`, the PlayerPrefs key holding the choice. |

Call it from the main thread (scripts, systems), not from jobs.

### From native code

`Localization/GameLocalization.hpp` offers the same table to C++: `GameLocalization::Get`, `Format` (`std::format` placeholders), `Has`, `SetLanguage`, `GetCurrentLanguage`, `GetAvailableLanguages`, `RegisterChangeCallback` and `GetRevision` (bumped by every language switch or reload). `SetLanguage` there does not store the player's choice; only the C# `Localization.SetLanguage` does.

### Checking translations

`funke validate` reports language files that aren't valid JSON or lack a `strings` object, Localized Text keys that the fallback language doesn't have (they would show the raw key) or that sit on an entity without a Text Renderer, and — as warnings — keys a language hasn't translated yet or has but the fallback doesn't (typos, leftovers).

---

## Summary

- Funke localization maps **keys to translated strings**, one **JSON file per language** (a `meta` block plus a flat `strings` object), in namespace `Funke::Localization`.
- **English (`en`) is the always-present fallback**; lookups resolve active → English → raw key, so missing keys are visible, never fatal.
- Three languages ship: **en**, **de** (bundled), and **ja** (bundled, needs the **CJK font**); `manifest.json` lists `de`/`ja` and the on-demand ~19 MB Noto Sans CJK font.
- The active language is read from **`%LocalAppData%/Funke/locale.json`**, can auto-detect the **system language**, and switches **live** via `SetLanguage` — except the CJK font, which **requires a restart** because the font atlas is baked at startup.
- Read strings with **`FNK_TR(key)`** / `Localization::Get`, use **`GetFallback`** for pre-font-load UI, format with **`Localization::Format(key, args...)`**, and pump **`Poll()`** each frame. These engine tables serve the **Launcher**.
- **Add a language** by dropping a `<code>.json` with a `meta` block into the bundled or user `Localization` folder — it auto-appears, with the user dir overriding bundled.
- **Games** keep their own tables in **`Assets/Localization/<code>.json`** (fallback `en` or the first language), read them from C# with **`Localization.Get` / `Format`**, let the **Localized Text** component fill Text Renderers, and switch with **`Localization.SetLanguage`**, which remembers the choice in **PlayerPrefs**; the game otherwise starts in the OS language when it has it. Unicode text needs a font containing the requested glyphs; game Text Renderers load them on demand.

## Related pages

- [Assets](../Assets/Assets.md) — the locale JSON files are content shipped next to each binary, like other engine assets.
- [Startup Processes](Startup-Processes.md) — the engine boot sequence, where `Localization::Initialize()` runs.
- [Third-Party Libraries](../Reference/Third-Party-Libraries.md) — the bundled OFL fonts and the on-demand Noto Sans CJK font.
- [Known Limitations](../Known-Limitations.md) — remaining font, text-shaping and localization-editor limits.

# Physics 2D

2D entities are simulated by [Box2D](https://box2d.org) (version 3). Every entity with a **Rigidbody 2D** or a collider is one Box2D body: a Rigidbody 2D makes it dynamic, kinematic or static, and a collider without a Rigidbody 2D is a static body. Colliders on child entities are separate bodies; join bodies with the joints below.

## Components

| Component | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Rigidbody 2D** | Body Type, Mass (pinned) or automatic mass from the colliders' density, Gravity Scale, Freeze Position X/Y, Freeze Rotation, Linear Damping (default 0.1), Angular Damping, Continuous (Bullet) for fast bodies. C#: `Inertia`, `LocalCenterOfMass`, `WorldCenterOfMass`, `ApplyForceAtPoint`, `ApplyImpulseAtPoint`, `ApplyTorque`, `ApplyAngularImpulse`. |
| **Box Collider 2D** | Box with **Offset** and **Size**. |
| **Circle Collider 2D** | Circle with **Offset** and **Radius**. |
| **Polygon Collider 2D** | One or more outlines (paths), see below. |
| **Revolute Joint 2D** | Hinge between two bodies, with limits, motor and spring. |
| **Prismatic Joint 2D** | Slider along an axis, with limits, motor and spring (suspensions, pistons, elevators). |
| **Weld Joint 2D** | Glues two bodies together, rigid or springy. |

An entity has at most one collider. Every collider has **Sensor**, **Contact Events**, **Friction**, **Bounciness**, **Density** (mass per area, default 1), **Layer**, **Collides With** and **Group Index** (Box2D groups: colliders with the same negative group never touch, for example the parts of one ragdoll or vehicle; the same positive group always touches; 0 leaves it to the layers). A Rigidbody 2D whose mass was never set weighs the sum of its colliders' density × area; setting **Mass** pins it.

## Polygon Collider 2D

A polygon collider is made of paths in the entity's frame (scaled by the transform and **Size**, moved by **Offset**):

- A path of up to 8 points that is convex, or whose points are not in outline order, becomes its convex hull. This is the classic behavior (**Sides** builds a regular polygon).
- Any other path is an outline in order and may be concave and have up to 16384 points. Funke splits it into convex pieces of at most 8 vertices (Box2D's limit), all on the same body. Use this for car bodies, rocks and terrain chunks.
- Several paths add up: each one collides, for example the two halves of a vehicle body.

**Edge (Open Line)** turns every path into an open line instead of a filled shape: ground, slopes, walls and one-way surfaces of any length. An edge has no area (no mass, never a sensor) and is smooth across its points, so wheels and balls roll over the joints without bumps. It collides on the left of the direction its points run, i.e. on top of a line drawn from left to right; a path needs at least 2 points. Scene key `"edge": true`.

The Editor View and the physics overlay (F8) draw every piece. In scene files the first path is `"points"` (`[{ "x": 0, "y": 0 }, …]`) and further paths are `"paths"`: an array of flat `[x0, y0, x1, y1, …]` arrays.

```csharp
var body = GetComponent<PolygonCollider2D>();
body.SetPoints(outline);                       // path 0, concave is fine
body.SetPaths(frontHalf, backHalf);            // replaces every path
Vector2[] first = body.GetPath(0);
body.Density = 2.5f;
```

## Joints

A joint component on an entity connects **body A** (the entity's own Rigidbody 2D or collider body) with **body B**, the **Connected Body**. Without a Connected Body the joint holds body A to the world.

- **Anchor** is the joint point in body A's frame, in meters (the transform's scale does not apply).
- **Auto Connected Anchor** (on by default) pins the joint where the anchor is when the joint is built. Turn it off to give **Connected Anchor** in body B's frame (world space without a Connected Body).
- **Collide Connected** lets the two bodies collide with each other (off by default).
- The joint is built when play starts, or as soon as both bodies exist (for spawned prefabs, on the next physics step). Angles and translations count from the pose the bodies have at that moment, so author the bodies in their rest pose. It is rebuilt when a body is recreated or Connected Body, an anchor, the axis or Collide Connected changes; motor, limit and spring settings change the live joint without a rebuild, so scripts can set the motor speed every frame.
- Destroying either entity or removing the component removes the joint.

| Joint | Settings |
|---|---|
| Revolute | **Use Limits** (Lower/Upper Angle, degrees in the Inspector), **Use Motor** (Motor Speed in degrees per second, Max Motor Torque), **Use Spring** (Frequency, Damping). |
| Prismatic | **Axis** (slide direction in body A's frame), **Use Limits** (Lower/Upper Translation in meters), **Use Motor** (Motor Speed in m/s, Max Motor Force), **Use Spring**. |
| Weld | **Linear/Angular Frequency** (0 = rigid) and **Damping**. |

An entity has at most one joint of each type. When a body needs several joints of the same type (a chassis welded to several parts), put the joints on the other bodies and set the chassis as their Connected Body.

```csharp
// A wheel: revolute joint from the wheel to its axle, driven by a motor.
var hinge = wheel.GetComponent<RevoluteJoint2D>();
hinge.EnableMotor = true;
hinge.MaxMotorTorque = 40f;
hinge.MotorSpeed = throttle * 30f;      // rad/s of body B relative to body A, counter-clockwise positive

// A suspension: the axle slides up and down in the chassis, a motor pushes it to its limit.
var spring = axle.GetComponent<PrismaticJoint2D>();
float compression = spring.JointTranslation;
Log.Info($"{spring.ReactionForce} {spring.IsCreated}");
```

In C# angles are in radians and speeds per second. `ConnectedBody` is an `Entity?`; `IsCreated`, `ReactionForce`, `ReactionTorque`, and per type `JointAngle`/`JointTranslation`, `JointSpeed`, `MotorTorque`/`MotorForce` read the live joint.

Scene keys: `RevoluteJoint2D`, `PrismaticJoint2D`, `WeldJoint2D` with `connectedBody` (entity id string), `anchorX/Y`, `connectedAnchorX/Y`, `autoConfigureConnectedAnchor`, `collideConnected`, and per type `enableLimit`, `lowerAngle`/`upperAngle` (radians) or `lowerTranslation`/`upperTranslation`, `enableMotor`, `motorSpeed`, `maxMotorTorque`/`maxMotorForce`, `enableSpring`, `springHertz`, `springDampingRatio`, `axisX/Y` (prismatic), `linearHertz`, `angularHertz`, `linearDampingRatio`, `angularDampingRatio` (weld).

## Gravity

`Physics2D.Gravity` reads and sets the world gravity (default `(0, -9.8)` m/s²). It is shared by every loaded scene and keeps its value until changed, so set it when your game starts.

## Queries

See [Scripting › Physics 2D](../Scripting/Scripting.md) for raycasts, overlap checks and layers.

# Platform Layer

Funke runs its window, input and operating-system services on **[SDL3](https://github.com/libsdl-org/SDL)** and renders through **WebGPU (Dawn)**. Together they cover Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS and the Web from one code base. This page explains what lives where and how to build SDL3 for each target.

## What SDL3 provides

| Area | Engine entry point | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Window, fullscreen, DPI, cursor, icon, clipboard, drag & drop | `Core/Window.{hpp,cpp}` | One SDL window. Exclusive fullscreen falls back to desktop fullscreen where the OS has no exclusive modes (Wayland, mobile, Web). |
| Keyboard, mouse, touch, text input | `Window::PollEvents` → `Input` | SDL scancodes are translated to the stable `KeyCode` values (`Core/Platform/SDLInputMapping.cpp`). Touch arrives as left-mouse input. |
| Gamepads | `Input` | Hot-plugged `SDL_Gamepad`s fill the four gamepad slots. Button names follow the Xbox layout; SDL's controller database maps other pads onto it. |
| Rendering surface | `Graphics/Backend/WebGPUSurfaceSource.cpp` | Builds the Dawn surface from the SDL window: HWND, Xlib or Wayland, CAMetalLayer, ANativeWindow or the HTML canvas. |
| OS services | `Core/Platform.{hpp,cpp}` (`Funke::Platform`) | Paths, message boxes, folder dialogs, opening files/URLs, file-manager reveal (Explorer `/select`, Finder `open -R`, the freedesktop `FileManager1` D-Bus call on Linux), locale, system theme, process memory, dynamic libraries, thread names, and the tool search path (`ExtendToolSearchPath` adds Homebrew, `/usr/local`, `~/.dotnet` and snap folders so a GUI-started editor finds `dotnet`, `cmake` and `git`). |
| Crash reports | `Core/CrashReporter.cpp` | Windows writes a minidump; Linux and macOS write `<app>-<time>.crash.txt` with a symbolized backtrace (signals on an alternate stack, plus `std::terminate`). Both land in `<user data>/Funke/CrashDumps`. |
| Progress popup | `Core/Platform/Win32BuildProgressWindow` | A native window on Windows; elsewhere the state is drawn by `EditorRuntime::RenderBuildProgressOverlay` (ImGui). |
| Editor UI | `imgui_impl_sdl3` | Consumers register `ImGui_ImplSDL3_ProcessEvent` through `Window::AddNativeEventHook`. |

The custom editor titlebar uses a Win32 window subclass on Windows (snap layouts, maximized inset, DWM shadow) and SDL's hit-test callback elsewhere. Both read the same caption regions (`Core/Platform/TitlebarRegions`).

## Platform macros

`Core/PlatformDetection.hpp` defines exactly one of `FNK_PLATFORM_WINDOWS`, `FNK_PLATFORM_MACOS`, `FNK_PLATFORM_LINUX`, `FNK_PLATFORM_ANDROID`, `FNK_PLATFORM_IOS` or `FNK_PLATFORM_WEB`. It also defines these helpers:

- `FNK_PLATFORM_DESKTOP`, `FNK_PLATFORM_MOBILE` and `FNK_PLATFORM_POSIX` (all `0`/`1`).
- `FNK_PLATFORM_HAS_PROCESSES`: child processes are desktop-only.
- `FNK_PLATFORM_HAS_DYNAMIC_LIBRARIES`: `0` on iOS and the Web. Native package layers are linked statically into the Android, iOS and Web players either way (see [Writing Packages](../Packages/Writing-Packages.md)).
- `FNK_PLATFORM_NAME` and `FNK_ARCH_NAME`, for example `"Windows"` and `"x64"`.

Premake still predefines the Windows, Linux and macOS macros. Other toolchains (Xcode, the Android NDK, Emscripten) rely on the compiler's own target macros. C# scripts get `FUNKE_WINDOWS`, `FUNKE_MACOS`, `FUNKE_LINUX`, `FUNKE_ANDROID`, `FUNKE_IOS`, `FUNKE_VISIONOS` or `FUNKE_WEB` as a define constant. In the editor that is the active build profile's platform, not the editor's own, so platform-specific script code can be played there; the native `FNK_PLATFORM_*` macros stay the real ones (see [Platform-specific code in the editor](../Editor/Testing.md#platform-specific-code-in-the-editor)).

## Building SDL3

SDL3 is the `External/SDL` submodule. It is built with its own CMake into `External/SDL-build/<target>-<arch>/install` (git-ignored). `Setup.bat` / `Setup.sh` run the host build automatically. To run a build yourself:

```bash
python scripts/sdl/SetupSDL.py                                   # host platform (shared library)
python scripts/sdl/SetupSDL.py --target android --android-abi arm64-v8a   # needs ANDROID_NDK_HOME
python scripts/sdl/SetupSDL.py --target ios                      # static library, Xcode generator
python scripts/sdl/SetupSDL.py --target web                      # static library, needs emcmake on PATH
```

Desktop targets use a shared library (`SDL3.dll`, `libSDL3.so.0`, `libSDL3.0.dylib`). Every executable ships it next to `Funke-Engine`, so engine and editor share SDL's global state. On Linux, SDL builds its X11 and Wayland backends from the development packages that Setup installs.

## Platform notes

- **Web:** the browser owns the frame loop. With `FUNKE_CUSTOM_MAIN`, `EntryPoint.hpp` exposes `FunkeRuntimeBegin` / `FunkeRuntimeFrame` / `FunkeRuntimeEnd`, and the Web package's entry point runs one frame per `requestAnimationFrame` through `emscripten_set_main_loop` (no ASYNCIFY). WebGPU adapter and device arrive asynchronously and are handed to the engine with `WebGPUBackend::ProvideDevice`. There are no threads: the job system runs jobs inline. The canvas fills the page and losing focus does not pause the game (browsers already stop hidden tabs).
- **Android / iOS:** the platform package's entry point includes `SDL_main.h` and calls `FunkeRuntimeMain`, so the app is launched through SDL (`SDLActivity` / `UIApplicationMain`). Text input, and with it the on-screen keyboard, is off by default; call `Window::SetTextInputActive(true)` while a text field is focused. Rendering pauses while the app is in the background.
- **macOS:** the window is created with `SDL_WINDOW_METAL`. Dawn renders into the `CAMetalLayer` of an `SDL_Metal_CreateView` view.

Exports for Android, iOS and Web come from platform packages; see [Platform Packages](../Editor/Platform-Packages.md). Those packages build SDL3 statically (iOS, Web) or as `libSDL3.so` (Android) for their target themselves.

# Scenes

A **scene** is a container for a slice of your game — a level, a menu, a screen. It holds entities (with their components) and **systems** (code that runs over them). This page explains how scenes are defined, loaded, saved, and how they behave while the game runs.

If you just want the short version: you design a scene in the editor, it's saved as a `.scene` file, and at runtime the engine loads it, wakes up its systems, and updates it every frame.

---

## Two halves: definition and instance

Funke separates a scene into two things:

| | **Scene Definition** | **Scene (instance)** |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | A *blueprint*: the scene's name, which systems it has, and load/unload callbacks. | The *live* scene: an actual entity world you can play. |
| When it exists | Registered up front, before anything loads. | Created when the scene is loaded. |

You **register** a definition once, then the engine **instantiates** it into a live `Scene` whenever it's loaded. Registering looks like this (conceptually):

```cpp
auto& def = SceneManager::RegisterScene("Level1");
def.AddSystem<MyEnemySpawnerSystem>();
def.OnLoad([](Scene& scene) { /* set the scene up */ });
def.SetAsStartupScene();   // this is the scene the game starts on
```

In practice, when you make scenes in the editor, the runtime wires all of this up for you from your project's scene list — you don't usually write registration code by hand.

Use `OnLoadFromFile` for a `.scene` file. This makes its file read and parsing available to asynchronous loads:

```cpp
def.OnLoadFromFile("Assets/Scenes/Level1.scene");
```

Use `OnLoad` for setup that cannot fail. Other validated setup should use `OnLoadChecked` and return whether the scene is usable:

```cpp
def.OnLoadChecked([](Scene& scene) {
    return LoadLevelData(scene);
});
```

Returning `false` rejects the staged scene with `SceneLoadStatus::LoadCallbackFailed`.

---

## Systems

A **system** is a piece of C++ code that lives in a scene and runs over its entities. Systems derive from `SceneSystem` and override the lifecycle hooks they need:

| Hook | When it runs |
|------|-------------|
| `Awake(scene)` | Once, when the scene is created — before `Start`. |
| `Start(scene)` | Once, right after every system's `Awake`. |
| `Update(scene)` | Every frame. |
| `FixedUpdate(scene)` | Every fixed step (physics-rate, independent of frame rate). |
| `OnPreRender(scene)` | Once per frame after `Update`, just before rendering. |
| `OnEnable` / `OnDisable` | When the system is turned on/off. |
| `OnDestroy(scene)` | When the scene unloads. |

Systems are **owned by the scene** — each scene has its own set, created when it loads and destroyed when it unloads. They can be enabled or disabled at runtime.

> Systems are the C++ way to run scene logic. The C# equivalent is a **SceneSystem** — see [Scripting](../Scripting/Scripting.md). They share the same `Awake`/`Start`/`Update` rhythm.

---

## The scene lifecycle

When a scene loads, things happen in a fixed order:

```
Load scene
 ├─ Instantiate     create systems + an empty entity world
 ├─ OnLoad callback / deserialize the .scene file (recreate entities)
 ├─ ScenePreStartEvent
 ├─ Awake   all systems      ← systems wake up
 ├─ Start   all systems      ← then start
 ├─ (scene is now "loaded")
 └─ ScenePostStartEvent

Every frame while loaded
 ├─ Update systems
 ├─ FixedUpdate systems (zero or more times)
 └─ OnPreRender systems

Unload scene
 ├─ ScenePreStopEvent
 ├─ OnDestroy systems   (in reverse order)
 ├─ OnUnload callback
 ├─ clear entities, clean up physics
 └─ ScenePostStopEvent
```

The **scene events** (`ScenePreStartEvent`, `ScenePostStartEvent`, `ScenePreStopEvent`, `ScenePostStopEvent`) let other code react to scenes coming and going — for example, a global manager that needs to know when a new level is ready.

---

## Loading and switching scenes

The **Scene Manager** controls which scenes are loaded. There's always **one active scene**, but you can have **several loaded at once** (handy for things like a persistent UI scene over a level).

| Action | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| `LoadScene("X")` | Unloads the other scenes and loads `X` as the active scene. |
| `LoadSceneAdditive("X")` | Loads `X` **without** unloading the others (becomes active only if nothing else is). |
| `SetActiveScene("X")` | Makes an already-loaded scene the active one. |
| `UnloadScene("X")` | Unloads a single scene. |
| `ReloadScene("X")` | Saves the scene's current state, reloads it, and restores that state. |

A scene definition can be marked **persistent**, meaning it survives `LoadScene` calls that would otherwise unload it — useful for managers or HUDs you want to keep across level changes.

Raw C++ callers that need failure details should use `TryLoadScene`, `TryLoadSceneAdditive`, or `TryReloadScene`:

```cpp
const SceneLoadResult result = SceneManager::TryLoadScene("Level2");
if (!result) {
    FNK_CORE_ERROR("Scene load failed: {}", result.Message);
}
```

`Succeeded()` is true for `Success` and `AlreadyLoaded`. Failure statuses are `ReentrantLoad`, `NotInitialized`, `NotRegistered`, `NotLoaded`, `InstantiationFailed`, `LoadCallbackFailed`, `SetupFailed`, `BeforeStartFailed`, `AwakeFailed`, `StartFailed`, `CommitFailed`, `AfterStartFailed`, `SnapshotFailed`, `WrongThread`, and `Cancelled`. `Message` carries the error context, while `LoadedScene` is expired when no usable scene was produced. A failed `TryReloadScene` can return the preserved original scene there, so always check the result before treating it as reload success. The legacy `LoadScene`, `LoadSceneAdditive`, and `ReloadScene` methods remain available and return an expired pointer on failure.

Raw C++ `SceneManager` APIs are main-thread-only. Off the main thread, the structured load methods return `WrongThread`; legacy loads and queries return empty, null, false, or zero results; and unload-style void methods do nothing. Registration and mutable-reference APIs throw a catchable `FunkeException` instead of asserting or touching live scene state. Marshal scene work back to the application thread before retrying it.

A non-additive load stages and validates its replacement through load callbacks and system startup before unloading the current non-persistent scenes. If any staged phase fails, the previous loaded scene set and active scene are preserved.

`TryReloadScene` replaces the scene atomically but keeps the same logical scene identity, so it does not emit scene loaded/unloaded events for the internal instance swap.

From a C# script you typically switch scenes through the scripting `SceneManager` API; see [Scripting](../Scripting/Scripting.md).

### Asynchronous loading

`SceneManager.LoadSceneAsync` returns a `Task<Scene?>`. Start it from the engine thread and `await` it so the application can keep updating and rendering while the scene file is prepared:

```csharp
Scene? level = await SceneManager.LoadSceneAsync("Level2", LoadSceneMode.Single);
if (level == null)
    Log.Error("Level2 could not be loaded.");
```

The name and asset GUID overloads both support `Single` and `Additive`. A successful task completes after activation; a load failure returns `null` and preserves the previous scenes. `Single` restarts an already loaded scene from its authored data, as the synchronous API does. Do not block the engine thread with `.Wait()` or `.Result`: activation needs a later frame.

For cancellation, pass a `CancellationToken` as the third argument:

```csharp
try
{
    Scene? level = await SceneManager.LoadSceneAsync(
        "Level2", LoadSceneMode.Single, cancellationToken);
}
catch (OperationCanceledException)
{
    // The existing scenes remain loaded.
}
```

Cancellation is cooperative until activation starts. An in-flight file read or parse is allowed to finish before the operation completes as canceled; cancellation does not interrupt system startup or roll back a successful activation.

The worker reads and parses JSON or binary scene files and referenced prefabs. Supported GUID references to textures, audio, fonts (32px bake) and meshes use the asynchronous asset loader for CPU preparation. Asset publication, including texture uploads, stays on the engine thread with a default limit of one publication and a cooperative 2ms budget per frame. Prepared assets remain retained until activation or cancellation.

Entity construction runs in an unpublished, suspended scene across frames: by default at most 128 top-level entity records or 2ms per batch. The current scenes keep updating and rendering. Activation initializes runtime component state, raises scene events and starts systems before committing the replacement. Each prefab tree, custom callback, hierarchy finalization, runtime setup, upload and old-scene teardown remains indivisible and can exceed the budget. Assets created dynamically by callbacks, legacy path references, material dependencies and font sizes other than the prepared size may still load on demand. This is cooperative loading, not a hard frame-time guarantee. File preparation requires thread support; current threadless Web builds report a load failure.

Pass `IProgress<SceneLoadProgress>` to drive a loading bar and phase label. `Progress` is a phase-weighted fraction from 0 to 1, not a time estimate:

```csharp
var progress = new Progress<SceneLoadProgress>(state =>
{
    loadingBar.Value = state.Progress;
    loadingLabel.Text = state.Phase.ToString();
});
Scene? level = await SceneManager.LoadSceneAsync(
    "Level2", LoadSceneMode.Single, cancellationToken, progress);
```

To prepare the next level while the player remains in the current one:

```csharp
using PreloadedScene? prepared = await SceneManager.PreloadSceneAsync(
    "Level2", cancellationToken, progress);
if (prepared != null)
    await prepared.ActivateAsync(LoadSceneMode.Single, cancellationToken, progress);
```

Keep the `PreloadedScene` until the game decides to switch. Preloading does not create entities, instantiate systems, invoke scene callbacks or change the loaded scene set. A ready preload does not block other requests. Activate it once, or dispose it on the engine thread to release its prepared content. Activation reuses the parsed scene snapshot; it does not re-read a subsequently edited scene file. The activation progress starts a new operation phase at 0.5. Cancellation during entity construction discards the unpublished scene. Script reload and play-mode exit cancel both pending loads and retained preloads.

Native callers register file stages explicitly and receive a completion callback on the main thread:

```cpp
SceneManager::RegisterScene("Level2")
    .OnLoadFromFile("Assets/Scenes/Level2.scene");

const uint64_t operation = SceneManager::LoadSceneAsync("Level2", false,
    [](uint64_t, const SceneLoadResult& result) {
        if (!result) FNK_CORE_ERROR("Scene load failed: {}", result.Message);
    });
```

`CancelSceneLoad(operation)` requests cancellation before activation. Both native calls are main-thread APIs. Ordinary `OnLoad` and `OnLoadChecked` callbacks always run on the main thread; wrapping `LoadFromFile` inside such a callback keeps that file read synchronous. Project scenes registered by the runtime and scripting API use `OnLoadFromFile` automatically.

Native callers can use `PreloadSceneAsync`, then `ActivatePreloadedScene(operation, additive, completion)`. The preload completion reports success with an empty `LoadedScene`; activation supplies the loaded instance. `GetSceneLoadProgress(operation)` exposes the current phase, fraction and entity/asset counts while the request is retained. It returns no value after cancellation/completion is delivered. `SetAsyncSceneLoadBudget(milliseconds, maxEntitiesPerFrame)` adjusts the cooperative entity budget; `AssetLoader::Pump(milliseconds, maxPublications)` controls asset publication. Unused native preloads must be cancelled explicitly.

---

## Saving scenes: the `.scene` file

Scenes are saved to disk as **`.scene` files** (JSON by default; a compact binary format is also available). A scene file stores:

- the scene's **name** and id, and a format **version**,
- the scene's **systems** (and any of their saved settings),
- every **entity** authored in the scene, with **all its components** and its **parent/child hierarchy**.

A couple of important details:

- **Runtime-spawned entities are not saved.** Only entities that belong to the scene (or are prefab instances) get written out. Things you spawn while playing vanish when the scene reloads — which is what you want.
- Saving and loading is a clean **round-trip**: what you save is exactly what you get back.

`.scene` files are [assets](../Assets/Assets.md) like any other, and they reference other assets (textures, audio, fonts) by **GUID**.

---

## Prefabs

A **prefab** is a saved entity (with its children and components) stored as a `.prefab` file, so you can reuse it many times. Drop a prefab into a scene and you get an **instance** of it; you can then tweak individual instances with **overrides** while still tracking which prefab they came from.

Editing the prefab asset updates every instance (except the parts an instance has deliberately overridden). The editor has dedicated support for creating, editing, and instantiating prefabs — see [Editor](../Editor/Editor.md#prefabs).

Script fields that point at the prefab's own entities follow each instance: an `Entity` field, a component field (`Image`, `Transform2D`, …) and also lists and arrays of them (`List<Entity> Slots`, `Image[] Icons`, inline objects with such fields) refer to that instance's children, not to the template's or another instance's. The same happens when entities are duplicated, pasted or cloned with `Entity.Instantiate(entity)`.

---

## Play mode (in the editor)

While you're editing, scene **scripts don't run** — your game logic only ticks when you press **Play**. When you do:

1. The editor writes a private snapshot of every loaded scene in `.funke/PlayMode`, including scenes with no unsaved edits; your `.scene` files are not modified.
2. Scripts and systems begin their `Awake` → `Start` → `Update` lifecycle on the scenes as you left them.

When you press **Stop**, the scenes are reloaded from those snapshots, discarding anything that happened during play; scenes that were unsaved before Play stay marked unsaved. A successful restore also keeps each scene's pre-Play undo and redo history. That's why changes you make to entities *while playing* don't stick — it's a safety net. (In a shipped [runtime](Startup-Processes.md), there's no editor, so the game is simply always "playing.")

A `.scene` file changed by another program while it is loaded in the editor is reloaded, or you are asked first if the scene has unsaved edits. See [Assets › Hot-reload](../Assets/Assets.md#hot-reload-editor).

---

## How the first scene is chosen

At startup the engine loads the **startup scene**. A scene definition is marked as the startup scene (`SetAsStartupScene()`), and the runtime picks it from your project settings — falling back to the last opened scene, then to a default, if none is set. Other scenes in the project's scene list are registered too, but only the startup scene loads automatically. See [Startup Processes](Startup-Processes.md#configure-scenes).

---

## Summary

- A scene is a **definition** (blueprint) that becomes a live **instance** when loaded.
- **Systems** (C++) and **SceneSystems** (C#) run a scene's logic with `Awake` → `Start` → `Update`.
- The Scene Manager keeps **one active scene** but can hold several loaded at once; scenes can be **persistent**.
- Scenes save to **`.scene` files** that round-trip entities, components, and hierarchy; **prefabs** are reusable saved entities.
- In the editor, scripts run only in **Play mode**, and stopping restores the pre-Play snapshot.

## Related pages

- [ECS](ECS.md) — the entities and components a scene contains.
- [Startup Processes](Startup-Processes.md) — when and how the startup scene loads.
- [Scripting](../Scripting/Scripting.md) — SceneSystems and switching scenes from code.
- [Editor](../Editor/Editor.md) — building scenes visually, prefabs, and Play mode.

# Spatial audio and headphones

Add an **Audio Source** to an entity, assign its clip, and enable **3D Sound → Spatial**.
The source follows the entity's world position. The main Camera3D supplies the listener's
position and orientation; a 2D scene uses its main Camera2D.

Enable **HRTF (Headphones)** for binaural playback. The measured ear filters include
front/back and elevation-dependent spectral cues, interaural delay, and level differences.
Listener rotation follows the camera, including pitch and roll. No separate audio assets
or external audio DLLs are required.

```csharp
var source = GetComponent<AudioSource>();
source.Spatial = true;
source.Hrtf = true;
source.MinDistance = 1f;
source.MaxDistance = 30f;
source.Rolloff = AudioRolloff.Linear;
source.Play();

// A one-shot at a fixed world position.
ImpactSound?.PlayOneShotAt(position, hrtf: true);
```

HRTF is off by default, including when loading older scenes. It replaces `Panning`;
volume, distance attenuation, pitch, looping, and `DopplerLevel` still apply. Stereo clips
are averaged to a mono point source before the two ear filters. Prefer mono recordings
for positioned effects; leave music and UI sounds non-spatial. HRTF can be changed during
playback. Directions interpolate between measurements and filter changes blend over 10 ms.

Use stereo headphones and disable additional system/headset spatialization to avoid
processing the signal twice. This is a generic head model, so perceived front/back and
height separation varies with the listener and headphones. It does not simulate walls,
reflections, or room reverb. The KEMAR measurements cover elevation -40° to +90°; directions
below -40° use the lowest measured elevation. The output must be stereo at 8–192 kHz;
otherwise initialization warns and retains ordinary spatial panning. Low sample rates
cannot reproduce the high-frequency elevation cues.

The engine embeds the diffuse-field equalized KEMAR measurements by **Bill Gardner and
Keith Martin, MIT Media Laboratory (1994)**. See the [original dataset and terms](https://sound.media.mit.edu/resources/KEMAR.html)
and `External/kemar/LICENSE`. Recreate the generated header with:

```powershell
Invoke-WebRequest https://sound.media.mit.edu/resources/KEMAR/diffuse.zip -OutFile diffuse.zip
python scripts/audio/GenerateHrtfData.py diffuse.zip
```

The generator checks the archive's SHA-256. The committed header makes builds independent
of network access. SDK/runtime license staging includes the attribution.

Verification: `scripts/dev/Test.ps1 -Suite Engine -Filter "*HRTF*,*spatial*"` mixes actual
audio without opening an output device and checks direction spectra, ear delays, camera
orientation, resampling, short clip tails, thread handoff, component playback, and scene
serialization. `scripts/dev/Test.ps1 -Suite CSharp -Filter SpatialAudioTests` checks the
managed one-shot packing and backward-compatible overload.

# Startup Processes

This page explains **what happens, step by step, when you launch a game made with Funke** — from double-clicking the `.exe` to the first frame your player sees.

If you just want the short version: the runtime boots the engine's subsystems in a fixed order, finds your project, loads your starting scene, runs your scripts, and then enters the main loop that draws every frame.

> This describes the **Runtime** (the shipped game), not the Editor. The Editor follows a very similar path but adds its tools on top.

---

## The big picture

A launched game goes through three stages:

1. **Boot** – start the engine and all its subsystems (window, graphics, audio, physics, …).
2. **Load** – find the project, load the startup scene, run packages and scripts.
3. **Run** – the main loop: read input, update the game, draw a frame, repeat — until the window closes.

```
Launch .exe
   │
   ▼
[1] Boot the engine ── window, graphics, audio, physics, jobs, assets …
   │
   ▼
[2] Load the game ──── project file → packages → startup scene → scripts
   │
   ▼
[3] Main loop ─────── input → update → physics → render → present  (every frame)
   │
   ▼
Window closed → shut everything down cleanly
```

---

## Stage 1 — Boot

### The entry point

Every Funke program (game or editor) starts in the same place: a single `Main()` function (in `EntryPoint.hpp`). The very first things it does are:

1. **Initialize the core** – low-level setup (memory, assertions, logging).
2. **Initialize localization** – the language/translation system.
3. **Capture the command line** – arguments like `--project="C:/path"` are stored so the rest of the engine can read them.
4. **Create the application** – calls `CreateApplication()`, which builds the game's `Application` object.

If anything throws an error during the whole run, it is caught here and logged, so the game fails cleanly instead of crashing silently.

### Finding your project

Before the engine fully starts, the runtime decides **which project to run** (in `RuntimeApplication`):

- If you pass `--project="<path>"`, that folder is used.
- Otherwise it looks **next to the `.exe`** for a project.

It then reads your project's `project.json`. This file holds everything the game needs to know about itself: the window size, the splash screen, which scenes exist, and which scene to start with. If no project is found, the runtime logs a warning and falls back to a built-in sample scene so it still boots.

### Starting the subsystems

Next, `Application::Initialize()` starts every engine subsystem **in a fixed order**. Order matters — later systems depend on earlier ones (for example, the renderer needs the window and graphics device to already exist).

| # | Subsystem | What it does |
|---|-----------|--------------|
| 1 | **Profiler** | Performance measurement (only in profiling builds). |
| 2 | **Job System** | The worker-thread pool for multithreaded work. See [Job System](Job-System.md). |
| 3 | **Frame Arenas** | Fast per-frame scratch memory. |
| 4 | **Window** | Opens the OS window and input via **SDL3**. |
| 5 | **Render API** | Starts the graphics device — **WebGPU (via Dawn)**, which picks Direct3D 12 / Vulkan / Metal under the hood. |
| 6 | **Texture Manager** | Loads built-in textures, manages GPU textures. |
| 7 | **Shader Manager** | Loads and manages shaders. |
| 8 | **Renderer2D** | The 2D sprite/quad renderer. |
| 9 | **Gizmo Renderer** | Debug shapes/lines (optional in runtime). |
| 10 | **GUI Renderer** | The ImGui layer used for on-screen UI/overlays. |
| 11 | **Physics 2D** | The 2D physics world. |
| 12 | **Font Manager** | Loads and bakes fonts for text rendering. |
| 13 | **Asset Registry** | Registers built-in engine assets and indexes your project's assets. See [Assets](../Assets/Assets.md). |
| 14 | **Audio Manager** | Starts the audio device (via miniaudio). |

Some of these can be turned off through the application's configuration (for example, a headless server build may disable the window and audio).

---

## Stage 2 — Load

Once the subsystems are up, the runtime prepares your actual game.

### Configure scenes

The runtime calls `ConfigureScenes()`, which:

1. Puts the game into **play mode** immediately (a shipped game is always "playing").
2. Decides the **startup scene** using this priority:
   1. `StartupScene` from `project.json`, otherwise
   2. the last opened scene, otherwise
   3. a scene literally named `"SampleScene"`.
3. **Registers** every scene listed in the project's build scene list, and wires each one so that loading it reads the matching `.scene` file from disk.

At this point scenes are *registered* (the engine knows they exist and how to load them) but **not yet loaded**.

### Load packages

The runtime then calls `PackageHost::LoadAll()`. This scans next to the executable for package DLLs (`Pkg.<Name>.Native.dll`) and loads each one, calling its `FunkePackage_OnLoad()` function.

**Packages must load before any scene loads**, because a scene may contain components that a package defines. If the package isn't loaded first, the engine wouldn't know how to recreate those components. See [Writing Packages](../Packages/Writing-Packages.md).

### Splash screen (optional)

If your project enables a splash screen, the runtime pushes a **splash layer** here. When a splash is shown, the engine **defers loading the startup scene** until the splash finishes — so the player sees your logo first, and the (possibly heavy) scene load happens behind it. When the splash fades out, the deferred scene load runs.

### Load the startup scene

Whether immediately or after the splash, the engine loads the startup scene. Loading a scene means:

1. **Instantiate** the scene (create its systems and an empty entity world).
2. **Deserialize** the `.scene` file — recreate every saved entity and its components.
3. **Awake** all systems, then **Start** all systems.
4. Fire scene events (`ScenePreStartEvent` → `ScenePostStartEvent`) so other code can react.

See [Scenes](Scenes.md) for the full scene lifecycle.

### Start scripting

When the game needs C# code, the **Scripting host** boots: it starts the .NET runtime (via hostfxr), loads `Funke-ScriptCore.dll` and your game's script assembly, and connects the native ↔ managed bridge. Then `OnApplicationStart` and the per-scene/per-entity script lifecycle begin running. See [Scripting](../Scripting/Scripting.md).

---

## Stage 3 — The main loop

Now the game is live. The engine runs the same loop every frame until the window is told to close. Each frame does this, in order:

```
┌────────────────────────────── one frame ──────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. Input    │ snapshot last frame's input, poll OS events, update state │
│ 2. Fixed    │ run FixedUpdate as many times as needed (physics-rate)    │
│    Update   │ — a fixed timestep, independent of frame rate             │
│ 3. Update   │ audio · global scripts · game logic · scene systems       │
│             │ · physics step · pre-render prep                          │
│ 4. Render   │ Renderer2D draws the scene · UI · gizmos                   │
│ 5. Present  │ swap the buffers — the finished frame appears on screen    │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

A few details worth knowing:

- **Fixed Update** uses an accumulator. If the game runs fast, fixed update might run zero or one time per frame; if a frame was slow, it may run several times to "catch up." This keeps physics and gameplay stable regardless of frame rate.
- **Update** is where most game logic happens — your scripts' `OnUpdate`, scene systems, and so on.
- If a splash was shown, the deferred scene load is triggered early in this stage on the first eligible frame.
- The loop ends when you close the window (or the game calls quit).

---

## Stage 4 — Shutdown

When the loop ends, the engine tears everything down in a clean order: scenes are unloaded (systems get their `OnDestroy`), packages run `FunkePackage_OnUnload`, subsystems shut down, and the core shutdown guard runs last. This ensures files are flushed and resources are released properly.

---

## Quick reference: the boot order

```
Main()
 ├─ InitializeCore, Localization, parse command line
 ├─ CreateApplication()  → load project.json
 └─ Application::Run()
     ├─ Initialize()
     │   ├─ Profiler → JobSystem → FrameArenas
     │   ├─ Window (SDL3) → Render API (WebGPU/Dawn)
     │   ├─ Textures → Shaders → Renderer2D → Gizmos → GUI
     │   ├─ Physics2D → Fonts → Asset Registry → Audio
     │   ├─ ConfigureScenes()   (choose + register startup scene)
     │   ├─ ConfigureLayers()   (push splash if enabled)
     │   ├─ PackageHost::LoadAll()
     │   └─ Load startup scene (now, or after splash) → start scripts
     └─ Main loop:  input → fixed update → update → render → present
```

---

## Related pages

- [Scenes](Scenes.md) — how scenes load and what their lifecycle looks like.
- [ECS](ECS.md) — entities and components, the contents of a scene.
- [Assets](../Assets/Assets.md) — how textures, audio, fonts, etc. are found and loaded.
- [Scripting](../Scripting/Scripting.md) — the C# scripts that run during the loop.
- [Writing Packages](../Packages/Writing-Packages.md) — code loaded at the package step.
- [Job System](Job-System.md) — the worker threads started early in boot.

# Terrain Renderer 2D

**Terrain Renderer 2D** draws ground along a line of points: a **fill** texture below the surface and an **edge** texture along it. Use it for hills in driving games, roads, cliffs and platforms that are not made of tiles. It only draws; give the ground a **Polygon Collider 2D** (concave outlines are fine, see [Physics 2D](Physics-2D.md)) or build the collider from the same points.

Each segment between two points is drawn as one quad sheared vertically, so neighbouring segments share their edges exactly and the edge texture follows every slope without gaps.

## Settings

| Setting | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Points** | The surface from left to right, in the entity's frame (moved, rotated and scaled by its Transform 2D). Set by a generator in the scene file (`points`) or from C# with `SetPoints`. Points must go left to right; a segment that doesn't is skipped. |
| **Fill Texture** | Texture below the surface. Give it **Wrap Repeat** in its import settings so it tiles. |
| **Fill Tile Size** | Width and height one repeat of the fill texture covers. |
| **Fill Mapping** | **World**: the texture is fixed in the entity's frame, its rows stay horizontal under the hills. **Draped**: the texture's top row follows the surface. |
| **Fill Depth** | How far the fill reaches below the surface. |
| **Edge Texture** | Strip along the surface (grass, curb, snow). Also Wrap Repeat. |
| **Edge Thickness**, **Edge Offset** | Height of the strip and of its top above the surface (negative sinks it into the fill). |
| **Edge Tile Length** | Surface length one repeat of the edge texture covers (measured along the slope). |
| **Edge Texture Offset** | Where along its texture the edge starts, in repeats. Set it to the end of the previous piece (`offset + length / tileLength`) so the pattern runs on without a seam across pieces built one after another. |
| **Fill/Edge Color** | Tint, as on a Sprite Renderer. |
| **Sorting Layer**, **Sorting Order**, **Edge Sorting Order** | Draw order against sprites; the edge has its own order so it can lie over the fill. |

Only the segments inside the camera view are drawn, so a long terrain costs little.

## C#

```csharp
var ground = GetComponent<TerrainRenderer2D>();
ground.SetPoints(surface);                  // Vector2[] in the entity's frame
ground.FillTexture = DirtTexture;           // public Texture? field wired in the scene
ground.FillTileSize = new Vector2(16f, 8f);
ground.EdgeOffset = 0.25f;
Vector2[] points = ground.GetPoints();
```

Scene key `TerrainRenderer2D`: `points` (flat `[x0, y0, x1, y1, …]`), `fillTexture` and `edgeTexture` (GUID strings), `fillColor` / `edgeColor` (`[r, g, b, a]`), `fillTileX`, `fillTileY`, `fillMapping` (0 World, 1 Draped), `fillDepth`, `edgeThickness`, `edgeOffset`, `edgeTileLength`, `edgeTextureOffset` (only when not 0), `sortLayer`, `sortOrder`, `edgeSortOrder`.
