# World-space UI

Add a `Transform2D` or `Transform3D` alongside `RectTransform2D` on a UI entity to place its UI hierarchy in the world. The two world transform types remain mutually exclusive.

- The world transform controls position, rotation and scale.
- The RectTransform controls UI size, pivot, anchors and local layout. Child UI entities need only their usual RectTransform and widget components.
- At unit world scale, 100 UI units occupy one world unit. World UI size does not change with the window resolution or safe area.
- A RectTransform without a world-transform canvas ancestor remains screen-space UI.

Images, text and widgets use the canvas transform for drawing. Mouse and touch hit tests project the pointer onto that same canvas plane; dragged widgets keep using their canvas coordinates. The active 3D camera is used when present, otherwise the main 2D camera.

In the Editor View, select the canvas to manipulate its world transform. Select a child to edit its local UI layout; the Rect tool edits its size. The 3D view also supports picking and framing world-space UI.

World-space images and text depth-test against scene meshes, so opaque geometry in front hides them. They render before postprocessing and MSAA resolve, without writing depth, preserving UI blending and canvas ordering. Screen-space UI is drawn over world-space canvases. Separate world canvases have stable canvas order; sorting layer/order controls elements within each canvas.

# Known Limitations (Beta)

Funke is in beta. This page records platform restrictions, core-only boundaries and remaining feature limits. **Optional external packages are part of Funke's available functionality:** a feature absent from the core is not necessarily missing from Funke. See the [package overview](README.md#packages) and each package's documentation before treating a core restriction as an engine-wide limitation. Please report unexpected behavior as a bug.

Reference games are also distributed separately through the Launcher's **Asset Library**, including **NeonStack** and **Voxtau**. The [Asset Library catalog](https://github.com/Ben-Scr/Funke-AssetLibrary) contains these projects; the empty starters under this repository's `templates/` directory are not the full set of examples.

## Platforms

- **Desktop games are exported for the editor's own platform.** The Windows editor builds Windows games, the Linux editor Linux games and the macOS editor macOS games (an `.app` bundle); there is no cross-export between desktop platforms yet.
- **Linux and macOS are new.** They have had far less testing than Windows. macOS games are ad-hoc signed but not notarized, so Gatekeeper asks before the first launch on other Macs (right-click › **Open**). Dragging assets from the Asset Browser to other applications works on Windows only.
- **Android, iOS and Web exports are new.** They come from platform packages ([Platform Packages](Editor/Platform-Packages.md)) and need extra SDKs. Android builds arm64-v8a only and has had little on-device testing; the iOS package needs a Mac and has not been verified on a device yet; Web needs a browser with WebGPU.
- **C# on Android, iOS and Web runs on Mono.** iOS and Web use the interpreter, which is noticeably slower than the desktop JIT, and culture-sensitive formatting uses invariant rules everywhere outside the desktop.
- Desktop builds include a private **.NET 10 Runtime** by default; disabling **Include .NET Runtime** requires players to install it separately. Windows players still need the **Visual C++ Redistributable**. Mobile and Web builds bundle their Mono runtime.
- **Web builds have additional limits.** C# games need the .NET 11 SDK with `wasm-tools`; scripts run interpreted, the class library is not trimmed, and jobs run sequentially in the current browser build. See [Platform Packages](Editor/Platform-Packages.md#web).

## Feature availability and remaining limits

| Feature | Current support and remaining limit |
|---|---|
| Animation blend trees, layers, avatar masks, root motion | The Animator plays one state machine layer with crossfades; drive extra motion from a script. |
| Tilemaps | Available through the optional external [Funke.Tilemap2D](https://github.com/Ben-Scr/Funke-PackageRegistry/tree/main/packages/Funke.Tilemap2D) package, with chunked tile storage, rendering, Inspector support and C++/C# APIs. Install through the Package Manager; consult the package README for its capabilities and limits. Sprite entities and prefabs remain an alternative for projects without the package. |
| 2D lighting | Available through the optional external `Funke.Lighting2D` package: ambient light, up to 32 point lights and 64 rectangular shadow occluders. This version has hard shadows, one lighting plane and no normal maps or per-layer light masks. Mobile/Web performance and device compatibility still need validation. See [Lighting 2D](Engine-Core/Lighting-2D.md). |
| Physics joint types | [2D physics](Engine-Core/Physics-2D.md#joints) provides revolute, prismatic and weld joints. Other joint types are not exposed by the built-in 2D components. |
| Model import | `.obj`, `.gltf` and `.glb` meshes and glTF skeletal animation are supported. FBX, glTF material/texture import and morph targets are not; assign Funke materials separately. See [3D](Engine-Core/3D.md#custom-meshes). |
| Standard 3D materials and lighting | The standard material has a base-color texture and scalar metallic/roughness values; dedicated normal/metallic/roughness maps and alpha-cutout settings are not exposed. Custom shaders can implement their own surface shading. Only the main directional light casts shadows; point/spot shadows are not available. MSAA 4x is available for 3D geometry. |
| Split screen and built-in camera-follow rigs | Multiple camera entities can exist, but each scene selects one main 2D camera and the game uses the first enabled 3D camera. Move the active camera from a script for following behavior. |
| Core audio mixing | Spatial Audio Sources and `Audio.PlayOneShotAt` are available; `AudioStream` streams files from disk. The core exposes per-source and master volume, without mixer groups. See the audio examples in [Scripting](Scripting/Scripting.md#what-scripts-can-do-the-api) for the optional mixer package. |
| Input action maps and rebinding | Available through the optional external [Funke.Input](https://github.com/Ben-Scr/Funke-PackageRegistry/tree/main/packages/Funke.Input) package, including keyboard/mouse/gamepad bindings and saved rebinding. Consult the package README for version-specific authoring tools and engine requirements. The core also supports direct polling (`Input.GetKey`, `Input.GetGamepadButton`). |
| Asynchronous scene activation and asset streaming | `LoadSceneAsync` reads and parses JSON/binary scene files on a worker. Entity/component creation, asset resolution, GPU uploads and lifecycle hooks still run on the main thread, so large scenes or uncached assets can cause an activation hitch. There is no progress or preload-only API. File preparation requires threads; current Web builds report a load failure. See [Scenes](Engine-Core/Scenes.md#asynchronous-loading). |
| Localization authoring | Games have string tables, a C# API and the Localized Text component, but no table editor or preview-language picker in the editor; Button labels, Dropdown options and Input Field placeholders are not localized automatically (set them from `Localization.Get`). |
| Text shaping and font coverage | Text Renderers load Unicode glyphs on demand from their assigned font. Use a font containing the required characters: the bundled IBM Plex fonts cover Latin Extended, but not Greek, Cyrillic or CJK. Missing glyphs use the font's replacement character or `?`. There is no fallback-font chain, bidirectional layout, OpenType shaping, combining-mark positioning or color-emoji rendering. First use of a glyph can cause a small rasterization/upload cost. |
| Creating prefab variants in the editor | Variants load correctly; create them by editing a prefab file. |

## Editor

- Undo and redo history belong to each loaded scene instance. Switching between loaded scenes, entering and leaving Prefab Mode, and a successful Play/Stop round trip preserve edit-scene histories. Closing, replacing or reloading a scene discards its history; closing Prefab Mode discards the prefab's own history. Failed play-mode restoration discards the suspended histories. Asset file operations are not covered by scene Undo.
- Moving entities between two loaded scenes cannot be undone.
- Large textures are decoded on the UI thread the first time they are selected, which can cause a short hitch.
- Hot reload keeps the previous working assembly when a replacement cannot be read or its types cannot be resolved. A first load without any working assembly still needs a successful build; script lifecycle callbacks can run again when instances restart after a reload attempt.

## Packages

- Native dependencies are resolved transitively and loaded before their dependents. Missing or incompatible dependencies prevent the affected packages from loading; inspect the package log for the reason.
- `packages-lock.json` records exact package versions. **Restore locked versions** restores registry releases with their recorded URL and SHA-256; Git and local packages still need to be reinstalled or copied manually. See [Packages](Packages/Package-System.md#packages-lockjson).

# Package System

This page explains how Funke's package system works **under the hood** — the loader, build outputs, runtime loading, the cloud registry, and the rules that aren't obvious from the outside.

If you just want to *write* a package, start with [Writing Packages](Writing-Packages.md). This page is the reference for how the machinery fits together.

If you want to **use an existing package**, start with the [package overview](../README.md#packages) or browse the [Funke Package Registry](https://github.com/Ben-Scr/Funke-PackageRegistry). Tilemaps (`Funke.Tilemap2D`) and input actions with saved rebinding (`Funke.Input`) are already available as external packages. This repository's `packages/` directory is not the complete catalog; use the editor's **Package Manager** to discover and install published packages.

> **Source of truth:** the loader/validator lives in `premake/package-loader.lua`. When anything here disagrees with that file, the file wins.

---

## The three install roots

A package can reach a project from three places:

| Root | Who ships it | When it's used |
|------|--------------|----------------|
| `<repo>/packages/<Name>/` | The engine itself | Always scanned. |
| `<project>/Packages/<Name>/` | The project (committed, or installed via the editor) | Used when project files are generated *for that project*. |
| Cloud registry | Third-party authors | Installed into `<project>/Packages/` by the editor's Package Manager. |

When generating project files for a specific game, the project path is passed to premake:

```sh
./vendor/bin/premake5.exe vs2022 --funke-project="C:/path/to/MyProject"
```

That absolute path tells the loader both where the project's `Packages/` folder is and where to read `project.json`.

---

## The layers, in detail

| Layer | Builds | Links engine? | Notes |
|-------|--------|---------------|-------|
| `native` | `Pkg.<Name>.Native` (C++ SharedLib) | Yes | Gets the engine include set, the import macro, and the matching EnTT entity-bits define. |
| `native_standalone` | the same `Pkg.<Name>.Native` SharedLib | No | Pure C++. No engine symbols — logging macros are unavailable; use `printf` or your own logger. |
| `csharp` | `Pkg.<Name>` (C# net10.0 SharedLib) | n/a | Always references `Funke-ScriptCore`. |

**`native` and `native_standalone` cannot coexist** in one package: they would both compile into the single `Pkg.<Name>.Native` DLL, but one links the engine and the other is explicitly the "no engine link" path. The loader rejects the combination at generation time, and the scaffolder refuses it upfront.

### Deprecated layer names

Older manifests used `engine_core` (→ `native`) and `standalone_cpp` (→ `native_standalone`). They still load but log a warning. Use the new names in new manifests.

---

## The project allow-list

When project files are generated for a project, `project.json`'s `packages` array decides which packages actually register as build projects:

```jsonc
{ "packages": ["Funke.Tilemap2D", "MyGame.Loot"] }
```

| State | Result |
|-------|--------|
| Field present, non-empty | Only the listed packages register. Their dependencies are pulled in automatically. |
| Field present but empty `[]` | No packages register (a fresh project). |
| Field absent / file missing | **No packages register** — fail-closed. Without an explicit list, intent is unknown. |
| No project passed at all | Engine-developer mode: scan everything under `<repo>/packages/`. |

Skipped packages produce a one-line log. A listed package with no matching manifest produces a warning.

> **Always regenerate project files after editing the allow-list** or adding/removing a package. The IDE solution does not update itself.

---

## Versions and dependencies

`version` is a [SemVer](https://semver.org) number: `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` with an optional pre-release (`1.2.0-beta.1`). Two optional manifest fields build on it:

```lua
engine = ">=2026.1.0 <2027.0.0",            -- engine versions the package supports
dependencies = {
    "MyGame.Core",                          -- any version
    "MyGame.Grid@^1.2.0",                   -- name@range
    { name = "MyGame.Ui", version = "~2.1" },
    ["MyGame.Audio"] = ">=0.3.0",
},
```

Ranges use npm syntax:

| Range | Means |
|---|---|
| `^1.2.3` | `>=1.2.3 <2.0.0` (below 1.0: `^0.2.3` is `<0.3.0`) |
| `~1.2.3` | `>=1.2.3 <1.3.0` |
| `1.2`, `1.x` | any `1.2.*` / `1.*` |
| `>=1.0.0 <2.0.0` | every comparator must hold |
| `1.0.0 - 2.0.0` | inclusive range |
| `^1.0.0 \|\| ^3.0.0` | either set |
| `*` or empty | any release |

A pre-release only matches when the range names that exact version with a pre-release (`>=2.0.0-beta`), so `^1.0.0` never picks up `2.0.0-beta`. For the `engine` check the engine's own pre-release suffix is ignored: `>=2026.1.0` accepts `2026.1.0-beta.1`.

The rules are checked in three places, all with the same resolver:

- **Project file generation** (`premake/package-loader.lua`) fails with an `[Funke Packages]` error naming the package, the range and the installed version.
- **Runtime loading** (`PackageHost`) pulls in dependencies that `project.json` does not list, loads dependencies before the packages that need them, and skips a package whose dependency is missing, outside its range or incompatible with the engine. Only that package and its dependents are skipped; the error is in the log.
- **The Package Manager** shows each package's requirements, marks unmet ones and lists dependency-only packages as *dependency*.

A package can also need [engine modules](../Engine-Core/Engine-Modules.md) (`modules = { "Funke.2D" }`). Installing it adds them to `project.json` `modules`; runtime loading skips a package whose module is off, and the game build fails with an error naming the package and the module. The engine modules themselves are listed in the Package Manager under **Engine Modules**.

### packages-lock.json

The editor writes `packages-lock.json` next to `project.json` whenever packages change. It records the exact version of every loaded package and where it came from (registry URL and SHA-256, git URL, local copy or engine). Commit it: `Packages/` is not committed, and on a fresh clone the Package Manager offers **Restore locked versions**, which downloads exactly those registry releases and checks their SHA-256.

---

## Build outputs

For each registered package:

- A **native** (or **native_standalone**) layer → one `Pkg.<Name>.Native` project (C++20 SharedLib).
  - Output: `bin/<config>/Pkg.<Name>.Native/Pkg.<Name>.Native.dll`
  - Compatibility metadata: the adjacent `Pkg.<Name>.Native.dll.funkeabi` file.
- A **csharp** layer → one `Pkg.<Name>` project (C# net10.0 SharedLib).
  - Output: `bin/<config>/Pkg.<Name>/Pkg.<Name>.dll`
  - Always references `Funke-ScriptCore` implicitly.

Configurations are **Debug / Release / Dist**. `Dist` strips symbols and is what shipped runtimes use.

---

## Runtime loading

The runtime side is `Funke-Engine/src/Core/PackageHost.{hpp,cpp}`:

- **`PackageHost::LoadAll()`** — scans the directory next to the running executable for `Pkg.<Name>.Native.dll` files and loads each one. Idempotent. This runs during [startup](../Engine-Core/Startup-Processes.md), **before any scene loads**, so package-defined components exist before a scene tries to deserialize them.
- **`PackageHost::LoadInstalled()`** — the editor's "I just installed a package, pick it up without restarting" hook. Filters against the project allow-list first.
- Each loaded DLL is queried for **`FunkePackage_OnLoad`** (called now) and optionally **`FunkePackage_OnUnload`** (called at shutdown). Both are plain C entry points.
- **`PackageHost::UnloadAll()`** — runs `FunkePackage_OnUnload` and frees modules in reverse order at shutdown.

Before loading, PackageHost validates the adjacent `.funkeabi` file. A `native`
package records the SHA-256 fingerprint of the exact `Funke-Engine.dll` it linked;
a missing or different fingerprint is rejected with rebuild guidance before any
package code can run. `native_standalone` records an engine-independent boundary.
Keep the sidecar with the DLL whenever package binaries are copied or shipped.

When the editor opens a project, it first checks every source package under
`<project>/Packages/` that has a native layer. If none of its builds (workspace
output or `Bin/` prebuilt) passes this check for the running engine, the editor
regenerates the package workspace and rebuilds it before `LoadAll()` runs. An
engine rebuild therefore costs one package build on the next editor start
instead of a manual rebuild (`PackageHost::FindStaleProjectNativePackages()`).

This guard detects C++ ABI drift; it does not make the C++ boundary stable.
Distribute `native` packages as source and rebuild them for each engine SDK/build.

On Android, iOS and the Web there are no package DLLs: the platform builder compiles
each native layer into the player (`funke_platform_sdk/native_packages.py` and
`funke_add_native_packages` in `cmake/FunkeEngine.cmake`) together with a generated
registry. The player calls it before startup, and `LoadAll()` then runs the linked
packages' `FunkePackage_OnLoad` in dependency order, before any DLL
(`Packages/StaticPackages.hpp`). Mono resolves `[DllImport("Pkg.<Name>.Native")]`
through `StaticPackages::FindSymbol` on Android and iOS; the Web relink generates its
own table from the package archives. See [Writing Packages](Writing-Packages.md#android-ios-and-web-native-layers-are-linked-statically).

### The package API surface

Inside `FunkePackage_OnLoad`, packages register their content through helpers:

- `Funke-Engine/src/Packages/PackageApi.hpp` — defines `FUNKE_PACKAGE_API` (the cross-DLL export marker) and the entry-point signatures.
- `Funke-Engine/src/Packages/PackageRegistration.hpp` — `Package::RegisterSerializableComponent<T>(...)` and `Package::DeclareComponentConflict<A, B>()`.

A registered component behaves exactly like a built-in one: it shows up in the Add Component menu, draws in the Inspector, and round-trips through scene serialization.

---

## Cloud registry

End users install packages through the editor's **Package Manager**, which reads a static `index.json` from a public GitHub repo (the **Funke Package Registry**). There is no server — it's a static file served over the GitHub CDN.

Install flow:

1. Fetch the registry `index.json` (atomic write to a cache file).
2. Plan the install: pick the newest release that supports this engine, then the newest fitting release of each dependency that is missing or outside its range. A plan that would push an installed package outside a range another installed package declares is refused, with the reason.
3. For each release in the plan (dependencies first): download the zip, **verify its SHA-256**, extract it (rejecting path-traversal and zip-bomb tricks), move the single top-level folder into `<project>/Packages/`, and check that it contains the expected name and version.
4. Add the requested package to the project's allow-list (dependencies load transitively) and update `packages-lock.json`.
5. Regenerate project files, rebuild, and call `PackageHost::LoadInstalled()` to load the new DLLs live.

**Updates** use the same plan: when the registry has a newer release that fits the engine and every installed dependent, the package shows **Update to x.y.z**. The old folder is moved to `.funke/package-backup/` and restored if any step fails, so a failed update leaves the previous set of packages in place.

To **publish**: zip your package folder (a single top-level folder containing `funke-package.lua`), host the zip somewhere fetchable, and add an entry to the registry's `index.json`:

```json
{ "packages": [ {
    "name": "MyGame.Grid", "description": "...", "layers": ["native", "csharp"],
    "version": "1.3.0", "downloadUrl": "https://.../grid-1.3.0.zip", "sha256": "<64 hex>",
    "engine": ">=2026.1.0", "dependencies": ["MyGame.Core@^2.0.0"],
    "versions": [
        { "version": "1.2.0", "downloadUrl": "https://.../grid-1.2.0.zip", "sha256": "<64 hex>", "engine": ">=2026.1.0" }
    ]
} ] }
```

The top-level `version` / `downloadUrl` / `sha256` describe one release; `versions` adds others, so projects on an older engine can still install a release that supports it. `minEngineVersion: "X"` is still read as `engine: ">=X"`. A release may list `"modules": ["Funke.2D"]`; the install then enables those modules, and a module this engine doesn't know or wasn't compiled with stops the install. Pushing that file is the only deploy step.

---

## The package CLI tool

`Funke-PackageTool` is a small stateless .NET command-line program the engine shells out to for network and archive work. It handles things like searching NuGet, downloading files with progress, zipping/unzipping projects, and the registry fetch/download/verify/extract operations above. The editor calls it behind the scenes — you rarely invoke it directly.

---

## Non-obvious rules (gotchas)

These break things in ways the error messages don't always explain:

1. **EnTT entity bits must match across DLLs.** The `native` layer automatically defines the engine's entity-bit width so the ECS types line up across the package boundary. A mismatch is undefined behavior that shows up as memory corruption when entities cross between the engine and a package. (Handled for you by the loader — only a concern if you hand-write a package project, which you shouldn't.)

2. **The native import macro is required.** The engine is a shared library; the `native` layer is set up to *import* engine symbols, not export them. The loader configures this automatically; `native_standalone` deliberately doesn't (it links nothing from the engine).

3. **Library paths are per-configuration.** The native layer links the WebGPU/Dawn library and `Funke-Engine.lib`, which live in per-config folders. The loader sets this up per configuration (Dist points at the Release Dawn library; each configuration links its own engine build first). A linker error here usually means a configuration mismatch.

4. **The csharp layer auto-references `Funke-ScriptCore`.** Don't list it in `dependencies` — that field is for *other packages*. Pure-managed packages pay nothing for the reference if they don't use it.

5. **The allow-list is fail-closed.** A missing `project.json` or absent `packages` field means *no* packages, not *all* packages.

6. **Regenerate after manifest/allow-list changes.** The scaffolder does this; manual edits don't.

7. **Native DLLs are tied to one engine binary.** The build writes a `.dll.funkeabi` sidecar and PackageHost refuses a missing or stale one. The editor rebuilds project source packages automatically on the next project open after the engine changes; engine packages under `packages/` are rebuilt with the engine. Do not publish one generic native DLL for multiple engine builds.

# Writing Packages

A **package** is how you add new functionality to Funke. Anything the engine core doesn't ship — a custom component, a gameplay system, a third-party integration — lives in a package. This page shows you how to write your own.

If you just want the short version: run the scaffolder, fill in your code, list the package in your project, and the editor builds and loads it.

> **See also:** [Package System](Package-System.md) covers the deeper architecture (the loader, build outputs, the CLI, and the non-obvious rules) once you've got the basics here.

---

## What is a package?

A package is a self-contained folder with:

- a **manifest** (`funke-package.lua`) that describes it, and
- one or more **layers** of code (C++ and/or C#).

When built, a package produces one or two DLLs that Funke loads at startup. Your package can register new components, systems, and behavior, and those show up in the editor just like the built-in ones.

### Where packages live

There are two places a package can live:

| Location | Who it's for |
|----------|--------------|
| `<engine repo>/packages/<Name>/` | Packages shipped with the engine itself. |
| `<your project>/Packages/<Name>/` | Packages that belong to *your* game. **This is where your packages go.** |

End users can also install packages from a cloud registry through the editor's Package Manager — more on that below.

---

## The three layers

A package is made of **layers**. Each layer is a kind of code, and you pick the ones you need:

| Layer | Language | Links the engine? | Use it for |
|-------|----------|-------------------|------------|
| `native` | C++ | **Yes** | Components, systems, anything that talks to the engine in C++. |
| `native_standalone` | C++ | No | Pure C++ with no engine dependency (e.g. wrapping a C library). |
| `csharp` | C# (.NET 10) | n/a (auto-links the script core) | Gameplay logic, managed APIs, tools. |

Two important rules:

- A package can mix `csharp` with `native`, but it **cannot have both `native` and `native_standalone`** — they conflict (one links the engine, the other deliberately doesn't).
- The `csharp` layer automatically references `Funke-ScriptCore`, so you get the scripting API for free.

---

## Quick start: scaffold a package

Don't hand-write the boilerplate — use the scaffolder. From the engine repo root:

```sh
# A C++ package for your project, with an example "Health" component wired end-to-end:
python scripts/packages/NewPackage.py MyGame.Combat --layers native --component Health \
    --project "C:/path/to/MyProject"
```

Other common variations:

```sh
# Pure C# package:
python scripts/packages/NewPackage.py MyGame.Tools --layers csharp --project "C:/path/to/MyProject"

# C++ and C# together, bridged via P/Invoke:
python scripts/packages/NewPackage.py MyGame.Loot --layers native+csharp --project "C:/path/to/MyProject"

# Depends on another package (optionally with a version range):
python scripts/packages/NewPackage.py MyGame.Combat --depends-on MyGame.Core@^1.0.0
```

The scaffolder creates the folder, the manifest, the entry point, the example code, **adds the package to your project's allow-list**, and regenerates the project files so it appears in your IDE. After that you can build from the editor (or your IDE) and it loads automatically.

> **Naming rule:** package names are `PascalCase.PascalCase`, with at least one dot. `MyGame.Loot` ✓, `MyGame.Loot.Combat` ✓, but `loot` ✗, `My-Game` ✗, `MyGame.loot` ✗. The folder name must match the package name.

---

## The manifest (`funke-package.lua`)

The manifest is a small Lua file that returns a table describing your package. A typical one:

```lua
return {
    name        = "MyGame.Loot",        -- required, PascalCase.PascalCase
    version     = "0.1.0",              -- required, MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH
    description = "Loot drops and tables.",
    engine      = ">=2026.1.0",         -- optional, engine versions this release supports

    layers = {
        native = {
            sources          = { "src/**.cpp", "src/**.hpp", "include/**.hpp" },
            includes         = { "include" },
            private_includes = { "src" },
        },
        csharp = {
            sources     = { "Source/**.cs" },
            pinvoke_dll = "Pkg.MyGame.Loot.Native",  -- only if calling into the native layer
        },
    },

    dependencies = { "MyGame.Core@^1.0.0" },   -- optional, other packages this one needs
    modules = { "Funke.2D" },                  -- optional, engine modules this one builds on
}
```

Key points:

- **`name`** and **`version`** are required; every layer needs a non-empty **`sources`** list. Bump `version` with `scripts/packages/BumpPackageVersion.py` when you publish a change: patch for fixes, minor for additions, major for anything that breaks packages or games using yours.
- **`dependencies`** lists *other packages* (not NuGet packages, not the script core), each optionally with a version range (`"MyGame.Core@^1.0.0"` or `{ name = "MyGame.Core", version = "^1.0.0" }`). Dependencies build and load first, and a project only needs to list your package; the rest comes along. The range syntax is in [Package System](Package-System.md#versions-and-dependencies).
- **`engine`** states which engine versions the release supports; a project on another engine gets a clear error instead of a crash.
- **`modules`** lists the [engine modules](../Engine-Core/Engine-Modules.md) your package uses (`"Funke.2D"`, `"Funke.3D"`). Installing the package turns them on in the project; a project with one of them off doesn't load the package and refuses to build it. Leave it out when you only use the core (UI, text, audio, input, assets). `NewPackage.py --modules Funke.2D` writes it for you.
- The manifest is validated when project files are generated — mistakes fail loudly with a clear `[Funke Packages]` message, so you'll know right away.

---

## Writing C++ code: the entry point

Every C++ package needs an **entry point** — a function Funke calls when it loads your package. Without it, the package won't be recognized.

```cpp
#include "Packages/PackageApi.hpp"
#include "Core/Log.hpp"

extern "C" FUNKE_PACKAGE_API int FunkePackage_OnLoad() {
    FNK_INFO_TAG("Pkg.MyGame.Loot", "Loaded.");
    return 0;   // 0 = success
}

// Optional — runs when the package unloads:
extern "C" FUNKE_PACKAGE_API void FunkePackage_OnUnload() {
}
```

`FUNKE_PACKAGE_API` is the marker that exports these functions across the DLL boundary. Always use it (not the engine's `FUNKE_API`).

### Registering a component

Most C++ packages exist to add a **component**. You register it inside `FunkePackage_OnLoad`:

```cpp
#include "MyLootComponent.hpp"
#include "Inspector/PropertyRegistration.hpp"
#include "Packages/PackageRegistration.hpp"

extern "C" FUNKE_PACKAGE_API int FunkePackage_OnLoad() {
    using namespace Funke;

    std::vector<PropertyDescriptor> props = {
        Properties::Make("DropChance", "Drop Chance", &MyLootComponent::DropChance),
        Properties::Make("TableId",    "Table Id",    &MyLootComponent::TableId),
    };

    Package::RegisterSerializableComponent<MyLootComponent>(
        /* display name    */ "Loot Drop",
        /* subcategory     */ "Gameplay",
        /* serialized name */ "LootDrop",
        /* draw inspector  */ nullptr,   // null = use the automatic inspector
        /* serialize       */ nullptr,
        /* deserialize     */ nullptr,
        /* category        */ ComponentCategory::Component,
        /* properties      */ std::move(props),
        /* icon            */ "particles");   // optional, see below

    return 0;
}
```

Once registered, your component appears in the editor's **Add Component** menu, draws its fields in the Inspector, and saves/loads with scenes automatically. The `props` list is what makes its fields editable — see the inspector documentation for the full set of field types (sliders, asset pickers, enums, references, and so on).

The optional **icon** is the name of an editor icon from `FunkeAssets/Textures/Editor/General` without size and extension (`audio_source`, `particles`, `light_point`, `collider_box_3d`, `rigidbody_2d`, `camera`, `grid`, ...). The Inspector shows it in the component's header. `Package::RegisterComponent` takes it as its last argument too, and `Package::SetComponentIcon<MyLootComponent>("particles")` sets it after registration. Without one the editor guesses an icon from the display name.

You can also declare that two components can't coexist:

```cpp
Package::DeclareComponentConflict<MyLootComponent, Funke::SomeOtherComponent>();
```

### Hooking into scenes and 2D physics

Components that own runtime state outside the registry (a physics body, a cache) need to know when scenes come and go. Register a `SceneExtension` (`Scene/SceneExtensions.hpp`) in `FunkePackage_OnLoad` and remove it in `FunkePackage_OnUnload`:

- `OnSceneCreated(Scene&)`: connect EnTT signals (`on_construct` / `on_destroy`) for your component types.
- `OnRuntimeStateInitialized(Scene&)`: build state for components that already exist (a staged load resumes, play mode copies the scene).
- `OnSceneDestroyed(Scene&)`: drop everything keyed by the scene and disconnect the signals. It can run more than once per scene.

The hooks run for every scene, detached ones included, so check `Scene::IsDetached()` / `IsLifecycleSuspended()` where it matters. `SceneExtensions::Register` applies the hooks to scenes that are already loaded.

A package can also add a 2D physics backend next to Box2D with `PhysicsSystem2D::RegisterExtension(PhysicsExtension2D)`: `SyncToPhysics` (push transform edits, runs in edit mode too), `Step`, `SyncFromPhysics` (write positions back, see `PhysicsSystem2D::DecomposeWorldToLocal`), `DispatchCollisions` (raises the usual `OnCollisionEnter2D/Stay2D/Exit2D` script callbacks), `DrawDebug` (the F8 physics overlay) and `Shutdown`. `BodyComponent` is the `entt::type_hash` of your body component; the transform hierarchy leaves entities with it to the backend. `Funke.Physics` in the package registry uses both hooks.

---

## Scripts in a C# package

A `csharp` layer can ship `EntityScript`s, `SceneSystem`s and `GlobalSystem`s like a game's own scripts. Scenes and prefabs name them by full class name (`"className": "MyGame.Loot.LootDrop"`), or by class name alone when no other package has a class with that name. Public fields show in the Inspector and are saved like any script field.

The editor lists them once the game's scripts are compiled: **Add Component › Packages › <package>** for scripts and components, the Inspector's script picker, the scene's **Add System** list and **Project Settings › Global Systems**. Only public, non-abstract classes with a parameterless constructor show up. Picking one saves its full class name; a plain `Component` (not an `EntityScript`) is saved by class name, because `GetComponent<T>()` looks it up that way.

---

## Bridging C# to C++ (P/Invoke)

If your package has **both** a native and a csharp layer, the C# side can call into the C++ side. This is useful when you want fast native data with a friendly managed API on top.

The conventions:

1. Set `pinvoke_dll = "Pkg.<Name>.Native"` in the manifest's csharp layer.
2. Prefix every exported C function with your package name (underscores instead of dots) so symbols don't collide: `MyGame.Loot` → `MyGame_Loot_GetDrop`.
3. Use `extern "C"` on the C++ side and `CallingConvention.Cdecl` on the C# side.

C++ side:

```cpp
extern "C" FUNKE_PACKAGE_API
int32_t MyGame_Loot_RollDrop(int32_t tableId) { /* ... */ return 0; }
```

C# side:

```csharp
using System.Runtime.InteropServices;

internal static class Native {
    private const string Lib = "Pkg.MyGame.Loot.Native";

    [DllImport(Lib, EntryPoint = "MyGame_Loot_RollDrop",
               CallingConvention = CallingConvention.Cdecl)]
    public static extern int RollDrop(int tableId);
}
```

The names and signatures **must match exactly** on both sides — there's no tool that checks this for you, and a mismatch shows up as a runtime error. If you need pointer/`Span` work, set `allow_unsafe = true` on the csharp layer. Prefer pointers and `int` over `out`/`ref` and `bool` in these signatures: blittable signatures work unchanged in the Web build.

### C# wrappers for native components

For `entity.GetComponent<LootDrop>()` and `AddComponent<LootDrop>()` on a component registered in C++, derive a wrapper from `Component`. The engine finds the component by the class name when it equals the serialized name; map the wrapper to the component's **display name** once, from a module initializer, so the script core also treats it as a native component (no managed field state) and name lookups such as `"Loot Drop"` resolve:

```csharp
using System.Runtime.CompilerServices;

public class LootDrop : Component
{
    public float DropChance
    {
        get => Native.GetDropChance(RequireComponent<LootDrop>());   // RequireComponent returns Entity.ID
        set => Native.SetDropChance(RequireComponent<LootDrop>(), value);
    }
}

internal static class Registration
{
    [ModuleInitializer]
    internal static void Register() => Entity.RegisterNativeComponent<LootDrop>("Loot Drop");
}
```

The script core runs a package's module initializer before it looks up a component type, so the mapping is there on first use. Native code that hands entities back to C# returns the script id (`GetEntityScriptId` from `Scripting/ScriptEntityReference.hpp`); `Entity.FromID(id)` turns it into an `Entity`, and `ResolveEntityReference` goes the other way in C++.

---

## Android, iOS and Web: native layers are linked statically

The Android, iOS and Web players cannot load package DLLs. Their builders compile your `native` (or `native_standalone`) layer from source and link it into the player, so the same package works everywhere without extra work. What that relies on:

- **Entry points** are renamed per package at compile time (`FunkePackage_OnLoad` becomes `FunkePackage_OnLoad_MyGame_Loot`), so several packages can link into one binary. Define them exactly as shown above, in a `.cpp` of the native layer.
- **Every function C# calls is marked `FUNKE_PACKAGE_API`** in a `.cpp` file. The builder scans for that marker to build the table that resolves `[DllImport("Pkg.<Name>.Native")]` on Android and iOS (and keeps those functions from being stripped). On the Web the .NET relink resolves them from the package's `Pkg.<Name>.Native.a` archive.
- **Globals and helper functions** share one binary with other packages: keep them in your own namespace or an anonymous namespace.
- Static initializers in your package may not run on these platforms; do setup in `FunkePackage_OnLoad`.

The builder logs `Native package layers linked into the player: …` for every build that includes one.

---

## Android: Java code, Maven libraries and manifest entries

A package can bring what an Android SDK needs: Java sources, AARs/JARs from Maven repositories and entries for the game's `AndroidManifest.xml`. Declare them in an `android` table of the manifest; the Android builder picks them up for every game that lists the package (no Gradle involved):

```lua
android = {
    java     = { "Android/Java/**.java" },                    -- compiled into the APK (Java 8 syntax)
    maven    = { "com.example:some-sdk:1.2.3" },              -- plus everything it depends on
    manifest = "Android/AndroidManifest.xml",                 -- merged into the game's manifest
    placeholders = { someAppKey = "default-value" },          -- ${someAppKey} in the manifest
},
```

- **`maven`** coordinates are resolved from Google's Maven repository and Maven Central, transitive dependencies included (the newest requested version of a library wins, as in Gradle). Pin the result with a lock file and ship it with the package; builds then download exactly those files and check their SHA-256:

  ```sh
  python <engine>/platforms/Funke.Platform.Android/Builder/android_maven.py lock Packages/MyGame.Billing
  ```

  This writes `Android/maven.lock.json`. Rerun it whenever the `maven` list changes; without a matching lock the build resolves the libraries again and warns. Downloads are cached per user, so only the first build needs internet access.
- **`manifest`** is a normal `AndroidManifest.xml`: activities, services, providers, `<meta-data>`, permissions and `<queries>` are merged into the game's, like the libraries' own manifests. `${applicationId}` is the game's application ID; every other `${name}` comes from the Android build profile option of that name, or from `placeholders` when the profile does not set it (Release builds warn about that, so a sample key never ships unnoticed).
- **Calling the Java code from C#:** a Java class exposes `public static String method(String)` methods, C# calls them with `AndroidBridge.Call(className, method, argument)`, and Java answers asynchronously with `dev.funke.player.FunkeBridge.send(channel, message)`, received by `AndroidBridge.Subscribe(channel, handler)` on the main thread. Strings are typically JSON. `FunkeBridge.getActivity()` returns the game's activity; SDK calls that touch views belong on its UI thread. See [Platform Packages](../Editor/Platform-Packages.md#ads-and-other-java-libraries-from-packages).

`Funke.Ads` in the package registry is a complete example: a C# API, a Java plugin, AdMob and UMP from Maven, and a manifest entry filled from the build option `admobAppId`.

---

## Turning a package on for your project

A project only builds the packages it explicitly lists. Open your project's `project.json` and add the package to the `packages` array:

```jsonc
{
  "packages": [
    "MyGame.Core",
    "MyGame.Loot"
  ]
}
```

- Only listed packages are built and registered. Their dependencies are pulled in automatically.
- An empty list (or a missing file) means **no** packages — this is deliberate (a fresh project ships with none).
- After editing the list, **regenerate project files** (the scaffolder does this for you; manual edits don't).
- Rebuilding the engine from the editor also regenerates and rebuilds every enabled native package before relaunch.

> If you used `NewPackage.py --project`, this entry was added for you.

---

## Sharing and installing packages

Packages can be shared through Funke's **cloud registry**. End users don't touch any of the above — they open the editor's **Package Manager**, browse the registry, and click install. The editor downloads the package, verifies it, drops it into the project's `Packages/` folder, adds it to the allow-list, rebuilds, and loads it — all without a restart.

To publish your own package to the registry, you zip the package folder and add an entry (download URL + checksum) to the registry index. The full publishing flow and the registry format are covered in [Package System](Package-System.md#cloud-registry).

---

## Common mistakes to avoid

These trip people up, so internalize them:

- **No entry point** → the package is silently ignored. Every C++ package needs `FunkePackage_OnLoad`.
- **Forgetting the allow-list** → the package never builds. Add it to `project.json` (and regenerate).
- **Editing files but not regenerating project files** → your IDE solution lags behind the manifest. Re-run premake (or use the scaffolder, which does it for you).
- **Copying only a native DLL** → PackageHost also requires its generated `.dll.funkeabi` sidecar. A `native` package must be rebuilt after the engine changes; for source packages under `<project>/Packages/` the editor does this when it opens the project.
- **Mixing `native` and `native_standalone`** → not allowed; pick one.
- **Wrong package name format** → must be `PascalCase.PascalCase`. The folder name must match.
- **P/Invoke name/signature mismatch** → runtime crash. Keep both sides identical.
- **An export without `FUNKE_PACKAGE_API`** → works on desktop if exported some other way, but Android and iOS can't resolve the `[DllImport]`.

---

- [Package System](Package-System.md) — the loader, build outputs, the package CLI, the cloud registry, and the deeper rules.
- [ECS](../Engine-Core/ECS.md) — what a component is and how the engine stores them.
- [Scripting](../Scripting/Scripting.md) — the C# API your csharp layer builds on.

# Funke Documentation

Welcome to the documentation for **Funke**, a modular 2D and 3D game engine supporting game development in **C++ and C#**. The native engine is implemented in C++20; projects can use C++ scripts, C# scripts, or both. These pages explain how the engine works and how to build games with it, from launching a game to writing your own packages.

New here? Start with **[Your First Game](Getting-Started.md)**, a 15-minute walkthrough from install to a desktop build. After that, a good reading order is **Editor → ECS → Scenes → Scripting**, then the rest as you need it. **[Known Limitations](Known-Limitations.md)** distinguishes core-only restrictions, available package features and remaining beta limitations.

**Funke includes an external package and project ecosystem.** This repository does not contain every available feature or reference game. Tilemaps and input actions/rebinding are available through [optional packages](#packages). For existing reference games, open the Launcher's **Asset Library**: **NeonStack** and **Voxtau** are game projects, and **FunkeBench** is a benchmark sample. The [Asset Library catalog](https://github.com/Ben-Scr/Funke-AssetLibrary) is maintained separately; `templates/` contains only the built-in empty starters.

---

## Engine Core

The foundational systems that make a game run.

- **[Startup Processes](Engine-Core/Startup-Processes.md)** — what happens, step by step, when a game launches: boot, load, and the main loop.
- **[ECS](Engine-Core/ECS.md)** — entities and components, the building blocks of everything in a scene.
- **[Scenes](Engine-Core/Scenes.md)** — scenes, systems, the scene lifecycle, saving, and prefabs.
- **[Engine Modules](Engine-Core/Engine-Modules.md)** — the optional `Funke.2D` / `Funke.3D` modules: turning them on in a project, what the editor offers, and how game builds leave unused modules out.
- **[Terrain Renderer 2D](Engine-Core/Terrain-2D.md)** — hills and roads along a line of points: tiled fill plus an edge strip.
- **[Physics 2D](Engine-Core/Physics-2D.md)** — Box2D bodies, colliders (concave polygons), revolute/prismatic/weld joints, density and gravity.
- **[Physics 3D](Engine-Core/Physics-3D.md)** — Jolt-based Rigidbody 3D, Box/Sphere/Capsule/Mesh Collider 3D, triggers, raycasts and the C# API.
- **[3D](Engine-Core/3D.md)** — Transform 3D, Camera 3D with skybox, Mesh Renderer and materials, directional/point/spot lights, shadows, the 3D renderer and the 3D Editor View.
- **[Animation](Engine-Core/Animation.md)** — keyframe clips for any component property or script field, Animator Controller state machines with crossfades, the Animation and Animator windows, record mode, events and the C# API.
- **[Custom Shaders](Engine-Core/Custom-Shaders.md)** — your own WGSL shaders for meshes, sprites and post effects: the `@property` header, materials, hot reload, errors, C# API and builds.
- **[Lighting 2D](Engine-Core/Lighting-2D.md)** — optional external package for ambient light, point lights and rectangular shadow occluders.
- **[Graphics Settings](Engine-Core/Graphics-Settings.md)** — render scale, post-processing, particles, shadows, texture quality, anisotropic filtering and anti-aliasing: project defaults and changing them at runtime with `RenderSettings`.
- **[Job System](Engine-Core/Job-System.md)** — running work across multiple CPU cores.
- **[Localization](Engine-Core/Localization.md)** — translating interface text, the per-language JSON files, supported languages, and on-demand downloads.
- **[Platform Layer](Engine-Core/Platform-Layer.md)** — SDL3 window/input, the portable OS services, platform macros, and building SDL3 for Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS and Web.

## Assets

- **[Assets](Assets/Assets.md)** — how textures, audio, fonts, scenes, and prefabs are identified, found, referenced, and loaded.
- **[Data Assets](Assets/Data-Assets.md)** — shared, reusable game data (Funke's ScriptableObject equivalent).

## Scripting

- **[Scripting](Scripting/Scripting.md)** — writing game logic in C# and C++: script types, lifecycle, Inspector integration, and compilation/reload workflows.
- **[Native C++ scripts](Scripting/Scripting.md#native-c-scripts)** — create and attach C++ gameplay scripts in the editor.
- **[C++ application and SDK guide](../../Funke-Engine/README.md)** — build a native application directly with Funke, including projects that do not use the editor.

## Packages

Optional packages provide existing Funke features as well as an extension mechanism for your own code. A feature being absent from the core does not mean it is unavailable in Funke.

| Feature | External package |
|---|---|
| Tilemaps | [Funke.Tilemap2D](https://github.com/Ben-Scr/Funke-PackageRegistry/tree/main/packages/Funke.Tilemap2D) — chunked tile storage, rendering, Inspector support and C++/C# APIs. |
| Input actions and rebinding | [Funke.Input](https://github.com/Ben-Scr/Funke-PackageRegistry/tree/main/packages/Funke.Input) — named actions, control maps, keyboard/mouse/gamepad bindings and saved rebinding. |
| 2D lighting | [Funke.Lighting2D](Engine-Core/Lighting-2D.md) — ambient light, point lights and shadow occluders. |
| Audio mixing | [Funke.AudioMixer](https://github.com/Ben-Scr/Funke-PackageRegistry/tree/main/packages/Funke.AudioMixer) — optional mixer functionality; see the [scripting examples](Scripting/Scripting.md). |

In the editor's **Package Manager**, refresh the registry, find the package and choose **Install**. Browse the [Funke Package Registry](https://github.com/Ben-Scr/Funke-PackageRegistry) for more packages. Consult each package's README for supported engine versions, prerequisites, APIs and limits; source versions can include features not yet in the published release.

- **[Writing Packages](Packages/Writing-Packages.md)** — a practical guide to authoring your own package.
- **[Package System](Packages/Package-System.md)** — how packages are built, loaded, and distributed (the internals).

## Editor

- **[Editor](Editor/Editor.md)** — the visual tool for building scenes, testing in Play mode, and producing a finished game.
- **[Building and Shipping](Editor/Building-and-Shipping.md)** — verified Windows game exports and standalone engine release bundles.
- **[Standalone Verification](Editor/Standalone-Verification.md)** — binary installation, managed package, Editor play mode, relocated exports and Windows Sandbox checks.
- **[Test Builds and Debug Tools](Editor/Testing.md)** — Debug/Development/Release, build profiles for test variants, the developer console with `[DevCommand]`, the physics overlay, isolated player data and scripted test runs with screenshots.
- **[Command-Line Tool](Editor/Command-Line.md)** — `funke create`, `funke build`, validate, convert, prefabs, sprite slicing and packages without opening the editor.
- **[Editor Bridge](Editor/Editor-Bridge.md)** — `funke editor`: drive the open editor from the command line (Play, taps and keys, offscreen screenshots at any resolution, console, recompile, logs), even while it is minimized.
- **[Platform Packages](Editor/Platform-Packages.md)** — Android, iOS and Web exports as installable packages, their requirements, C# through Mono, and the builder protocol for writing your own.
- **[Platform Export Testing](Editor/Platform-Export-Testing.md)** — run actual Web, Android and iOS simulator exports and check script execution and rendered output.

## Reference

- **[Third-Party Libraries](Reference/Third-Party-Libraries.md)** — the open-source libraries Funke is built on.

---

## How the pieces fit together

```
        ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │                   Editor                     │  ← you build the game here
        │   Hierarchy · Inspector · Viewport · Build   │
        └───────────────────────┬─────────────────────┘
                                 │ produces
                                 ▼
        Scenes ── contain ──► Entities ── have ──► Components
          │                                            ▲
          │ run                                        │ add your own via
          ▼                                            │
        Systems / Scripts (C#) ──────────────► Packages
          │
          │ heavy work →  Job System
          │ content    →  Assets
          ▼
        Runtime  ── boots everything in →  Startup Processes
```

- The **Editor** is where you author; the **Runtime** is what ships and runs your game (see [Startup Processes](Engine-Core/Startup-Processes.md)).
- A game is made of **Scenes**, which contain **Entities** built from **Components** ([ECS](Engine-Core/ECS.md)).
- **Scripts** ([Scripting](Scripting/Scripting.md)) and systems give entities behavior; **Packages** ([Writing Packages](Packages/Writing-Packages.md)) add new components and features.
- **Assets** ([Assets](Assets/Assets.md)) are the content; the **Job System** ([Job System](Engine-Core/Job-System.md)) parallelizes heavy work.

# Third-Party Libraries

Funke is built on a small set of well-established open-source libraries. This page lists what they are and what each one does in the engine, so you know where a given capability comes from.

Funke's philosophy is to keep mandatory dependencies few and focused — each library below earns its place by doing one job well.

---

## Rendering & windowing

| Library | Role in Funke |
|---------|---------------|
| [WebGPU via Dawn](https://dawn.googlesource.com/dawn) | The graphics backend. Dawn implements the WebGPU API and **picks the right native backend at runtime** — Direct3D 12, Vulkan, or Metal — depending on the platform. |
| [SDL3](https://github.com/libsdl-org/SDL) | Opens the OS window and handles keyboard, mouse, touch and gamepad input, plus dialogs, clipboard, paths and other platform services on every target. |
| [Dear ImGui](https://github.com/ocornut/imgui) | The immediate-mode UI used to build the editor's panels and the runtime's on-screen overlays. |
| [ImGuizmo](https://github.com/CedricGuillemet/ImGuizmo) | The editor's move/rotate/scale gizmos in the Viewport. |

---

## Simulation & gameplay

| Library | Role in Funke |
|---------|---------------|
| [EnTT](https://github.com/skypjack/entt) | The Entity Component System — how entities and components are stored and iterated. See [ECS](../Engine-Core/ECS.md). |
| [Box2D](https://github.com/erincatto/box2d) | 2D physics — rigid bodies, colliders, and collision detection. The lightweight Fast Body 2D physics is the optional Funke.Physics package. |
| [Jolt Physics](https://github.com/jrouwe/JoltPhysics) | 3D physics — Rigidbody 3D, box/sphere/capsule/mesh colliders, triggers and raycasts. See [Physics 3D](../Engine-Core/Physics-3D.md). |

---

## Audio & assets

| Library | Role in Funke |
|---------|---------------|
| [miniaudio](https://github.com/mackron/miniaudio) | The audio backend — device output and sound playback. |
| [GLM](https://github.com/g-truc/glm) | Vector and matrix math. |
| [STB](https://github.com/nothings/stb) | Image loading (decoding PNG/JPG/etc. into textures). |

---

## Scripting

| Library | Role in Funke |
|---------|---------------|
| [.NET 10 LTS / hostfxr](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/) | Hosts the C# scripting runtime. The engine boots .NET through hostfxr and loads the scripting assemblies. See [Scripting](../Scripting/Scripting.md). |

---

## A note on supported frameworks

For C# scripting, Funke targets **.NET 10.0 LTS**. Scripts and C# packages build against that runtime.

## Related pages

- [Startup Processes](../Engine-Core/Startup-Processes.md) — where these libraries are initialized during boot.
- [Scripting](../Scripting/Scripting.md) — the .NET scripting host.
- [ECS](../Engine-Core/ECS.md) — how EnTT is used.

Funke is a lightweight, modular game engine with **C++ and C# support** for game development, focused on performance and supporting both 2D and 3D projects. The native engine is implemented in C++20; game logic and packages can be written in C++, C#, or a combination of both. > **Beta.** The editor and launcher run on **Windows x64**, **Linux x64** and **macOS** (Apple Silicon and Intel), and each exports games for its own desktop platform. Android, iOS and Web exports come from platform packages. See [Known Limitations](Github-Docs/Documentation/Known-Limitations.md). **Making a game?** Download the latest build for Windows, Linux or macOS from [Releases](https://github.com/Ben-Scr/Index/releases), install the [.NET 10 SDK](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/10.0), and follow **[Your First Game](Github-Docs/Documentation/Getting-Started.md)**. **License:** Funke is free and open source under the [MIT License](LICENSE.txt). Use it for any project, commercial or not; just keep the license notice with copies of the engine (game builds already include it in their `Licenses` folder). ## Develop with C++ and C# - **C#:** write game logic with `EntityScript`, `SceneSystem` and `GlobalSystem`, Inspector integration and hot reload. Start with [Your First Game](Github-Docs/Documentation/Getting-Started.md) and the [scripting guide](Github-Docs/Documentation/Scripting/Scripting.md). - **C++:** create native scripts in the editor with `NativeScript`, Inspector integration and native rebuild/reload, or build an application directly with the native SDK. See [Native C++ scripts](Github-Docs/Documentation/Scripting/Scripting.md#native-c-scripts) and the [C++ application/SDK guide](Funke-Engine/README.md). - **Combine both:** use C++ and C# scripts in the same project and author [packages with native and/or managed layers](Github-Docs/Documentation/Packages/Writing-Packages.md). The languages have distinct APIs and build requirements; follow the guide for your chosen workflow. ## Packages and reference games Funke's available features span the engine and separately distributed packages. This repository's built-in components and empty project templates are not the full catalog. - **Tilemaps** are available through [Funke.Tilemap2D](https://github.com/Ben-Scr/Funke-PackageRegistry/tree/main/packages/Funke.Tilemap2D). - **Input actions, control maps and saved rebinding** are available through [Funke.Input](https://github.com/Ben-Scr/Funke-PackageRegistry/tree/main/packages/Funke.Input). - Install optional packages through the editor's **Package Manager**; see the [package overview](Github-Docs/Documentation/README.md#packages) for discovery and installation. - **Reference games already exist:** open the Launcher's **Asset Library** to download projects such as **NeonStack** and **Voxtau**, or the **FunkeBench** sample. They are distributed through the separate [Funke Asset Library](https://github.com/Ben-Scr/Funke-AssetLibrary), not the engine repository's `templates/` folder. Check the package documentation and Asset Library alongside [Known Limitations](Github-Docs/Documentation/Known-Limitations.md) when evaluating Funke's capabilities. A feature supplied by an optional package is available in Funke even when it is not built into the core. ## Preview Images ### Editor

## Getting Started Clone with submodules: ```bash git clone --recurse https://github.com/Ben-Scr/Index.git cd Funke ``` Then follow the steps for your platform. Re-run setup after pulling changes that touch dependencies, submodules, Premake files, or C# projects.
Windows (MSVC v143 / Visual Studio 2022 toolchain) **Prerequisites:** Visual Studio 2022 (MSVC v143 toolset + Windows SDK), .NET 10 SDK, Python 3.10+, Git, and CMake. Opening Funke's `net10.0` game projects in Visual Studio requires Visual Studio 2026 (18.0+) even though the native build continues to use the VS2022/v143 toolchain. After a fresh clone, fetch and build the git-ignored Dawn/WebGPU dependency once: ```bat scripts\dawn\SetupDawn.bat ``` Generate the project files: ```bat scripts\Setup.bat ``` Setup checks every prerequisite and asks `[Y/n]` before installing a missing one via winget: Python, Git, the .NET 10 SDK, CMake, Premake, and (default *no*, several GB) the Visual Studio 2022 Build Tools with the C++ workload. Pass `-y` to accept all, or `--no-install` to only report what is missing. Build managed projects with the .NET 10 SDK and native projects with the Visual Studio 2022 toolchain: ```powershell .\scripts\BuildWindows.ps1 -Configuration Release ``` Create and verify the standalone engine bundle: ```powershell .\scripts\BuildWindows.ps1 -PublishBundle ``` Create the Windows setup with selectable packages, templates and command-line tools: ```powershell .\scripts\BuildInstaller.ps1 -DownloadCompiler ``` See [Installer development](installer/README.md) for build and signing options, and [Install Funke on Windows](Github-Docs/Documentation/Editor/Installer.md) for the setup workflow. See [Building and Shipping](Github-Docs/Documentation/Editor/Building-and-Shipping.md) for game exports, prerequisites, and the clean-machine release checklist.
Linux (GNU Make) **Prerequisites:** a C++20 compiler (GCC or Clang; Dawn's source build needs Clang), GNU Make, CMake, the .NET 10 SDK, Python 3.10+, Git, and the X11 / Wayland development packages SDL3 builds against. Running the editor needs a Vulkan driver (Mesa or the GPU vendor's). Generate the makefiles: ```bash chmod +x scripts/Setup.sh ./scripts/Setup.sh ``` Setup asks `[Y/n]` before installing anything missing through apt, dnf, pacman or zypper: Python, Git, the .NET 10 SDK, CMake, and the C++ toolchain with the X11/Wayland/GL development headers. It then builds SDL3 (`scripts/sdl/SetupSDL.py`). Distribution-built .NET SDKs (e.g. Ubuntu's `dotnet-sdk-10.0`) work as well as Microsoft's. Build Dawn (WebGPU) once, then everything else. `Funke-Managed` builds the C# projects (Funke-ScriptCore, the hot-reload compiler and the package tool) with `dotnet`; the Launcher target also bundles the Editor, Runtime, `funke` tool and EngineSDK next to the Launcher: ```bash ./scripts/dawn/SetupDawn.sh make config=dist -j"$(nproc)" Funke-Runtime make config=release -j"$(nproc)" Funke-Launcher ./bin/Release-linux-x86_64/Funke-Launcher/Funke-Launcher ``` `python3 scripts/PackagePosix.py` packs that folder into `Funke-Editor--Linux-x64.tar.gz`.
macOS (Apple Silicon or Intel, GNU Make) **Prerequisites:** macOS 11 or later, the Xcode Command Line Tools (`xcode-select --install`), CMake, the .NET 10 SDK, Python 3.10+ and Git. Rendering uses Metal through Dawn. ```bash chmod +x scripts/Setup.sh ./scripts/Setup.sh ``` Setup offers to install missing tools through [Homebrew](https://brew.sh) and opens the Command Line Tools installer when they are missing. The quickest start is `brew install python3 cmake premake make` first. Setup finds versioned Pythons (`python3.13`), installs the .NET SDK into `~/.dotnet` without administrator rights (the Homebrew cask needs them), and replaces a premake that can't run on Apple Silicon with Homebrew's. Then build Dawn once and the rest: ```bash ./scripts/dawn/SetupDawn.sh make config=dist -j"$(sysctl -n hw.ncpu)" Funke-Runtime make config=release -j"$(sysctl -n hw.ncpu)" Funke-Launcher ./bin/Release-macosx-arm64/Funke-Launcher/Funke-Launcher ``` On managed Macs where `make` fails with *Permission denied*, use GNU make (`brew install make`) and write `gmake` instead of `make`; the editor then uses `gmake` too. On Intel Macs the folder is `Release-macosx-x86_64`. `python3 scripts/PackagePosix.py` packs it into `Funke-Editor--macOS-.tar.gz`.
## Documentation Guides for building games with Funke live in **[`Github-Docs/Documentation`](Github-Docs/Documentation/README.md)**. ## Built With - [WebGPU via Dawn](https://dawn.googlesource.com/dawn) — rendering (picks D3D12 / Vulkan / Metal at runtime) - [SDL3](https://github.com/libsdl-org/SDL) — windowing, input, gamepads & platform services - [Box2D](https://github.com/erincatto/box2d) — 2D physics - [EnTT](https://github.com/skypjack/entt) — ECS - [Miniaudio](https://github.com/mackron/miniaudio) — audio - [GLM](https://github.com/g-truc/glm) / [STB](https://github.com/nothings/stb) — math & image loading - [.NET 10 LTS / hostfxr](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/) — C# scripting host ![Views](https://komarev.com/ghpvc/?username=ben-scr-repo-name&label=Repo%20views&color=218a45&style=flat)
SECURITY.md:
# Security Policy

## Supported versions

Only the latest published release (including the current beta) receives fixes.

## Reporting a vulnerability

Please do **not** open a public issue. Use GitHub's private reporting instead:
[Report a vulnerability](https://github.com/Ben-Scr/Index/security/advisories/new).

Include the Funke version, what an attacker could do, and steps or a file that reproduces it.

Areas where reports are especially useful: loading untrusted scene, prefab or project files; the package installer and registry downloads; the Launcher's Asset Library downloads; and the release signing and checksum verification.

# Imagegen icon concepts

Three alternatives per asset. Each folder includes the generated master and transparent PNG exports at 16, 32, 64, 128, and 256 pixels. Masters are scaled to fit the square without stretching.

- Folder: 01 open pocket; 02 closed folder with label panel; 03 open folder with visible sheet.
- C# file: 01 code brackets; 02 braces; 03 C#.
- Scene file: 01 clapperboard; 02 landscape; 03 stage.

These are candidate assets, not installed in the editor. The actual regular-folder asset is under [Editor/General/open_folder](../../../../Funke-Runtime/FunkeAssets/Textures/Editor/General/open_folder); C# and scene assets are under [Editor/FileIcons](../../../../Funke-Runtime/FunkeAssets/Textures/Editor/FileIcons). Their existing files have been preserved.

Image generation: built-in imagegen, using isolated flat 2D editor icon prompts on transparent backgrounds; amber folders, purple documents for C#, blue documents for scenes. C# variants were regenerated in purple to avoid transparency artifacts.

# Windows installer

`scripts/BuildInstaller.ps1` packages an existing Windows x64 release bundle with Inno Setup 6.7.3. It does not compile the engine. The setup targets Windows 10/11 x64, installs Funke for the current Windows user and can install the official Microsoft .NET 10 SDK and Visual C++ runtimes when needed. Both runtime architectures are required: x64 for the engine applications and x86 for the bundled Premake package generator. Windows on Arm is not currently an installer target.

The default installer contains binaries, assets, templates, package tools and `EngineSDK/FunkeSDK.json`; it excludes engine sources, native headers and link libraries. `-IncludeNativeSdk` adds the staged native headers and libraries for C++ scripts and packages, without engine implementation sources. The input bundle must have been staged with native development support. For direct payload preparation the equivalent option is `--include-native-sdk`. Upgrading to the binary installer removes obsolete engine-source/native-SDK directories inside the application SDK; project directories are separate.

`scripts/BuildWindows.ps1 -PublishBundle` and `scripts/PackagePosix.py` also produce binary distributions by default. Their opt-in native SDK switches are `-IncludeNativeSdk` and `--include-native-sdk`. Developer launcher staging retains native support by default; `scripts/CopyEngineSdk.py ... --binary-only` stages a managed-only SDK. The manifest advertises only runtime folders actually staged, and the release verifier requires complete Development and Release payloads.

The default installer contains binaries, assets, templates, package tools and `EngineSDK/FunkeSDK.json`; it excludes engine sources, native headers and link libraries. `-IncludeNativeSdk` adds the staged native headers and libraries for C++ scripts and packages, without engine implementation sources. The input bundle must have been staged with native development support. For direct payload preparation the equivalent option is `--include-native-sdk`. Upgrading to the binary installer removes obsolete engine-source/native-SDK directories inside the application SDK; project directories are separate.

`scripts/BuildWindows.ps1 -PublishBundle` and `scripts/PackagePosix.py` also produce binary distributions by default. Their opt-in native SDK switches are `-IncludeNativeSdk` and `--include-native-sdk`. Developer launcher staging retains native support by default; `scripts/CopyEngineSdk.py ... --binary-only` stages a managed-only SDK. The manifest advertises only runtime folders actually staged, and the release verifier requires complete Development and Release payloads.

User instructions: [Install Funke on Windows](../Github-Docs/Documentation/Editor/Installer.md).

## Build

From the repository root, first produce a complete Release + Dist bundle:

```powershell
scripts/BuildWindows.ps1 -PublishBundle
scripts/BuildInstaller.ps1 -DownloadCompiler
```

The first command builds the engine and stages its publish bundle. The second explicitly allows downloading the pinned Inno compiler into `bin-int`, then prepares the installer payload and compiles setup. Subsequent installer builds can reuse the staged bundle and compiler. Native engine changes require a fresh bundle first.

The packaging machine also needs Windows SDK `mt.exe` (found automatically, or supplied with `-ManifestToolPath`). Both installer packaging and `BuildWindows.ps1 -PublishBundle` use `scripts/PrepareBundledPremake.ps1` to merge the UTF-8 process manifest into staged Premake before publishing, so installation and project paths containing non-ASCII characters work. The vendor executable remains unchanged; the installer payload inventory records both hashes. Users of the finished installer or ZIP do not need the Windows SDK.

To use an existing compiler and bundle:

```powershell
scripts/BuildInstaller.ps1 `
    -BundleDirectory 'C:\Builds\FunkeBundle' `
    -CompilerPath 'C:\Program Files (x86)\Inno Setup 6\ISCC.exe' `
    -OutputDirectory 'C:\Builds\Installers'
```

Defaults are `bin/Release-windows-x86_64/Funke-Launcher` for the input and `bin/installer` for output. Release identity comes from the bundle metadata. The outputs are:

- `FunkeSetup-<version>-Windows-x64.exe`
- The executable's `.sha256` checksum
- The executable's `.manifest.json` payload inventory and `.dependencies.json` dependency record

The finished setup contains its payload and prerequisite installers; it does not download them during installation. Preparing that payload requires network access unless its locked inputs are already available locally. `-PrerequisiteDirectory` supplies the Microsoft installers from an existing directory; `-CatalogPath` selects an alternate package catalog. These inputs are validated against their expected metadata and hashes.

## Optional packages

The package catalog in `windows/packages.lock.json` pins the package versions, download locations and checksums. The initial selection contains five packages implemented in C#:

| Package | Version |
|---|---|
| Funke.AudioMixer | 1.1.1 |
| Funke.Cryptography | 0.1.0 |
| Funke.Serialization | 0.1.1 |
| Funke.Tween | 1.0.0 |
| Funke.Networking | 1.0.0 |

Selected sources are installed under `EngineSDK/packages`. They appear in the editor's Package Manager, where the user enables them separately for each project. Installation does not modify existing projects or enable all packages in new projects. Source files must remain in the payload: the project package workspace compiles them with the .NET SDK when enabled.

The initial catalog excludes native packages and platform exporters. Native packages need matching engine ABI artifacts and possibly C++ build tools. Android, Web and iOS exporters also need platform toolchains and a complete native engine SDK; copying their manifests into this desktop bundle is insufficient.

## Installation modes

The recommended installation includes the core application and templates. Full installation also includes the CLI and all five catalog packages; custom installation permits individual choices. Setup selects English or German from the system language. The default location is `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Funke`.

Inno's standard `/VERYSILENT /SUPPRESSMSGBOXES /NORESTART /LOG` and `/COMPONENTS` options are supported. Silent mode does not bypass Windows administrator approval for missing Microsoft prerequisites. For an unattended deployment, preinstall those prerequisites or provide an appropriately elevated deployment context. Exit code 3010 from a prerequisite requests a restart, and setup defers launching Funke until the restart is resolved.

Rerunning setup preserves the previous location and selections. Deselecting an optional component during an upgrade does not delete its existing files. Uninstall uses tracked application files; it does not remove project folders, preferences or shared Microsoft runtimes.

## Signing and CI

Public release builds must sign the engine bundle before packaging and sign both setup and its uninstaller. Use the same identity for both stages:

```powershell
scripts/BuildWindows.ps1 -PublishBundle -RequireSigning `
    -SigningCertificatePath 'C:\Signing\funke.pfx' `
    -SigningTimestampUrl 'https://your-rfc3161-timestamp-service.example'
scripts/BuildInstaller.ps1 -DownloadCompiler -RequireSigning `
    -SigningCertificatePath 'C:\Signing\funke.pfx' `
    -SigningTimestampUrl 'https://your-rfc3161-timestamp-service.example'
```

Set the PFX password through `FUNKE_SIGNING_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD`, or pass the name of another secret environment variable using `-SigningPasswordEnvironmentVariable`. Do not put the password in the command line. Alternatively, use `-SigningCertificateThumbprint` for a certificate with an accessible private key in `CurrentUser\My` or `LocalMachine\My`.

`BuildInstaller.ps1` passes the signing configuration to `SignInstaller.ps1` through process environment variables. Inno calls that helper for setup and the uninstaller. It locates Windows SDK `signtool.exe`, signs using SHA-256, verifies the signature and expected signer, and checks the timestamp when configured. The helper suppresses native diagnostics that could expose signing arguments.

The Windows CI job builds the installer after the signed publish bundle, using the existing certificate secrets and timestamp setting. Tags require signing; builds without configured credentials remain unsigned for testing. CI uploads setup, checksum, payload inventory and dependency record. The tag release job adds them to the existing draft release.

## Release checks

Run the installer integration smoke test on a test account with the prerequisites installed and no existing Funke installation:

```powershell
scripts/ci/installer_smoke_test.ps1 `
    -InstallerPath 'bin/installer/FunkeSetup-<version>-Windows-x64.exe'
```

The test uses an isolated path containing spaces and a non-ASCII character. It checks selective package installation, adding components, removing obsolete installer-owned package sources, enabling Tween in a new project, compiling its Dist assembly during a Release game export, and uninstalling while preserving separate projects. These checks passed locally. Windows CI runs the same test; it retains its logs and the separate test projects for inspection.

Exercise setup on clean Windows x64 with a standard user account, including a machine without .NET or the Visual C++ runtimes. Also test with only the x64 Visual C++ runtime installed: setup must install the x86 runtime and the installed `EngineSDK/premake5.exe --version` must succeed. Check prerequisite cancellation and restart handling, a path containing spaces and non-ASCII characters, upgrading an existing install, and uninstalling while retaining projects. Create a project, enable one selected package, run it, and export a Windows Release build. Verify a signed installer and its installed uninstaller. CI packaging alone does not establish those clean-machine results.
